addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- refine-writing: Refine a section of academic systems writing (paper section, abstract, intro, motivation, rebuttal) to the measured register of a top ML-systems venue, then iterate with diverse critic agents until it converges (a full round with no new suggestions). - User asks to rewrite, polish, refine, or "make academic" a paper section, abstract, intro, motivation, related work, or rebuttal; complains the writing is awkward / wordy / colloquial / "weird" / not natural; asks to match the tone of reference papers; 'rewrite this section', 'polish the writing', 'make this read like a top conference paper', 'fix the tone', 'too colloquial', 'check against related work'.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). 1	# motivation_v2 — Background & Motivation (§2): titles + rhetoric
2	# (2026-07-26 DirectKV-SHAPED RESTRUCTURE)
3	
4	(Supersedes the 2026-07-25 six-flat-subsection structure. The new
5	structure copies DirectKV's §2 LOGIC exactly, with our content:
6	definitions → the incumbent approach and its voided premise → the
7	promising direction, endorsed → the naive version of that direction
8	failing, measured → per-technique opportunity units, each microbench +
9	trade-off + bold Takeaway. §3's sectioning is FIXED (mentor-approved);
10	only §3 content/pointers adapt. Kevin's seven content points map as:
11	(1)+(2)→§2.2, (3)→§2.4.2, (4)→§2.3+§2.4.1, (5)→§2.4.3,
12	(6)→§2.4.4, (7)→§2.4.5. 2026-07-26b: the 2.2.1/2.2.2 taxonomy is
13	DROPPED — the streaming line is inference serving, not a peer training
14	system, so coordinating them under one "existing systems" split was
15	forced. §2.2 = the training systems alone; §2.3 absorbs the
16	endorsement and then runs the carry-over test.)
17	
18	DELEGATION RULE (unchanged): §2 answers every WHY with micro-scale
19	evidence; §3 answers WHAT and HOW with at most one-clause whys + §2
20	pointers. A reviewer who stops after §2 knows every problem and why
21	our approach solves it.
22	
23	THE DIRECTKV TEMPLATE (what each piece is FOR):
24	- §2.1 = definitions only, zero claims (their attention math).
25	- §2.2 = the existing training systems (model-state offloading) with
26	  their mechanism stated fairly, then the premise voided — no taxonomy
27	  with the streaming line (different domain).
28	- §2.3 = ENDORSE then the CAPABILITY GAP + ACCOUNTING: first the
29	  streaming direction from inference serving (asymmetric GEMM, regime
30	  argument), then ONE paragraph: concede the trivial re-aim runs, then the
31	  three structural commitments it cannot touch (pipeline ownership /
32	  parallelism source / output retirement), each broken by LoRA, with
33	  the closer that fixing any one breaks the other two — then the
34	  accounting consequence: the only executable path
35	  under offloading today is staging back, whose copy re-spends the
36	  offloaded bytes at exactly the peak. NOTE vs DirectKV: their §2.3
37	  measures naive zero-copy because the naive option RUNS; our
38	  inference kernels mostly CANNOT run the training dataflows, so the
39	  honest evidence is absence + arithmetic, and the microbench lives
40	  entirely in §2.4.1 (single owner, no synthetic 'Inference' bar).
41	- §2.4 = opportunity units, each: revisit the lever → microbench with
42	  deltas in prose → trade-off naming both sides AND the absorbing
43	  resource → bold **Takeaway:** one-liner (their tiling / pipelining /
44	  fusion). Ours has five opportunities, one per §3 module.
45	
46	---
47	
48	## §2.1 Background: LoRA Fine-Tuning on Superchips   [defs only]
49	
50	R: Pure definitions, zero claims — the vocabulary every later section
51	spends. (a) LoRA: $Wx$ gains $BAx$, $A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d}$,
52	$B\in\mathbb{R}^{d'\times r}$, $r{\ll}d$ (64 here); trainable state a
53	fraction of a percent; every pass still runs the full frozen model.
54	(b) Long-context SFT: tens of thousands to beyond 1M tokens; per-layer
55	gradient checkpointing standard (forward saves each layer's input;
56	backward recomputes the layer's forward before differentiating it; at
57	most one layer's activations live). Define the placement granularity WITHOUT minting a noun: placement
58	acts on each TYPE of activation a layer produces (attention
59	projections, normalization inputs, MLP intermediates), uniformly
60	across layers — say 'activation type', never 'class'. (c) The machine: GB200
61	couples two Blackwell GPUs ([X] GB HBM each) to one Grace CPU ([Y]
62	GB); each GPU has its OWN coherent NVLink-C2C link (~450 GB/s [450 spec REMOVED from prose per author — link stated qualitatively; measured ~212 GB/s H2D stays], well
63	below [Z] TB/s HBM); links independent; GPU kernels read CPU memory
64	directly, no staging copy; each GPU thereby reaches [Y] GB of CPU memory, [R]x its own HBM. [[Y] GB / [R]x capacity numbers REMOVED from prose per author — prose says "well beyond a single GPU's HBM"]
65	
66	## §2.2 Model-State Offloading and the Activation Bottleneck   [existing training systems; points 1+2]
67	
68	R: OPEN with the two-sentence problem statement (the target models
69	overflow GPU memory: at the large end weights alone exceed it, [~470]
70	GB bf16 vs [X] GB; across the rest, weights plus long-context
71	activations together do from [N] tokens on — prose numbers, NO figure (M1 is CUT: growth-with-length is trivial and M0b already shows activations dominating); part of the
72	training state must live in CPU memory). THEN the existing systems'
73	mechanism, stated fairly and precisely: they move MODEL STATE — ZeRO-Offload homes optimizer states and gradients in CPU memory and runs the update there, ZeRO-Infinity moves the parameters as well, SuperOffload tunes the design for superchips (speculative optimizer execution overlapped with the backward, Grace-tuned Adam, gradient bucketization) — and the runtime machinery centers on the optimizer step, correct for full-parameter training where fp32 master weights and moments exist for every parameter. THEN the premise voided TWICE, measured: (i) under LoRA the adapters are the only trainable state, the optimizer is a few percent of step time, overlap changes nothing (Figure M0a); FIGURES OF THIS UNIT: M0a + M0b only (2 panels); (ii) everything these systems move is PARAMETER-PROPORTIONAL — static once homed; the recurring traffic is the rank-width adapter exchange plus (where params are CPU-homed) a read-only weight fetch FIXED IN BYTES while compute grows with tokens, so at long context the fetch fills [X]% of the step's link-seconds and the link+cores idle for the rest (ONE CLAUSE, arithmetic consequence — NO figure; M0c/M0d are RETIRED, the idleness is argued, and §2.4.2/§2.4.3 carry measured evidence via M3 and M4b). THEN what binds: the TOKEN-PROPORTIONAL term — activations, linear in tokens, one live layer's classes at [tens of] GB at 1M tokens plus checkpoint inputs beneath (M0b). CLOSE: the binding term is activation peak, which model-state offloading addresses only at the CHECKPOINT BOUNDARY (whole saved tensors offloaded or recomputed); the within-layer classes dominating the peak stay on the GPU. (Never say 'leaves activations on the GPU' flat — §3.4 cites the same systems for checkpoint-boundary offload.)
74	
75	## §2.3 Streaming Kernels Fall Short for Training   [ONE paragraph; adapter dataflows only]
76	
77	SETTING: a GEMM is general, so the inference streaming kernel can be
78	trivially re-aimed at LoRA's dataflows (concede this up front; also
79	the operand rule in one clause with the math: $Y{=}XW^\top$ streams
80	$W$; $S{=}XA^\top$ and $dA{=}dS^\top X$ stream $X$ — the ~1 MB
81	adapters always stay resident, the large once-read operand streams) —
82	and deleting the reuse loop looks like it should be enough.
83	
84	TAKEAWAY (long, the paragraph's spine): it is not enough, because
85	reuse is not a loop but the kernel's three structural commitments,
86	and LoRA breaks each one:
87	(1) WHO OWNS THE PIPELINE — the kernel gives its multi-buffered
88	shared-memory pipeline to the STREAMED operand because that operand
89	is reused; in LoRA the reused operand is the RESIDENT adapter, so the
90	memory roles must invert (the stream takes a fetch-once slot at full
91	link width, the adapter takes the pipeline) — a rewiring of the
92	kernel's memory hierarchy, not a deletion.
93	(2) WHERE PARALLELISM COMES FROM — the grid is keyed to output width;
94	a rank-64 output is 64 columns, one thread block's worth, so the GPU
95	serializes; parallelism must be re-extracted from the TOKEN ROWS (the
96	stream itself is partitioned), changing the launch geometry and how
97	partials combine.
98	(3) WHEN OUTPUTS MAY RETIRE — the kernel retires output tiles as the
99	reduction advances, valid because the reduction axis is resident; the
100	adapter gradient reduces OVER THE STREAMED AXIS, so nothing may
101	retire until the whole stream has passed, forcing an

# motivation_v2 — Background & Motivation (§2): titles + rhetoric
# (2026-07-26 DirectKV-SHAPED RESTRUCTURE)

(Supersedes the 2026-07-25 six-flat-subsection structure. The new
structure copies DirectKV's §2 LOGIC exactly, with our content:
definitions → the incumbent approach and its voided premise → the
promising direction, endorsed → the naive version of that direction
failing, measured → per-technique opportunity units, each microbench +
trade-off + bold Takeaway. §3's sectioning is FIXED (mentor-approved);
only §3 content/pointers adapt. Kevin's seven content points map as:
(1)+(2)→§2.2, (3)→§2.4.2, (4)→§2.3+§2.4.1, (5)→§2.4.3,
(6)→§2.4.4, (7)→§2.4.5. 2026-07-26b: the 2.2.1/2.2.2 taxonomy is
DROPPED — the streaming line is inference serving, not a peer training
system, so coordinating them under one "existing systems" split was
forced. §2.2 = the training systems alone; §2.3 absorbs the
endorsement and then runs the carry-over test.)

DELEGATION RULE (unchanged): §2 answers every WHY with micro-scale
evidence; §3 answers WHAT and HOW with at most one-clause whys + §2
pointers. A reviewer who stops after §2 knows every problem and why
our approach solves it.

THE DIRECTKV TEMPLATE (what each piece is FOR):
- §2.1 = definitions only, zero claims (their attention math).
- §2.2 = the existing training systems (model-state offloading) with
  their mechanism stated fairly, then the premise voided — no taxonomy
  with the streaming line (different domain).
- §2.3 = ENDORSE then the CAPABILITY GAP + ACCOUNTING: first the
  streaming direction from inference serving (asymmetric GEMM, regime
  argument), then ONE paragraph: concede the trivial re-aim runs, then the
  three structural commitments it cannot touch (pipeline ownership /
  parallelism source / output retirement), each broken by LoRA, with
  the closer that fixing any one breaks the other two — then the
  accounting consequence: the only executable path
  under offloading today is staging back, whose copy re-spends the
  offloaded bytes at exactly the peak. NOTE vs DirectKV: their §2.3
  measures naive zero-copy because the naive option RUNS; our
  inference kernels mostly CANNOT run the training dataflows, so the
  honest evidence is absence + arithmetic, and the microbench lives
  entirely in §2.4.1 (single owner, no synthetic 'Inference' bar).
- §2.4 = opportunity units, each: revisit the lever → microbench with
  deltas in prose → trade-off naming both sides AND the absorbing
  resource → bold **Takeaway:** one-liner (their tiling / pipelining /
  fusion). Ours has five opportunities, one per §3 module.

---

## §2.1 Background: LoRA Fine-Tuning on Superchips   [defs only]

R: Pure definitions, zero claims — the vocabulary every later section
spends. (a) LoRA: $Wx$ gains $BAx$, $A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d}$,
$B\in\mathbb{R}^{d'\times r}$, $r{\ll}d$ (64 here); trainable state a
fraction of a percent; every pass still runs the full frozen model.
(b) Long-context SFT: tens of thousands to beyond 1M tokens; per-layer
gradient checkpointing standard (forward saves each layer's input;
backward recomputes the layer's forward before differentiating it; at
most one layer's activations live). Define the placement granularity WITHOUT minting a noun: placement
acts on each TYPE of activation a layer produces (attention
projections, normalization inputs, MLP intermediates), uniformly
across layers — say 'activation type', never 'class'. (c) The machine: GB200
couples two Blackwell GPUs ([X] GB HBM each) to one Grace CPU ([Y]
GB); each GPU has its OWN coherent NVLink-C2C link (~450 GB/s [450 spec REMOVED from prose per author — link stated qualitatively; measured ~212 GB/s H2D stays], well
below [Z] TB/s HBM); links independent; GPU kernels read CPU memory
directly, no staging copy; each GPU thereby reaches [Y] GB of CPU memory, [R]x its own HBM. [[Y] GB / [R]x capacity numbers REMOVED from prose per author — prose says "well beyond a single GPU's HBM"]

## §2.2 Model-State Offloading and the Activation Bottleneck   [existing training systems; points 1+2]

R: OPEN with the two-sentence problem statement (the target models
overflow GPU memory: at the large end weights alone exceed it, [~470]
GB bf16 vs [X] GB; across the rest, weights plus long-context
activations together do from [N] tokens on — prose numbers, NO figure (M1 is CUT: growth-with-length is trivial and M0b already shows activations dominating); part of the
training state must live in CPU memory). THEN the existing systems'
mechanism, stated fairly and precisely: they move MODEL STATE — ZeRO-Offload homes optimizer states and gradients in CPU memory and runs the update there, ZeRO-Infinity moves the parameters as well, SuperOffload tunes the design for superchips (speculative optimizer execution overlapped with the backward, Grace-tuned Adam, gradient bucketization) — and the runtime machinery centers on the optimizer step, correct for full-parameter training where fp32 master weights and moments exist for every parameter. THEN the premise voided TWICE, measured: (i) under LoRA the adapters are the only trainable state, the optimizer is a few percent of step time, overlap changes nothing (Figure M0a); FIGURES OF THIS UNIT: M0a + M0b only (2 panels); (ii) everything these systems move is PARAMETER-PROPORTIONAL — static once homed; the recurring traffic is the rank-width adapter exchange plus (where params are CPU-homed) a read-only weight fetch FIXED IN BYTES while compute grows with tokens, so at long context the fetch fills [X]% of the step's link-seconds and the link+cores idle for the rest (ONE CLAUSE, arithmetic consequence — NO figure; M0c/M0d are RETIRED, the idleness is argued, and §2.4.2/§2.4.3 carry measured evidence via M3 and M4b). THEN what binds: the TOKEN-PROPORTIONAL term — activations, linear in tokens, one live layer's classes at [tens of] GB at 1M tokens plus checkpoint inputs beneath (M0b). CLOSE: the binding term is activation peak, which model-state offloading addresses only at the CHECKPOINT BOUNDARY (whole saved tensors offloaded or recomputed); the within-layer classes dominating the peak stay on the GPU. (Never say 'leaves activations on the GPU' flat — §3.4 cites the same systems for checkpoint-boundary offload.)

## §2.3 Streaming Kernels Fall Short for Training   [ONE paragraph; adapter dataflows only]

SETTING: a GEMM is general, so the inference streaming kernel can be
trivially re-aimed at LoRA's dataflows (concede this up front; also
the operand rule in one clause with the math: $Y{=}XW^\top$ streams
$W$; $S{=}XA^\top$ and $dA{=}dS^\top X$ stream $X$ — the ~1 MB
adapters always stay resident, the large once-read operand streams) —
and deleting the reuse loop looks like it should be enough.

TAKEAWAY (long, the paragraph's spine): it is not enough, because
reuse is not a loop but the kernel's three structural commitments,
and LoRA breaks each one:
(1) WHO OWNS THE PIPELINE — the kernel gives its multi-buffered
shared-memory pipeline to the STREAMED operand because that operand
is reused; in LoRA the reused operand is the RESIDENT adapter, so the
memory roles must invert (the stream takes a fetch-once slot at full
link width, the adapter takes the pipeline) — a rewiring of the
kernel's memory hierarchy, not a deletion.
(2) WHERE PARALLELISM COMES FROM — the grid is keyed to output width;
a rank-64 output is 64 columns, one thread block's worth, so the GPU
serializes; parallelism must be re-extracted from the TOKEN ROWS (the
stream itself is partitioned), changing the launch geometry and how
partials combine.
(3) WHEN OUTPUTS MAY RETIRE — the kernel retires output tiles as the
reduction advances, valid because the reduction axis is resident; the
adapter gradient reduces OVER THE STREAMED AXIS, so nothing may
retire until the whole stream has passed, forcing an
output-stationary design (the rank-sized output pinned in registers

23	## 2.1 Background: LoRA Fine-Tuning on Superchips
24	
25	LoRA fine-tuning replaces each trained weight update with a pair of
26	low-rank factors: a projection $Wx$ gains a correction $BAx$ with
27	$A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d}$, $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d' \times r}$, and
28	rank $r \ll d$ (64 throughout this paper), so the trainable state is a
29	fraction of a percent of the parameters while every forward and
30	backward pass still runs the full frozen model~\cite{lora}.
31	Long-context supervised fine-tuning drives sequence lengths from tens
32	of thousands of tokens to beyond a million, and at these lengths
33	per-layer gradient checkpointing is standard: the forward saves only
34	each layer's input, and the backward recomputes a layer's forward
35	immediately before differentiating it, so at most one layer's
36	activations are live at a time. Placement will act on each type of
37	activation a layer produces (its attention projections, its
38	normalization inputs, its MLP intermediates), uniformly across layers.
39	In MoE models a router assigns each token to a few expert MLPs per
40	layer; a grouped GEMM runs all of a layer's experts in one launch and
41	returns outputs grouped by expert rather than by token.
42	
43	A Grace--Blackwell superchip couples two Blackwell GPUs, each with
44	189~GB of HBM, to one Grace CPU with 72 cores and a memory pool well
45	beyond a single GPU's HBM. Each GPU reaches the CPU's memory over its
46	own coherent NVLink-C2C link: host-to-device streams on our machine
47	achieve about 212~GB/s from the GPU's local memory socket (roughly
48	half from the far socket), well below the [8]~TB/s of the GPU's HBM.
49	The two links are independent, though both draw on the CPU memory's
50	[500]~GB/s, which caps what the two streams and the Grace cores' own
51	kernels can pull from it together. Coherence means a GPU kernel reads
52	CPU memory directly, with no staging copy and no driver round trip;
53	each GPU thereby addresses the whole CPU pool, well beyond its own
54	HBM.
55	
56	## 2.2 Model-State Offloading and the Activation Bottleneck
57	
58	The models we target overflow GPU memory. At the large end the weights
59	alone exceed it, a 235B-parameter model holding about 470~GB in bf16
60	against 189~GB of HBM per GPU; across the rest, the weights and the
61	long-context activations together do from [N] tokens on. Part of the
62	training state must therefore live in CPU memory.
63	
64	Existing offloading systems move model states.
65	ZeRO-Offload~\cite{zero-offload} homes the optimizer states and
66	gradients in CPU memory and runs the update there;
67	ZeRO-Infinity~\cite{zero-infinity} moves the parameters as well;
68	SuperOffload~\cite{superoffload} tunes the design for superchips with
69	speculative optimizer execution overlapped with the backward pass, a
70	Grace-tuned Adam, and gradient bucketization over the interconnect.
71	The runtime machinery centers on the optimizer step, and for
72	full-parameter training this is the right center: fp32 master weights
73	and Adam moments exist for every parameter, and their update dominates
74	an offloaded step.
75	
76	LoRA voids this premise twice. First, the adapters are the only
77	trainable state, so the optimizer accounts for a few percent of step
78	time on dense (Qwen3-32B) and MoE (Qwen3-30B-A3B) models alike, and
79	overlapping it with the backward leaves end-to-end step time
80	essentially unchanged (Figure M0a). Second, everything these systems
81	move is parameter-proportional and static once homed: the recurring
82	traffic that remains under LoRA is the rank-width adapter exchange
83	plus, where the parameters live in CPU memory, a read-only weight
84	fetch whose bytes are fixed while the step's compute grows with
85	tokens, so as context grows the fetch occupies a shrinking fraction of
86	the step and the interconnect and the Grace cores idle through the
87	rest. What grows is the token-proportional term. Activations scale
88	linearly in tokens: one bf16 activation of hidden width 5120 spans
89	10.7~GB at a million tokens, a layer produces several such types plus
90	MLP intermediates five times wider, and every layer's saved checkpoint
91	input accumulates beneath the one live layer (Figure M0b). For
92	long-context LoRA fine-tuning the binding term is therefore the
93	activation peak, and model-state offloading reaches it only at the
94	checkpoint boundary, where whole saved tensors are offloaded or
95	recomputed~\cite{zero-infinity, superoffload}; the within-layer
96	activation types beneath that boundary, which dominate the peak, stay
97	on the GPU.
98	
99	## 2.3 Streaming Kernels Fall Short for Training
100	
101	A different use of the superchip streams operands instead of moving
102	state. An asymmetric GEMM keeps one operand in CPU memory and reads it
103	tile-by-tile over the interconnect while the multiplication proceeds:
104	the streamed operand occupies no GPU memory and needs no staging
105	buffer. The AsymGEMM inference line realizes this for
106	serving~\cite{asymgemm, directkv, c2cserve}. The regime suits the
107	link: the kernel reads the streamed operand in shared-memory-sized
108	tiles and pipelines them beneath the multiplication, so many tiles are
109	in flight at once, per-access latency is hidden, and what the stream
110	asks of the interconnect is sustained bandwidth, which each GPU's
111	private link supplies. CPU memory as operand capacity with the compute
112	staying on the GPU is exactly the shape of the activation problem, if
113	the kernels carry over to training.
114	
115	They do not carry over, though the trivial re-aim runs: a GEMM is
116	general, and the operand rule is a single clause, the large once-read
117	operand streams while the small reused one stays resident, so the
118	frozen path $Y{=}XW^\top$ streams $W$, and the adapter contractions
119	$S{=}XA^\top$ and $dA{=}dS^\top X$ stream the activation $X$ while the
120	megabyte-scale adapters stay resident; deleting the weight-reuse loop
121	looks like all that is left. It is not enough, because reuse in these
122	kernels is not a loop but three structural commitments, and LoRA's
123	dataflows break each one. First, who owns the pipeline: the kernel
124	gives its multi-buffered shared-memory pipeline to the streamed
125	operand because the streamed operand is the reused one; in the adapter
126	contractions the reused operand is the resident factor, so the memory
127	roles must invert, the stream taking a fetch-once slot at full link
128	width and the adapter taking the pipeline, a rewiring of the kernel's
129	memory hierarchy rather than a deletion. Second, where parallelism
130	comes from: the launch grid is keyed to output width, and a rank-64
131	output is 64 columns, one thread block's worth of work, so the GPU
132	serializes; parallelism must be re-extracted from the token rows by
133	partitioning the stream itself, which changes the launch geometry and
134	how partial results combine. Third, when outputs may retire: the
135	kernel retires output tiles as its reduction advances, valid because
136	its reduction axis is resident; the adapter gradient reduces over the
137	streamed axis, so nothing may retire until the whole stream has
138	passed, forcing an output-stationary dataflow, the rank-sized output
139	pinned in registers for the stream's entire lifetime, which the
140	inference kernels do not contain. Fixing any one commitment breaks the
141	other two's assumptions: what results is a rebuilt kernel, not a
142	patched one. The accounting consequence follows: with no streaming
143	kernel for these dataflows, the only fast path under offloading today
144	is staging the activation back, and the staged copy is the offloaded
145	tensor rematerializing in GPU memory at exactly the backward's peak,
146	so the peak saving offloading bought is spent at the moment it binds.
147	Streaming's memory promise is real, and for training it is so far
148	uncollectable; collecting it takes rebuilt kernels (§2.4.1).
149	
150	## 2.4 Opportunities: Rebuilding Long-Context Activation Offloading for Superchips
151	
152	The superchip supplies exactly the resources model-state offloading
153	leaves idle (§2.2): both directions of each C2C link and the Grace
154	cores. And kernels control their own dataflows: nothing in §2.3's
155	failure is fundamental to the hardware. \emph{The ideal execution
156	would use CPU memory purely for capacity, run each operator at full
157	rate on the processor where it wins, and pay no step time for the
158	placement.} Five opportunities close the distance to that ideal.
159	
160	### 2.4.1 Kernels Rebuilt for Training Dataflows
161	
162	The first opportunity is kernel structure, not tuning. Rebuilt for
163	training, the streaming kernels (i) invert the operand roles of §2.3,
164	the once-read activation taking the fetch-once stream slot and the
165	small resident factor taking the shared-memory pipeline; (ii)
166	accumulate token-axis reductions output-stationary, the rank-sized
167	result living in registers until the stream ends; (iii) fold the
168	routing scatter into the streamed grouped GEMM's epilogue, forward and
169	backward: a grouped GEMM returns outputs in expert order, and where
170	that output is streamed or offloaded, the separate re-ordering pass
171	first materializes an expert-ordered copy of it, so the epilogue
172	instead writes each result, scaled by its routing weight, to its
173	token-order address, and both the copy and the pass disappear (the
174	input-side gather stays a staged pass; its fused variant measured
175	about 75$\times$ slower and was rejected); and (iv) instantiate
176	transposed variants for the backward's rereads of the frozen weights.
177	
178	Figure M2a measures what the rebuild collects, on one adapter GEMM as
179	a case study: the attention LoRA-A projection $S{=}XA^\top$ at rank 64
180	and hidden width 5120, the activation $X$ CPU-resident, at 32K and
181	256K token rows. Three executions: Resident, both operands pre-placed
182	in HBM, the cuBLAS ceiling; Staged, $X$ copied to HBM and cuBLAS run
183	on the copy; Streamed, the rebuilt kernel reading $X$ in place. At 32K
184	rows they take 0.053, 1.651, and 1.598~ms; at 256K rows, 0.402,
185	13.080, and 12.701~ms. Both off-GPU executions are link-bound,
186	sustaining the link's achieved rate (about 210~GB/s), because at rank
187	64 the arithmetic is negligible next to moving $X$; Staged then moves
188	the bytes twice, over the link and again out of HBM, which is why
189	Streamed runs about 3\% faster. The decisive difference is what the
190	execution holds: Staged holds the returned activation, 0.34~GB at 32K
191	rows and 2.69~GB at 256K, re-spent at exactly the backward's peak,
192	where Streamed holds the 0.7~MB adapter. Under offloading, the one
193	executable path paid the link and re-bought the memory; the rebuilt
194	kernel pays the same link time and keeps the memory saving the offload
195	was for. The 30$\times$ gap to Resident is
196	the residency premium, the throughput price of any off-GPU placement;
197	it argues for keeping tensors resident whenever they fit (§2.4.4), not
198	for staging.
199	
200	The routed-expert legs measure the scatter fusion (Figure M2b):
201	Qwen3-30B-A3B expert GEMMs under the streamed recipe at 128K tokens
202	(top-8 of 128 experts, 1.05M routed rows), the fused epilogue against
203	an unfused grouped GEMM plus separate scatter pass. Fusion eliminates
204	the expert-ordered fp32 output copy on both legs, 8.59~GB per leg at
205	this length, and the forward leg also runs 13\% faster (41.9 to
206	36.4~ms); the backward leg pays 12\% (44.0 to 49.1~ms), because its
207	streamed weight is read transposed and the fused mainloop pays more
208	for that than the folded scatter saves. The fusion's claim is
209	therefore the eliminated copy on both legs, with a faster forward, and
210	the backward's 12\% is the stated price of its 8.59~GB.
211	
212	The rebuilt kernels' trade-off is that every streamed tile crosses the
213	interconnect; the GPU-bound C2C direction, idle under model-state
214	offloading (§2.2), absorbs that traffic (§2.4.2). Streaming also fixes
215	a direction, moving the data to the compute; §2.4.3 opens the inverse
216	route. **Takeaway:** rebuilt for once-read operands and backward
217	dataflows, streaming runs at staged execution's speed with streamed
218	execution's memory: the promise §2.3 called uncollectable, collected.
219	
220	### 2.4.2 Idle Interconnect as Activation Capacity
221	
222	The second opportunity spends the idle link on activations. Below the
223	checkpoint boundary, each activation type is independently offloaded,
224	leaving the GPU in the forward and returning beneath the backward's
225	compute, restaged or consumed in place by the kernels of §2.4.1 and
226	§2.4.3, or recomputed, regenerated by the layer's forward inside the
227	backward window. The per-type mix inside one layer is the composition
228	prior systems lack: they choose once per saved tensor at the
229	checkpoint boundary (§2.2). Attention shows why the mix pays: its two
230	small normalization inputs regenerate the wide normalized projections,
231	so offloading the parents moves a fraction of the bytes of the
232	children they rebuild.
233	
234	Figure M3 measures one full Qwen3-32B layer, forward and backward, at
235	128K tokens under three per-type policies, recompute-all (pure
236	checkpointing), offload-all (every offloadable type leaves and
237	restages), and the composed mix the system ships, with peak HBM, link
238	bytes, and backward-window time split by module (attention, MLP). In
239	the MLP the composition does what the levers promise: offload-all cuts
240	the module's backward peak from recompute-all's 44.0~GiB to 26.6,
241	composed holds 31.5 (the 5-GiB gap is a prefetch trade: gate and up
242	staged early, their gradients kept on the GPU), and composed moves
243	0.67$\times$ offload-all's link bytes (51.3 versus 76.3~GiB) while
244	running 11\% faster than it over the backward window (1230 versus
245	1360~ms). In attention the win
246	moves to the
247	wires. Composed moves 0.48$\times$ offload-all's link bytes (14.6
248	versus 30.5~GiB), the parent-to-child ratio visible directly, and
249	holds 7.8~GiB of pinned host memory to offload-all's 16.9; but no
250	policy lowers this module's GPU peak at this length, because in every
251	policy the peak instant sits inside the query-norm backward, where the
252	fp32 upcasts and their gradient chain hold about six 4-GiB tensors at
253	once: offload-all restages the two fp32 saves at exactly that instant,
254	re-spending the bytes it freed, and composed rebuilds the same chain
255	inside its recompute while its side-stream staging runs beside it
256	(36.5 versus 30.5~GiB). At this length the composition's attention win
257	is link and host bytes; its peak win lives in the MLP. On time, the
258	figure reports the backward window, where the composition acts
259	(forward time is policy-independent): composed beats offload-all in
260	both modules (4\% faster in attention, 11\% in the MLP).
261	Recompute-all is the fastest policy in this isolated single-layer run,
262	12\% ahead of composed in attention and 77\% in the MLP: with the
263	whole GPU and an idle link, its extra FLOPs cost nothing while the
264	offload policies wait on restages. What it cannot shed is residency, the
265	44.0~GiB MLP backward above, which is the term that does not scale
266	(§2.2).
267	
268	The trade-off is that freed GPU memory returns as link traffic,
269	absorbed while each transfer fits inside its layer's dependency
270	window, the span the layer's compute opens between an operand's
271	production and its consumption. **Takeaway:** spent on activations,
272	the idle interconnect becomes GPU-memory headroom at no step-time cost
273	over offloading, and the per-type composition cuts the bytes that
274	conversion pays to half to two-thirds.
275	
276	### 2.4.3 Idle Grace Cores as a Second Compute Engine
277	
278	Streaming moves the operand to the compute; the third opportunity is
279	the inverse, moving the compute to the operand. The Grace cores idle
280	outside the few-percent optimizer step (§2.2), 72 cores against the
281	CPU memory's [500]~GB/s, and memory-bound gradient work fits them when
282	its operands already live in CPU memory. Two placements ship, both SVE
283	kernels built for Grace. The CPU adapter-gradient kernel computes $dA$
284	where the offloaded activation lies, contracting it in place and
285	depositing the fp32 result directly into the optimizer's pinned
286	buffer, so all that crosses the link is the rank-width projection
287	gradient, 34~MB at 256K rows against the 2.7~GB activation a GPU-side
288	gradient would restage. The gradient-ingestion kernel fuses the
289	bf16-to-fp32 widen into the gradient-norm reduction the optimizer
290	already performs: gradients cross the link in bf16, half the fp32
291	bytes, and one SVE pass replaces the stock two, 7.2$\times$ faster on
292	a 1-GiB gradient batch (12.1 versus 86.7~ms). Table~\ref{tab:cpu-scope}
293	scopes the CPU's role against SuperOffload's:
294	GraceAdam~\cite{superoffload} runs the fp32 update loop on these cores
295	and leaves the ingestion pass untouched, and Superchip-Aware
296	Casting~\cite{superoffload} chose to cast on the GPU and transmit
297	fp32, a conclusion that inverts once the CPU cast is fused into a
298	reduction the optimizer already requires. (A fused SwiGLU elementwise
299	kernel for the same placement is built and bit-accurate but ships
300	disabled: the device-to-host transfer it removes is fully overlapped
301	on this machine, so removing it buys no step time, a negative result
302	that sharpens the gating below.)
303	
304	Figure M4b measures the deposit at its shipped site, MoE attention
305	$dA$, across 64K, 256K, and 1M projection rows. Against stock PyTorch
306	CPU matmuls at the same 96-thread budget, the kernel runs 1.8$\times$,
307	2.4$\times$, and 31$\times$ faster (12.3 versus 21.6~ms, 33.3 versus
308	79.8, and 137 versus 4336: the stock bf16 path collapses at scale).
309	Placement, however, is not settled by serial time: run in isolation,
310	the GPU route, restage plus GPU gradient kernel plus gradient
311	transfer, is faster at every size; the shipped question is what each
312	route adds to the critical path of a backward that is already using
313	the SMs and the link. Run concurrently with such a context (63.6~ms of
314	streamed GEMMs), the CPU route adds 1.36~ms at 64K rows to the GPU
315	route's 1.29, parity; 1.32~ms at 256K to the GPU's 5.19, four times
316	less; and 87.8~ms at 1M to the GPU's 20.7, because 137~ms of serial
317	CPU work no longer fits a 64~ms window. The crossover falls between
318	256K and 1M rows, and the shipped policy arms the CPU placement only
319	through the 256K point (262{,}144 rows), the last where it wins. The
320	boundary is a time window, not a bandwidth limit: the idle cores
321	absorb CPU seconds only while the backward's dependency window is
322	open, extending the step once it closes, and row count predicts the
323	closure. **Takeaway:** with the optimizer light, the Grace cores
324	absorb gradient work, but only inside the backward's dependency
325	windows; a gradient computable on either processor, with a measured
326	crossover between them, is exactly why kernel dispatch exists (§3.4).
327	
328	### 2.4.4 One Placement Does Not Fit All Jobs
329	
330	The fourth opportunity is the choice among the first three. Every
331	placement off the GPU frees memory and costs throughput: a streamed
332	weight holds no GPU memory where a staged one holds a layer's buffer,
333	an offloaded activation type frees its bytes but pays a restage, a
334	recomputed type pays FLOPs instead, and beneath them all sits §2.4.1's
335	30$\times$ residency premium. The placements also share a wire: a
336	configuration's weight streams, activation streams, and restages all
337	ride the same GPU-bound link, so their costs add, and the
338	configuration measurements of Figure M6 price them together. Overlap
339	narrows these costs but does not erase them, so configurations, each
340	an assignment of a placement to every weight and activation type,
341	order from most resident, the fastest, to fully streamed, the leanest.
342	Shorter jobs fit near-resident configurations and run fastest there;
343	only the longest need the streamed end: at 32K the most resident of
344	the three measured configurations is the fastest and holds the most
345	GPU memory (2063 versus 1524 versus 698~tok/s; 14.1 versus 11.8
346	versus 8.4~GiB; Qwen3-32B, batch 1), and at 512K the most resident
347	aborts out of memory in an attempted run, so the best feasible
348	configuration shifts to the partial one, 327 versus the streamed
349	one's 264~tok/s, a near-wall fit at 172 of the GPU's 184~GiB
350	(Figure M6). Near the capacity wall a wrong pick ends in an
351	out-of-memory abort, not a slowdown, and beyond a short anchor zone
352	where kernel behavior still shifts with length, peak GPU memory is
353	linear in token count for a fixed model and configuration, so records
354	of past runs predict whether a candidate fits. Within a feasible
355	configuration, throughput rises with batch size only to a knee, [the
356	batch where the step's kernels reach full device occupancy, reached at
357	small batch for long sequences], and is flat past it, so the largest
358	fitting batch is not worth taking past the knee (§3.3). The leanest
359	configurations also trade GPU memory for CPU memory, bounded in turn
360	by its own capacity, a bound the dense families reach first in
361	recorded runs (§3.4). **Takeaway:** the fastest feasible configuration
362	shifts with model and sequence length, and it is predictable from
363	records: selection must precede launch, and can.
364	
365	### 2.4.5 Two GPUs, One Memory: Balancing MoE Without Moving Data
366	
367	The last opportunity uses the second GPU. MoE routing concentrates
368	tokens on different experts at every step, so under a static expert
369	partition the GPU holding the cold experts finishes early and idles,
370	its private link unused (Figure M5a). Conventional rebalancing moves
371	data, either the tokens, exchanged all-to-all before every expert
372	layer through collectives that stall both GPUs (expert
373	parallelism~\cite{expert-parallelism}), or the expert weights,
374	repartitioned. On a superchip neither has to move: the expert weights
375	already sit in memory both GPUs address over independent links, and
376	under the activation-offloading configurations the long jobs run, the
377	routed tokens sit there too, so what moves is the work list, one
378	shared list of expert workloads per grouped launch, collective-free.
379	We measure four executions of the expert GEMM across routing skew $z$
380	(larger $z$ concentrates more tokens on fewer experts): the static
381	expert partition; a data-parallel split, each GPU running its own
382	tokens through every expert; and the shared list cut two ways, a
383	computed cut, both GPUs deriving the same balanced split from routing
384	counts they already hold, and a counter-raced cut, both claiming work
385	from the list's opposite ends until they meet. At $z{=}1.5$ on
386	Qwen3.5-122B the computed cut runs the expert GEMM in 31.2~ms against
387	39.0 raced, 42.8 data-parallel, and 44.6 expert-partitioned; the
388	static partition pays the skew itself, the data-parallel split runs
389	every expert at half its rows and streams every expert bank over both
390	links, and the raced cut pays coherence traffic on its shared counters
391	where the computed cut's counters are private. The saving carries
392	through to the MoE block, the two GPUs finish near-balanced across the
393	skew sweep, and both GPUs stream from the same CPU memory throughout,
394	so the shared [500]~GB/s ceiling of §2.1 is priced into the numbers
395	(Figure M5b). The gain needs skew to bind: where per-expert work
396	already saturates both GPUs under the data-parallel split, sharing
397	adds nothing, which sets the per-expert row ceiling above which it is
398	left off, and on Llama-4-Scout, where the data-parallel split is as
399	fast at every skew we sweep, it adds nothing at all. **Takeaway:** on
400	a superchip, wherever the routed tokens reside in the shared memory,
401	MoE balance is a scheduling property, not a communication cost.
402

## 2.1 Background: LoRA Fine-Tuning on Superchips

LoRA fine-tuning replaces each trained weight update with a pair of
low-rank factors: a projection $Wx$ gains a correction $BAx$ with
$A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d}$, $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d' \times r}$, and
rank $r \ll d$ (64 throughout this paper), so the trainable state is a
fraction of a percent of the parameters while every forward and
backward pass still runs the full frozen model~\cite{lora}.
Long-context supervised fine-tuning drives sequence lengths from tens
of thousands of tokens to beyond a million, and at these lengths
per-layer gradient checkpointing is standard: the forward saves only
each layer's input, and the backward recomputes a layer's forward
immediately before differentiating it, so at most one layer's
activations are live at a time. Placement will act on each type of
activation a layer produces (its attention projections, its
normalization inputs, its MLP intermediates), uniformly across layers.
In MoE models a router assigns each token to a few expert MLPs per
layer; a grouped GEMM runs all of a layer's experts in one launch and
returns outputs grouped by expert rather than by token.

A Grace--Blackwell superchip couples two Blackwell GPUs, each with
189~GB of HBM, to one Grace CPU with 72 cores and a memory pool well
beyond a single GPU's HBM. Each GPU reaches the CPU's memory over its
own coherent NVLink-C2C link: host-to-device streams on our machine
achieve about 212~GB/s from the GPU's local memory socket (roughly
half from the far socket), well below the [8]~TB/s of the GPU's HBM.
The two links are independent, though both draw on the CPU memory's
[500]~GB/s, which caps what the two streams and the Grace cores' own
kernels can pull from it together. Coherence means a GPU kernel reads
CPU memory directly, with no staging copy and no driver round trip;
each GPU thereby addresses the whole CPU pool, well beyond its own
HBM.

## 2.2 Model-State Offloading and the Activation Bottleneck

The models we target overflow GPU memory. At the large end the weights
alone exceed it, a 235B-parameter model holding about 470~GB in bf16
against 189~GB of HBM per GPU; across the rest, the weights and the
long-context activations together do from [N] tokens on. Part of the
training state must therefore live in CPU memory.

Existing offloading systems move model states.
ZeRO-Offload~\cite{zero-offload} homes the optimizer states and
gradients in CPU memory and runs the update there;
ZeRO-Infinity~\cite{zero-infinity} moves the parameters as well;
SuperOffload~\cite{superoffload} tunes the design for superchips with
speculative optimizer execution overlapped with the backward pass, a
Grace-tuned Adam, and gradient bucketization over the interconnect.
The runtime machinery centers on the optimizer step, and for
full-parameter training this is the right center: fp32 master weights
and Adam moments exist for every parameter, and their update dominates
an offloaded step.

LoRA voids this premise twice. First, the adapters are the only
trainable state, so the optimizer accounts for a few percent of step
time on dense (Qwen3-32B) and MoE (Qwen3-30B-A3B) models alike, and
overlapping it with the backward leaves end-to-end step time
essentially unchanged (Figure M0a). Second, everything these systems
move is parameter-proportional and static once homed: the recurring
traffic that remains under LoRA is the rank-width adapter exchange
plus, where the parameters live in CPU memory, a read-only weight
fetch whose bytes are fixed while the step's compute grows with
tokens, so as context grows the fetch occupies a shrinking fraction of
the step and the interconnect and the Grace cores idle through the
rest. What grows is the token-proportional term. Activations scale
linearly in tokens: one bf16 activation of hidden width 5120 spans
10.7~GB at a million tokens, a layer produces several such types plus
MLP intermediates five times wider, and every layer's saved checkpoint
input accumulates beneath the one live layer (Figure M0b). For
long-context LoRA fine-tuning the binding term is therefore the
activation peak, and model-state offloading reaches it only at the
checkpoint boundary, where whole saved tensors are offloaded or
recomputed~\cite{zero-infinity, superoffload}; the within-layer
activation types beneath that boundary, which dominate the peak, stay
on the GPU.

## 2.3 Streaming Kernels Fall Short for Training

A different use of the superchip streams operands instead of moving
state. An asymmetric GEMM keeps one operand in CPU memory and reads it
tile-by-tile over the interconnect while the multiplication proceeds:
the streamed operand occupies no GPU memory and needs no staging
buffer. The AsymGEMM inference line realizes this for
serving~\cite{asymgemm, directkv, c2cserve}. The regime suits the
link: the kernel reads the streamed operand in shared-memory-sized
tiles and pipelines them beneath the multiplication, so many tiles are
in flight at once, per-access latency is hidden, and what the stream
asks of the interconnect is sustained bandwidth, which each GPU's
private link supplies. CPU memory as operand capacity with the compute
staying on the GPU is exactly the shape of the activation problem, if
the kernels carry over to training.

They do not carry over, though the trivial re-aim runs: a GEMM is
general, and the operand rule is a single clause, the large once-read
operand streams while the small reused one stays resident, so the
frozen path $Y{=}XW^\top$ streams $W$, and the adapter contractions
$S{=}XA^\top$ and $dA{=}dS^\top X$ stream the activation $X$ while the
megabyte-scale adapters stay resident; deleting the weight-reuse loop
looks like all that is left. It is not enough, because reuse in these
kernels is not a loop but three structural commitments, and LoRA's
dataflows break each one. First, who owns the pipeline: the kernel
gives its multi-buffered shared-memory pipeline to the streamed
operand because the streamed operand is the reused one; in the adapter
contractions the reused operand is the resident factor, so the memory
roles must invert, the stream taking a fetch-once slot at full link
width and the adapter taking the pipeline, a rewiring of the kernel's
memory hierarchy rather than a deletion. Second, where parallelism
comes from: the launch grid is keyed to output width, and a rank-64
output is 64 columns, one thread block's worth of work, so the GPU
serializes; parallelism must be re-extracted from the token rows by
partitioning the stream itself, which changes the launch geometry and
how partial results combine. Third, when outputs may retire: the
kernel retires output tiles as its reduction advances, valid because
its reduction axis is resident; the adapter gradient reduces over the
streamed axis, so nothing may retire until the whole stream has
passed, forcing an output-stationary dataflow, the rank-sized output
pinned in registers for the stream's entire lifetime, which the
inference kernels do not contain. Fixing any one commitment breaks the
other two's assumptions: what results is a rebuilt kernel, not a
patched one. The accounting consequence follows: with no streaming
kernel for these dataflows, the only fast path under offloading today
is staging the activation back, and the staged copy is the offloaded
tensor rematerializing in GPU memory at exactly the backward's peak,
so the peak saving offloading bought is spent at the moment it binds.
Streaming's memory promise is real, and for training it is so far
uncollectable; collecting it takes rebuilt kernels (§2.4.1).

## 2.4 Opportunities: Rebuilding Long-Context Activation Offloading for Superchips

The superchip supplies exactly the resources model-state offloading
leaves idle (§2.2): both directions of each C2C link and the Grace
cores. And kernels control their own dataflows: nothing in §2.3's
failure is fundamental to the hardware. \emph{The ideal execution
would use CPU memory purely for capacity, run each operator at full
rate on the processor where it wins, and pay no step time for the
placement.} Five opportunities close the distance to that ideal.

### 2.4.1 Kernels Rebuilt for Training Dataflows

The first opportunity is kernel structure, not tuning. Rebuilt for
training, the streaming kernels (i) invert the operand roles of §2.3,
the once-read activation taking the fetch-once stream slot and the
small resident factor taking the shared-memory pipeline; (ii)
accumulate token-axis reductions output-stationary, the rank-sized
result living in registers until the stream ends; (iii) fold the
routing scatter into the streamed grouped GEMM's epilogue, forward and
backward: a grouped GEMM returns outputs in expert order, and where
that output is streamed or offloaded, the separate re-ordering pass
first materializes an expert-ordered copy of it, so the epilogue
instead writes each result, scaled by its routing weight, to its
token-order address, and both the copy and the pass disappear (the
input-side gather stays a staged pass; its fused variant measured
about 75$\times$ slower and was rejected); and (iv) instantiate
transposed variants for the backward's rereads of the frozen weights.

Figure M2a measures what the rebuild collects, on one adapter GEMM as
a case study: the attention LoRA-A projection $S{=}XA^\top$ at rank 64
and hidden width 5120, the activation $X$ CPU-resident, at 32K and
256K token rows. Three executions: Resident, both operands pre-placed
in HBM, the cuBLAS ceiling; Staged, $X$ copied to HBM and cuBLAS run
on the copy; Streamed, the rebuilt kernel reading $X$ in place. At 32K
rows they take 0.053, 1.651, and 1.598~ms; at 256K rows, 0.402,
13.080, and 12.701~ms. Both off-GPU executions are link-bound,
sustaining the link's achieved rate (about 210~GB/s), because at rank
64 the arithmetic is negligible next to moving $X$; Staged then moves
the bytes twice, over the link and again out of HBM, which is why
Streamed runs about 3\% faster. The decisive difference is what the
execution holds: Staged holds the returned activation, 0.34~GB at 32K
rows and 2.69~GB at 256K, re-spent at exactly the backward's peak,
where Streamed holds the 0.7~MB adapter. Under offloading, the one
executable path paid the link and re-bought the memory; the rebuilt
kernel pays the same link time and keeps the memory saving the offload
was for. The 30$\times$ gap to Resident is
the residency premium, the throughput price of any off-GPU placement;
it argues for keeping tensors resident whenever they fit (§2.4.4), not
for staging.

The routed-expert legs measure the scatter fusion (Figure M2b):
Qwen3-30B-A3B expert GEMMs under the streamed recipe at 128K tokens
(top-8 of 128 experts, 1.05M routed rows), the fused epilogue against
an unfused grouped GEMM plus separate scatter pass. Fusion eliminates
the expert-ordered fp32 output copy on both legs, 8.59~GB per leg at
this length, and the forward leg also runs 13\% faster (41.9 to
36.4~ms); the backward leg pays 12\% (44.0 to 49.1~ms), because its
streamed weight is read transposed and the fused mainloop pays more
for that than the folded scatter saves. The fusion's claim is
therefore the eliminated copy on both legs, with a faster forward, and
the backward's 12\% is the stated price of its 8.59~GB.

The rebuilt kernels' trade-off is that every streamed tile crosses the
interconnect; the GPU-bound C2C direction, idle under model-state
offloading (§2.2), absorbs that traffic (§2.4.2). Streaming also fixes
a direction, moving the data to the compute; §2.4.3 opens the inverse
route. **Takeaway:** rebuilt for once-read operands and backward
dataflows, streaming runs at staged execution's speed with streamed
execution's memory: the promise §2.3 called uncollectable, collected.

### 2.4.2 Idle Interconnect as Activation Capacity

The second opportunity spends the idle link on activations. Below the
checkpoint boundary, each activation type is independently offloaded,
leaving the GPU in the forward and returning beneath the backward's
compute, restaged or consumed in place by the kernels of §2.4.1 and
§2.4.3, or recomputed, regenerated by the layer's forward inside the
backward window. The per-type mix inside one layer is the composition
prior systems lack: they choose once per saved tensor at the
checkpoint boundary (§2.2). Attention shows why the mix pays: its two
small normalization inputs regenerate the wide normalized projections,
so offloading the parents moves a fraction of the bytes of the
children they rebuild.

Figure M3 measures one full Qwen3-32B layer, forward and backward, at
128K tokens under three per-type policies, recompute-all (pure
checkpointing), offload-all (every offloadable type leaves and
restages), and the composed mix the system ships, with peak HBM, link
bytes, and backward-window time split by module (attention, MLP). In
the MLP the composition does what the levers promise: offload-all cuts
the module's backward peak from recompute-all's 44.0~GiB to 26.6,
composed holds 31.5 (the 5-GiB gap is a prefetch trade: gate and up
staged early, their gradients kept on the GPU), and composed moves
0.67$\times$ offload-all's link bytes (51.3 versus 76.3~GiB) while
running 11\% faster than it over the backward window (1230 versus
1360~ms). In attention the win
moves to the
wires. Composed moves 0.48$\times$ offload-all's link bytes (14.6
versus 30.5~GiB), the parent-to-child ratio visible directly, and
holds 7.8~GiB of pinned host memory to offload-all's 16.9; but no
policy lowers this module's GPU peak at this length, because in every
policy the peak instant sits inside the query-norm backward, where the
fp32 upcasts and their gradient chain hold about six 4-GiB tensors at
once: offload-all restages the two fp32 saves at exactly that instant,
re-spending the bytes it freed, and composed rebuilds the same chain
inside its recompute while its side-stream staging runs beside it
(36.5 versus 30.5~GiB). At this length the composition's attention win
is link and host bytes; its peak win lives in the MLP. On time, the
figure reports the backward window, where the composition acts
(forward time is policy-independent): composed beats offload-all in
both modules (4\% faster in attention, 11\% in the MLP).
Recompute-all is the fastest policy in this isolated single-layer run,
12\% ahead of composed in attention and 77\% in the MLP: with the
whole GPU and an idle link, its extra FLOPs cost nothing while the
offload policies wait on restages. What it cannot shed is residency, the
44.0~GiB MLP backward above, which is the term that does not scale
(§2.2).

The trade-off is that freed GPU memory returns as link traffic,
absorbed while each transfer fits inside its layer's dependency
window, the span the layer's compute opens between an operand's
production and its consumption. **Takeaway:** spent on activations,
the idle interconnect becomes GPU-memory headroom at no step-time cost
over offloading, and the per-type composition cuts the bytes that
conversion pays to half to two-thirds.

### 2.4.3 Idle Grace Cores as a Second Compute Engine

Streaming moves the operand to the compute; the third opportunity is
the inverse, moving the compute to the operand. The Grace cores idle
outside the few-percent optimizer step (§2.2), 72 cores against the
CPU memory's [500]~GB/s, and memory-bound gradient work fits them when
its operands already live in CPU memory. Two placements ship, both SVE
kernels built for Grace. The CPU adapter-gradient kernel computes $dA$
where the offloaded activation lies, contracting it in place and
depositing the fp32 result directly into the optimizer's pinned
buffer, so all that crosses the link is the rank-width projection
gradient, 34~MB at 256K rows against the 2.7~GB activation a GPU-side
gradient would restage. The gradient-ingestion kernel fuses the
bf16-to-fp32 widen into the gradient-norm reduction the optimizer
already performs: gradients cross the link in bf16, half the fp32
bytes, and one SVE pass replaces the stock two, 7.2$\times$ faster on
a 1-GiB gradient batch (12.1 versus 86.7~ms). Table~\ref{tab:cpu-scope}
scopes the CPU's role against SuperOffload's:
GraceAdam~\cite{superoffload} runs the fp32 update loop on these cores
and leaves the ingestion pass untouched, and Superchip-Aware
Casting~\cite{superoffload} chose to cast on the GPU and transmit
fp32, a conclusion that inverts once the CPU cast is fused into a
reduction the optimizer already requires. (A fused SwiGLU elementwise
kernel for the same placement is built and bit-accurate but ships
disabled: the device-to-host transfer it removes is fully overlapped
on this machine, so removing it buys no step time, a negative result
that sharpens the gating below.)

Figure M4b measures the deposit at its shipped site, MoE attention
$dA$, across 64K, 256K, and 1M projection rows. Against stock PyTorch
CPU matmuls at the same 96-thread budget, the kernel runs 1.8$\times$,
2.4$\times$, and 31$\times$ faster (12.3 versus 21.6~ms, 33.3 versus
79.8, and 137 versus 4336: the stock bf16 path collapses at scale).
Placement, however, is not settled by serial time: run in isolation,
the GPU route, restage plus GPU gradient kernel plus gradient
transfer, is faster at every size; the shipped question is what each
route adds to the critical path of a backward that is already using
the SMs and the link. Run concurrently with such a context (63.6~ms of
streamed GEMMs), the CPU route adds 1.36~ms at 64K rows to the GPU
route's 1.29, parity; 1.32~ms at 256K to the GPU's 5.19, four times
less; and 87.8~ms at 1M to the GPU's 20.7, because 137~ms of serial
CPU work no longer fits a 64~ms window. The crossover falls between
256K and 1M rows, and the shipped policy arms the CPU placement only
through the 256K point (262{,}144 rows), the last where it wins. The
boundary is a time window, not a bandwidth limit: the idle cores
absorb CPU seconds only while the backward's dependency window is
open, extending the step once it closes, and row count predicts the
closure. **Takeaway:** with the optimizer light, the Grace cores
absorb gradient work, but only inside the backward's dependency
windows; a gradient computable on either processor, with a measured
crossover between them, is exactly why kernel dispatch exists (§3.4).

### 2.4.4 One Placement Does Not Fit All Jobs

The fourth opportunity is the choice among the first three. Every
placement off the GPU frees memory and costs throughput: a streamed
weight holds no GPU memory where a staged one holds a layer's buffer,
an offloaded activation type frees its bytes but pays a restage, a
recomputed type pays FLOPs instead, and beneath them all sits §2.4.1's
30$\times$ residency premium. The placements also share a wire: a
configuration's weight streams, activation streams, and restages all
ride the same GPU-bound link, so their costs add, and the
configuration measurements of Figure M6 price them together. Overlap
narrows these costs but does not erase them, so configurations, each
an assignment of a placement to every weight and activation type,
order from most resident, the fastest, to fully streamed, the leanest.
Shorter jobs fit near-resident configurations and run fastest there;
only the longest need the streamed end: at 32K the most resident of
the three measured configurations is the fastest and holds the most
GPU memory (2063 versus 1524 versus 698~tok/s; 14.1 versus 11.8
versus 8.4~GiB; Qwen3-32B, batch 1), and at 512K the most resident
aborts out of memory in an attempted run, so the best feasible
configuration shifts to the partial one, 327 versus the streamed
one's 264~tok/s, a near-wall fit at 172 of the GPU's 184~GiB
(Figure M6). Near the capacity wall a wrong pick ends in an
out-of-memory abort, not a slowdown, and beyond a short anchor zone
where kernel behavior still shifts with length, peak GPU memory is
linear in token count for a fixed model and configuration, so records
of past runs predict whether a candidate fits. Within a feasible
configuration, throughput rises with batch size only to a knee, [the
batch where the step's kernels reach full device occupancy, reached at
small batch for long sequences], and is flat past it, so the largest
fitting batch is not worth taking past the knee (§3.3). The leanest
configurations also trade GPU memory for CPU memory, bounded in turn
by its own capacity, a bound the dense families reach first in
recorded runs (§3.4). **Takeaway:** the fastest feasible configuration
shifts with model and sequence length, and it is predictable from
records: selection must precede launch, and can.

### 2.4.5 Two GPUs, One Memory: Balancing MoE Without Moving Data

The last opportunity uses the second GPU. MoE routing concentrates
tokens on different experts at every step, so under a static expert
partition the GPU holding the cold experts finishes early and idles,
its private link unused (Figure M5a). Conventional rebalancing moves
data, either the tokens, exchanged all-to-all before every expert
layer through collectives that stall both GPUs (expert
parallelism~\cite{expert-parallelism}), or the expert weights,
repartitioned. On a superchip neither has to move: the expert weights
already sit in memory both GPUs address over independent links, and
under the activation-offloading configurations the long jobs run, the
routed tokens sit there too, so what moves is the work list, one
shared list of expert workloads per grouped launch, collective-free.
We measure four executions of the expert GEMM across routing skew $z$
(larger $z$ concentrates more tokens on fewer experts): the static
expert partition; a data-parallel split, each GPU running its own
tokens through every expert; and the shared list cut two ways, a
computed cut, both GPUs deriving the same balanced split from routing
counts they already hold, and a counter-raced cut, both claiming work
from the list's opposite ends until they meet. At $z{=}1.5$ on
Qwen3.5-122B the computed cut runs the expert GEMM in 31.2~ms against
39.0 raced, 42.8 data-parallel, and 44.6 expert-partitioned; the
static partition pays the skew itself, the data-parallel split runs
every expert at half its rows and streams every expert bank over both
links, and the raced cut pays coherence traffic on its shared counters
where the computed cut's counters are private. The saving carries
through to the MoE block, the two GPUs finish near-balanced across the
skew sweep, and both GPUs stream from the same CPU memory throughout,
so the shared [500]~GB/s ceiling of §2.1 is priced into the numbers
(Figure M5b). The gain needs skew to bind: where per-expert work
already saturates both GPUs under the data-parallel split, sharing
adds nothing, which sets the per-expert row ceiling above which it is
left off, and on Llama-4-Scout, where the data-parallel split is as
fast at every skew we sweep, it adds nothing at all. **Takeaway:** on
a superchip, wherever the routed tokens reside in the shared memory,
MoE balance is a scheduling property, not a communication cost.
