# system_writing v2 — System Design (§3): the section skeleton

(2026-07-26: main sections RESYNCED to `system_writing_full_v2.md`
(the ground truth) after the offline/online restructure, the WHY→§2
delegation, and the three convergence passes. Subsection titles are
working names pending Kevin's confirmation. Back-matter (tables,
gates) retained below. §2 skeleton: `motivation_v2.md`.)

STRUCTURE RULE: two levels only — subsections §3.1–§3.6 + bold run-in
paragraph titles; §3.1 and §3.6 untitled flow. §3 carries WHAT and
HOW only: every WHY lives in §2 (motivation_v2.md), and §3 sentences
carry at most a one-clause why plus a §2 pointer. Sections run
fixed-before-launch → per-step: kernels (§3.2) and configuration
selection (§3.3) precede the runtime pair (§3.4, §3.5).

---

## §3.1 System Overview   [untitled flow, 3 ¶s]

RHETORIC: (P1) The machine and the target, as fact: Grace–Blackwell
superchips (two Blackwell GPUs + one Grace CPU, coherent NVLink-C2C,
both GPUs read CPU memory directly); long-context LoRA fine-tuning of
dense and MoE models at tens of thousands to beyond 1M tokens, where
weights and activations together exceed GPU memory. (P2) The givens
and the guarantee: base weights homed in CPU memory (as prior offload
systems); per-layer checkpointing enabled (forward saves only each
layer's input, backward recomputes before differentiating, at most one
layer's activations live); under a memory budget AsymLoRA determines
where every tensor resides and how it reaches its consumer; no
approximations — same optimization step as standard LoRA up to
floating-point reduction order. (P3) Figure walk, numbered like the
figure: (1)–(2) fixed before launch (the kernel portfolio §3.2, the
configuration via the Profiler §3.3); (3)–(4) act during the step (the
Dispatcher §3.4 enacts placements and routes operators; the Expert
Balancer §3.5 shares one routed-expert work list between the GPUs).

## §3.2 Training Kernels for CPU-Resident Tensors

RHETORIC: Lead (3 sentences): our kernels stream a CPU-resident
operand tile-by-tile during the GEMM, no GPU-memory copy — the
streaming scheme of the AsymGEMM inference library (trailing
attribution, never "builds on"); training shifts the streamed operand
from the reused frozen weight to the once-read activation and adds the
backward's transposed rereads and token-axis reductions (§2.3); the
kernels below serve these dataflows.

- **AsymLoRA Adapter Kernels.** — R: TWO GPU streaming kernels: (1)
  the forward-projection kernel (once-read activation in the
  fetch-once shared-memory slot, small resident factor pipelined;
  grid over row segments, since an expert-keyed grid collapses at
  rank 64); (2) the GPU adapter-gradient kernel (token-axis
  reduction, so rank-sized accumulators stay in registers across the
  whole segment, written once). ONE clause closes the bullet: whether
  this gradient runs here or on the Grace cores (CPU kernels below)
  is a dispatch decision (§3.4). [The CPU adapter-gradient kernel is
  described ONLY in the CPU bullet — consistency with §2.4.1/§2.4.3.]
- **Scatter-Fused Asymmetric Grouped GEMMs for Routed Experts.** — R:
  grouped GEMMs return expert-ordered outputs, so a separate scatter
  pass would materialize a permuted copy of streamed activations; our
  kernels fold the scatter into the streamed epilogue, forward and
  backward (§2.4.1): (1) forward kernel scales by routing weights and
  writes token-order addresses; (2) backward kernel likewise for
  gate/up input gradients. Streamed configurations dispatch these
  (§3.4); resident ones use the unfused grouped GEMM + cheap on-GPU
  scatter.
- **CPU Kernels for Host-Resident Data.** — R: memory-bound operators
  over CPU-resident operands run on the Grace cores in SVE kernels
  (in place, nothing crosses the link, §2.4.3). Three ship, all
  described here: (1) the CPU adapter-gradient kernel — the Grace
  counterpart of the GPU adapter-gradient kernel above: contracts the
  offloaded activation in place, only the rank-width projection
  gradient crosses inbound, fp32 result deposited into the
  optimizer's pinned buffer; (2) the gradient-ingestion kernel
  (bf16→fp32 widen fused into the optimizer's gradient-norm
  reduction; gradients cross in bf16); (3) the SwiGLU-activation
  kernel (gated product beside offloaded operands) [toconfirm #1].

Closer: the portfolio of three execution targets (streamed AsymLoRA
GEMMs, resident cuBLAS GEMMs, Grace CPU kernels); the streamed family
covers the frozen path both directions (transposed instantiations,
degrading to a staged GEMM where transposed tiling constraints fail);
which target runs which operator = the configuration (§3.3) and its
dispatch (§3.4).

## §3.3 Offline Profiling for Configuration Selection

RHETORIC: Lead: a configuration assigns every weight a TRANSPORT (staged or streamed) and every activation type (§2.1) a placement (kept, offloaded, recomputed); from records alone the Profiler answers (model, max seq len, budget) with config + batch maximizing throughput in the capacity the budget leaves free; never profiled before launch (near the wall: one guarded probe). COLD START closed: a family enters the store once via an anchor sweep ([k] short runs per config at [two] lengths); every run's manifest + peaks feed the store (§3.6).

- **Peak-Memory Prediction.** — R: a linear model of peak GPU memory
  in token count per (model, configuration) (§2.4.4), fitted to past
  runs, plus CPU-side capacity anchors; leaner configurations trade
  GPU memory for CPU memory so BOTH capacities are checked; the budget
  is a reservation subtracted before the check; measured tables where
  fits are invalid (short-sequence anchor zone); near the wall,
  decisions in a fixed band are flagged and shipped with an exact
  probe command. (NO metrics figures in §3 — F5 is RELOCATED: its
  linear-fits evidence joins §2.4.4/M6, its accuracy/probe-band story
  goes to the evaluation; §3 keeps only the system diagram and
  mechanism illustrations.)
- **Configuration Search.** — R: the configurations form a FIXED LADDER per family (each = previous with one more class off the GPU → residency is a total order); faster-first confirmed (§2.4.4, M6), so first-fit needs no runtime timing; largest batch passing both checks, capped at the knee (in recorded runs the knee sits below every feasible ceiling, so the cap forfeits nothing [verify]); constants changes gated by self-tests + replay (replay catches would-have-changed decisions; machine drift is caught by fresh measurements feeding the store).

## §3.4 Runtime Placement and Kernel Dispatch

RHETORIC: Lead: the Dispatcher executes each step under the selected
configuration (§3.3), reading only runtime state (free GPU memory,
per-operator shapes); it enacts each placement (staging, streaming,
offloading, recomputation) and routes each operator to the kernel of
the device holding its operands. THE TRADEOFF punchline: every
placement off the GPU trades throughput for memory — freed memory
comes back as transfers, restages, or recomputation (§2.4.4); the
Dispatcher narrows this cost by overlapping into the backward's
dependency windows; the remaining cost is why more resident
configurations stay faster and why the Profiler picks the most
resident fit (§3.3).

- **Enacting the Placement.** — R: weights and activations placed
  independently (bullets): weights staged (copy in for the GEMM,
  release after, ≤1 layer held) or streamed (tile-by-tile, no copy);
  activations recomputed by default (forward saves only inputs, §3.1)
  and, within that recompute, each class kept resident once produced,
  offloaded+restaged, or left to recompute; offloaded classes ride
  pinned buffers, completion events, and a guarded prefetch stream
  (restage only when free memory clears the guard, §2.4.2). Closing
  fact: a kept class has no CPU copy, so CPU-reading kernels (§3.2)
  apply only to offloaded classes.
- **Combining Recomputation with Offloading.** — R: prior systems
  treat each activation below the checkpoint boundary as either
  recomputed or offloaded; we compose them — regenerate a class in the
  backward window from a smaller offloaded save (attention's
  normalized projections rebuilt exactly from two small normalization
  inputs); the composition rides the idle interconnect (Figure M3,
  §2.4.2), turning idle bandwidth into freed GPU memory.
- **Asynchronous CPU Execution.** — R: for adapter gradients the
  gradient transfer is removed: a persistent CPU worker computes them
  on Grace cores during the backward, writing fp32 straight into the
  optimizer's pinned buffer; only the rank-sized projection gradient
  crosses; the computation hides inside dependency windows, whereas
  the GPU alternative underfills a GEMM and adds transfer to a busy
  link (§2.4.3).
- **Kernel Dispatch.** — R: every operator runs where its operands
  sit; arithmetic intensity settles clear cases (compute-bound frozen
  GEMMs on GPU, memory-bound ingestion on CPU); the rest fall to
  measured thresholds on rows/bytes/tokens gated by model class and
  free GPU memory; CPU-placement thresholds in rows, the quantity
  predicting window exhaustion (§2.4.3, Figure M4b); dense families disabled wholesale (CPU capacity first AND every-token adapter-gradient sites past M4b's crossover — the bridging premise is stated, §2.4.4/§2.4.3); prefetch shares the transport guard; rules fixed once, serving every configuration.

## §3.5 Dynamic Expert Load Balancing

RHETORIC: Lead: each GPU reads the shared CPU memory over its own
~450 GB/s link; per-step routing skew leaves a static expert split
idling one GPU and its link (§2.4.5); AsymLoRA keeps the weights still
and shares the work — one shared list of expert workloads per grouped
launch, agreed through the memory both GPUs address, no collectives.

- **A Shared Expert Work List.** — R: each launch executes the union
  of both GPUs' expert work; sharing applies under configurations that
  offload the routed activations (§3.4) — the tokens then sit in
  shared CPU memory and either GPU streams them plus expert weights
  directly; other launches take the data-parallel split; each expert
  bank streams once regardless of consumer; sharing covers only the
  frozen grouped GEMM (adapters and gradients untouched, semantics
  unchanged).
- **Collective-Free Coordination.** — R: every cross-GPU agreement
  runs through shared memory: both GPUs derive the same balanced cut
  from routing counts they already hold (common case exchanges
  nothing); results land in the peer's staging buffers, visible via
  host flag polling + GPU acquire/release; counter-raced variant when
  counts are unknown; Figure M5 (§2.4.5) is the measured basis for the
  computed cut; arming ceiling on per-expert rows, floor = the
  unshared launch, gains concentrate where skew binds.

## §3.6 Implementation   [untitled flow, 2 ¶s]

RHETORIC: (P1) components + KLOC placeholders (CUDA/C++ kernels of
§§3.2+3.5; Python placement/transport of §3.4; the Profiler of §3.3),
integrated into the [stack] stack; the integration is narrow (replaces
frozen-GEMM dispatch, activation-offload hooks, optimizer ingestion;
leaves trainer loop, data pipeline, attention, adapter math
untouched). (P2) every mechanism individually switchable and off by
default; launch configuration = explicit flags emitted by the
Profiler; per-run manifest; pinned memory via per-family accounting
degrading to pageable; every reported configuration reproducible from
its manifest.

grouped_expert_lora_cpu_left
  ADOPTION 🟡: attention LoRA-A forward at dense T2/T3 + MoE T2B/T3;
  MLP forward at dense T3. Not at T1/keep-acts; MoE expert forward
  pinned to GPU. Ledger cap-denial degrades to a staged GPU GEMM
  (lossless).
  GOAL: upstream amortizes the slow link through operand reuse; a
  rank-64 stream has almost none, so the requirement becomes fetch-once
  at full link bandwidth.
  IMPL: the shared-memory roles are swapped vs upstream — the host
  activation gets the fetch-once singleton slot (one tile per (M,K)
  step, reused across the output loop), the GPU factor gets the staged
  pipeline — and the launch grid is re-keyed to row chunks, without
  which rank-64 collapses to one GPU block per expert.

sm100_grouped_lora_a_grad_bf16_cpu_right
  ADOPTION 🟡: dense T3 MLP dA; MoE T2B/T3 down-projection dA. Not
  where activations stay on GPU (T1/keep-acts).
  GOAL: the gradient reduces over the token axis, so the host stream
  must feed a running accumulation, not retire-as-you-go tiling.
  IMPL: output-stationary — the [rank × k-tile] accumulators live in
  registers across a segment's whole token stream and write once at
  stream end; upstream retires partial tiles to memory at every
  reduction step (TMA reduce-add).

asym_bf16_cpu_right_matmul
  ADOPTION 🟡: base host-weight GEMMs wherever attention/dense offload
  runs; the inverted (activation-resident) case at the attention dA
  site at shed tiers.
  GOAL: single (non-grouped) GEMM against a CPU-resident operand for
  the offloaded attention/dense paths.
  IMPL: streams the pinned host tensor as the GEMM's right operand; at
  the attention dA site that operand is the OFFLOADED ACTIVATION — the
  one non-grouped inverted-residency site.

grouped_expert_lora_pair_cpu_left (+ pair-grad twin)
  ADOPTION ❌: env-gated off everywhere — launcher comment "Not on the
  current best benchmark paths; retained for experimental paired
  CPU-left LoRA-A runs"; the shipped default calls the single kernel
  twice, streaming the same activation twice. Gate C4 governs how the
  paper may mention it.
  GOAL: rank-64 gives zero reuse, so manufacture it — one activation
  fetch must serve both gate and up GEMMs.
  IMPL: a second weight/output descriptor set and doubled output loop
  with per-half descriptor selection through the shared
  accumulator/epilogue pipeline — a wrapper over two calls would stream
  the activation twice.

grouped_expert_lora / grouped_expert_lora_pair (GPU)
  ADOPTION ✅ (all fg tiers, both families) — but NOT our kernel:
  composition over torch grouped_mm; claimed as dispatch engineering
  only.
  GOAL: one launch for all experts' adapters instead of per-expert
  loops. IMPL: torch grouped_mm over concatenated operands — saves

#### A.2 MoE / additional asym kernels

| Kernel | Used? | In writing? | Notes |
|---|:--:|:--:|---|
| Route fusion `fwd-scatter` | 🟡 | ✔ §3.2 routed forward kernel (1) | scatter-add epilogue while streaming weights |
| Route fusion `gateup-dx-scatter` | 🟡 | ✔ §3.2 routed backward kernel (2) | same for gate/up input grads |
| Route fusion `down-dx-gather` | ❌ | ✗ | rejected (~75×); negative result |
| `ep_steal` grouped GEMM (2 policies) | 🟡 | ✔ §3.5 shared work list | plan (default) + queue (fallback) |
| `qwen3_gate_up_windowed_bwd` | ❌ | ✗ | unreachable in shipped tiers |
| Expert-blocked tiling mode | ❌ | ✗ | superseded by the route fusions |

```
Route fusion: fwd-scatter
  ADOPTION 🟡: MoE T3 only (the ker101 recipe); MoE T2/T2B run the
  resident path; dense never.
  GOAL: feeding routed tokens to upstream's kernels needs a permuted
  input copy, and un-permuting outputs needs a separate scatter pass.
  IMPL: block-tile TMA cannot follow a token permutation, so the
  prologue stages rows BY INDEX with per-lane loads into the swizzled
  shared-memory layout (folding the routing weight into the gather) and
  the epilogue scatter-ADDS results to token-order addresses — inside a
  mainloop simultaneously streaming host weights.

Route fusion: gateup-dx-scatter
  ADOPTION 🟡: MoE T3 only (same recipe).
  GOAL/IMPL: the same design applied to the gate/up gradient leg
  (scatter-add epilogue in the backward direction).

Route fusion: down-dx-gather
  ADOPTION ❌: measured and REJECTED (~5.5 s/call vs 72 ms staged);
  ker101's middle digit disarms it. Do not claim its "gather" argument
  for the shipped pair.
  GOAL: the same fusion idea for the down-projection gradient input.
  IMPL: the gather-prologue variant lost to the staged resident path by
  ~75× on measurement — kept in code as the negative result.

ep_steal grouped GEMM (m_grouped_…_ep_steal) — TWO SPLIT POLICIES
  ADOPTION 🟡: ONLY the 2-GPU expert-parallel mode (validated in the
  GB200 EP campaign; gate C7); never in the single-GPU tier system.
  Both policies share every line of transport; they differ only in how
  the union list is cut:
    · COMPUTED CUT ("plan") — PREFERRED, measured best on all three
      Qwen models, and the variant the paper should present as shipped.
      Expert GEMM at skew z=1.5: Qwen3.5-122B 31.2 ms vs 39.0 (raced)
      / 42.8 (sDP) / 44.6 (EP); Qwen3-235B −32% vs EP, −12% vs sDP
      (raced: −27% / −6%). Qwen3-30B at z=2.0: 15.2 ms vs 18.2 raced.
    · RACED CUT ("queue") — the counts-free variant; ties the computed
      cut at low skew and loses from z≈1.5 up; marginally better only
      on Llama-4-Scout, where neither policy beats sDP at all (sDP is
      already flat across skew — sEP adds nothing for that model).
  DEFAULT: `ASYM_EP_SEP_MODE` now defaults to "plan" (flipped from
  "queue" on 2026-07-23 to match the measurements); the raced cut stays
  available as the counts-free fallback.
  GOAL: static expert splits idle one GPU under per-step routing
  imbalance, and collective-based balancing pays synchronization
  stalls; upstream only statically assigns blocks.
  IMPL: both GPUs execute one union expert work list per launch;
  results are published with system-scope release/acquire ordering into
  staging at the peer's row offsets and a host pinned-flag protocol
  replaces every collective, while expert weights never move (each bank
  streams once). The computed cut derives the row-balanced segment
  boundary identically on both GPUs from the routing counts and gives
  each a PRIVATE counter (zero cross-GPU counter traffic), with
  hysteresis snapping to a fully local launch when the cut lands within
  one segment of the natural boundary; the raced cut instead pops one
  shared counter from both ends and lets the meeting point define the
  split. Arming: measured rows-per-expert ceiling; un-armed launches fall
  through to the data-parallel own-rows split (sDP) — THAT is the
  guaranteed floor, not the expert-partitioned baseline.

qwen3_gate_up_windowed_bwd
  ADOPTION ❌: unreachable in shipped tiers (full-fg configs force the
  expert-recompute policy that never calls it).
  GOAL: bound how many gradient bytes are alive at once in the gate/up
  backward — a training-only memory axis.
  IMPL: backward restructured into windows; dormant because the shipped
  recompute policy bypasses its caller.

Expert-blocked tiling mode
  ADOPTION ❌: pinned off in every MoE recipe; hard-errors if combined
  with the route fusions — superseded by them.
  GOAL: bound live routed bytes by processing experts in blocks.
  IMPL: an alternative iteration mode of the grouped kernels, not a
  separate kernel.
```

cpu_widen_bf16_sqsum (fused widen + squared-sum)
  ADOPTION ✅: all tiers, both model families (optimizer path,
  always-on under the policy).
  GOAL: the optimizer needs fp32 gradients and a gradient-norm sum —
  normally two passes over every gradient.
  IMPL: one fused SVE pass does the bf16→fp32 widen and the squared-sum
  reduction together (~13× over the unfused pair). Engineering claim,
  not a research kernel — and MUST cite SuperOffload twice: (1)
  GraceAdam (§4.6) is the published Grace optimizer kernel — theirs
  covers the fp32 Adam UPDATE loop; ours fuses the bf16 INGESTION pass
  (widen + norm reduction) GraceAdam does not touch; our update step is
  DeepSpeed's CPU-AdamW. (2) Their Superchip-Aware Casting (§4.5)
  chose cast-on-GPU-then-transmit-fp32 because on their stack the CPU
  cast was a separate slow pass and transfer-then-cast forced unpinned
  buffers; we take the OPPOSITE side — transmit bf16 (half the bytes),
  cast on CPU — and both of their reasons are engineered away: the cast
  is fused into the norm pass the optimizer needs anyway, over pinned
  staging. Positioning sentence for prose: SAC's conclusion inverts
  when the CPU cast is fused into an already-required reduction over
  pinned staging. (The deposit path beats both: gradients born fp32 in
  the CPU buffer — no cast, no transfer.)

cpu_grouped_lora_a_grad_bf16 (SVE deposit dA)
  ADOPTION 🟡: ONE shipped site — MoE attention dA at short sequences

  GOAL: skip the link entirely — compute the gradient where the data
  and the optimizer live; only the rank-64 dS ever crosses.
  IMPL: SVE-intrinsic CPU kernel (128-bit-vector microkernel, OpenMP,

  directly into the optimizer's pinned buffer at GPU-side segment

cpu_fused_silu_backward_bf16
  ADOPTION ❌: measured, LOST (+7.7% end-to-end), permanently rejected.

  IMPL: correct kernel, but the backward has no dependency window to

  ADOPTION ❌: same cold trigger as the fused forward; superseded by

### B. Non-kernel caveats

- Policy-rejected features (byte-diet, save-dedup, LoRA-B deposit,
  per-socket pools): eval negative-results only, never design claims.
- Keep-acts precedence is a DESIGN fact (in the §3.4 Enacting-the-
  Placement paragraph), not a caveat: an activation type kept in GPU
  memory has no CPU copy, so the kernels that stream or compute from
  CPU memory apply only to classes the configuration offloads.
- The measurement protocol lives in the eval setup; the design part's
  first measured number carries one "(protocol in §N)" pointer.
- Honest limit (state ONCE, in limits/eval — not in the design
  rhetoric, where it undercuts the scaling story): the 70B-dense family
  has no deepest streamed rung — its host-capacity line inverts the
  ladder before the leanest configuration is reached, so its deepest
  shipped state is the middle rung, by measurement.

21	## 3.1 System Overview
22	
23	AsymLoRA is a fine-tuning system for Grace–Blackwell superchips, which
24	couple two Blackwell GPUs to a Grace CPU over the coherent NVLink-C2C
25	interconnect, so that both GPUs read the CPU's memory directly. It
26	targets long-context LoRA fine-tuning of large language models, dense
27	and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) alike, at sequence lengths from tens of thousands of tokens to beyond a million, where model weights and long-context activations together exceed GPU memory (from [N] tokens on; at the largest models the weights alone do).
28	
29	AsymLoRA therefore trains with the base weights homed in CPU memory,
30	as prior offload systems do~\cite{zero-infinity, superoffload}, and with per-layer gradient checkpointing enabled: the
31	forward saves only each layer's input, and the backward recomputes a
32	layer's forward before differentiating it, so at most one layer's
33	activations are live at a time. Under a memory budget, AsymLoRA
34	determines where each of these tensors resides across a run and how
35	each reaches its consumer. AsymLoRA introduces no approximations:
36	training computes the same optimization step as standard LoRA fine-tuning, up to floating-point reduction order [and device rounding].
37	
38	Figure~SYS shows the four modules: (1)–(2) are fixed before launch,
39	the kernel portfolio and the configuration; (3)–(4) act during the
40	step. (1) The training kernels (§3.2) run GEMMs that stream
41	CPU-resident operands over the interconnect and CPU kernels that
42	consume them in place. (2) The Profiler (§3.3) searches measured past
43	runs for the configuration and batch size that maximize throughput
44	under the user's model, maximum sequence length, and memory budget.
45	(3) The Dispatcher (§3.4) enacts the configuration's placements each
46	step and routes every operator to the kernel where its operands sit.
47	(4) The Expert Balancer (§3.5) shares one routed-expert work list
48	between both GPUs through the shared CPU memory, absorbing routing
49	skew without moving weights.
50	
51	## 3.2 Training Kernels for CPU-Resident Tensors
52	<!-- was "Kernels"; MorphServe-style function title; confirm -->
53	
54	Our kernels stream a CPU-resident operand tile-by-tile over the
55	interconnect during the GEMM, holding no copy in GPU memory, the
56	streaming scheme of the AsymGEMM inference library~\cite{asymgemm}.
57	Training keeps the frozen-weight stream and adds a second streamed role, the once-read activation, together with the backward's token-axis reductions and transposed rereads (§2.3, §2.4.1); the kernels below serve these dataflows.
58	
59	**AsymLoRA Adapter Kernels.** The adapter path has three kernels.
60	(1) The forward-projection kernel computes the low-rank projections on
61	the GPU, directly against CPU-resident activations. The once-read
62	activation takes the fetch-once slot in shared memory while the small
63	resident factor is pipelined. This arrangement inverts the inference
64	kernels, whose reused weight is the streamed operand. Its launch grid
65	is partitioned over row segments rather than experts: at rank 64, an
66	expert-partitioned grid would collapse to one thread block per expert.
67	(2) The GPU adapter-gradient kernel streams the activation as one
68	operand of the weight-gradient contraction. Because that contraction
69	reduces over the token axis, no output can retire until the stream has
70	passed, so the kernel holds its rank-sized accumulators in registers
71	across the entire segment and writes them once. (3) The CPU
72	adapter-gradient kernel computes the same gradient on the Grace cores
73	instead, writing fp32 results directly into the optimizer's pinned
74	buffer, so that only the rank-width projection gradient, not the activation, crosses the link. Whether kernel (2) or (3) computes an operator's
75	adapter gradient is a dispatch decision, deferred to §3.4.
76	
77	**Scatter-Fused Asymmetric Grouped GEMMs for Routed Experts.** A grouped
78	GEMM computes an MoE layer's experts in a single launch but returns
79	each expert's outputs in expert order, so a separate pass must scatter
80	them back to token order; when its output is streamed or offloaded, that pass materializes an expert-ordered copy of it first. Our kernels fold the
81	token-order scatter into the epilogue of the streamed grouped GEMM,
82	forward and backward (§2.4.1): the epilogue scatters each result while
83	the mainloop is still streaming weight tiles across the interconnect. (1) The forward kernel multiplies each
84	expert's partial results by their routing weights and writes them
85	straight to token-order addresses, so the output leaves the GEMM
86	already in token order, with no separate pass and no permuted copy. (2)
87	The backward kernel does the same for the gate and up projections'
88	input gradients. Both stream weights and scatter results within one
89	launch. The fusion covers the output side only; the expert-order input
90	gather remains a separate staged pass (§2.4.1). Under configurations
91	that stream the routed activations, the Dispatcher (§3.4) uses these
92	kernels, chosen for the expert-ordered output copy they eliminate
93	(§2.4.1); where the activations stay GPU-resident, the scatter is a
94	cheap on-GPU pass and the unfused grouped GEMM is used instead.
95	
96	**CPU Kernels for Host-Resident Data.** Memory-bound gradient work
97	whose operands already reside in CPU memory runs on the Grace cores;
98	computing it on the GPU would cross the link twice, to fetch the
99	operands and return the result. We compute it in kernels written for
100	the length-agnostic vector model of Arm's Scalable Vector Extension
101	(SVE), operating on the bf16 operands in place (§2.4.3). Two such
102	kernels ship. (1) The CPU adapter-gradient kernel is kernel (3) of the
103	adapter path above. (2) The gradient-ingestion kernel converts each
104	incoming gradient from bf16 to fp32 and fuses this conversion with the
105	gradient-norm reduction the optimizer already performs, so the
106	gradient is read once rather than twice, 7.2$\times$ faster than the
107	stock two-pass path (§2.4.3). The backward emits gradients in bf16, so
108	transferring them in bf16 rather than fp32 is exact, and the
109	conversion introduces no additional pass over memory.
110	
111	Together these form a portfolio of three execution targets: streamed
112	AsymLoRA GEMMs, resident cuBLAS GEMMs, and Grace CPU kernels. The
113	streamed family covers the frozen path in both directions: the
114	base-weight GEMMs ship transposed instantiations for the backward's
115	input gradients, reading the same CPU-resident weight under the
116	transposed access pattern and degrading to a staged GEMM where the
117	transposed tiling constraints do not hold. Which target executes
118	which operator, and under which placement, is fixed by the
119	configuration (§3.3) and its dispatch (§3.4).
120	
121	## 3.3 Offline Profiling for Configuration Selection
122	<!-- was "Profiler"; mirrors MorphServe "Offline Profiling for Layer
123	Swapping Sequence"; confirm -->
124	
125	A configuration assigns every weight a transport, staged or streamed, and every activation type (§2.1) a placement: kept in GPU memory, offloaded to CPU memory, or recomputed (transport in §3.4). From measured past runs alone, the
126	Profiler answers a job request (model, maximum sequence length, memory
127	budget) with the configuration and batch size predicted to maximize
128	throughput within the capacity the budget leaves free; no profiling sweep precedes launch; the one exception, near the capacity wall, is a single guarded feasibility probe. A model family enters the record store once, through an anchor sweep of [k] short runs per configuration, at [two] sequence lengths beyond the anchor zone from which the linear fits extrapolate plus [j] in-zone lengths that seed the verbatim tables; every later run appends its manifest and measured peaks to the store (§3.6).
129	
130	**Peak-Memory Prediction.** For every model and configuration the
131	Profiler maintains a linear model of peak GPU memory in the token count (§2.4.4), fitted to past runs, alongside CPU-side peaks recorded the same way [verify: linear fit versus anchor scaling in the shipped checker]. A configuration that offloads more to CPU memory uses less
132	GPU memory but more CPU memory, so it can run out of either, and the
133	Profiler checks both. The user's budget is a reservation,
134	subtracted from each physical capacity before the fits are checked, so
135	headroom for anything else on the machine is expressed in the check
136	itself. Where linear fits are invalid (the short-sequence anchor zone, where
137	kernels change behavior), measured tables are used verbatim. Near the capacity wall the Profiler does not trust either:
138	any decision within a fixed band of the limit is flagged, and the
139	emitted configuration carries the exact probe command that validates it with a short run, [a few] steps at the job's maximum sequence length, at the emitted batch and one below. (Figure F5: predicted versus measured
140	peak GPU memory across sequence lengths for each configuration of
141	one model: the linear fits, the anchor zone, and the probe band near
142	the wall.)
143	
144	**Configuration Search.** The configurations form a fixed ladder per model family, each the previous with one more activation type moved off the GPU, so residency orders them totally; more residency is faster, a property the measurements confirm for every family we ship (§2.4.4, Figure M6). The search therefore needs no runtime timing; the
145	Profiler considers configurations from most to least resident and takes
146	the first that fits. It then chooses the largest batch that passes
147	both capacity checks; where a measured throughput knee exists (§2.4.4,
148	Figure M6), the batch is capped there, because larger batches no longer pay; in recorded runs the knee falls below every feasible configuration's batch ceiling, so the cap forfeits nothing a leaner configuration could reclaim [verify against M6]. Every change to the fitted constants is
149	gated by self-tests over the prediction properties and by replay of all recorded decisions, so a change that would have altered a past decision is caught before it can misconfigure a run.
150	
151	## 3.4 Runtime Placement and Kernel Dispatch
152	<!-- was "AsymScheduler"; "Runtime" marks the online half, mirrors
153	MorphServe "LayerSwapper: Runtime Layer Swapping"; confirm -->
154	
155	The Dispatcher executes each training step under the configuration
156	the Profiler selected (§3.3), reading only the runtime state: free GPU
157	memory and per-operator shapes. It enacts each placement through
158	staging, streaming, offloading, or recomputation, and routes each
159	operator to the kernel of the device holding its operands.
160	Every placement off the GPU trades throughput for memory: the freed
161	memory comes back as transfers, restages, or recomputation (§2.4.4).
162	The Dispatcher narrows this cost by overlapping the added work with
163	the dependency windows the backward pass opens; the cost that remains
164	is why more resident configurations stay faster and why the Profiler
165	selects the most resident one that fits (§3.3) (Figure~SYS, center).
166	
167	**Enacting the Placement.** Weights and activations are placed
168	independently.
169	
170	\begin{itemize}
171	\item \textbf{Weights} are staged or streamed (§3.2). Staging copies a
172	weight into GPU memory for its GEMM and releases it after, holding at
173	most one layer's weights at once. Streaming leaves it in CPU memory and
174	reads it tile-by-tile during the GEMM, holding no copy in GPU memory
175	but moving every tile across the interconnect.
176	
177	\item \textbf{Activations} are recomputed by default: the forward saves
178	only each layer's input, and the backward regenerates the rest (§3.1).
179	Within that recompute, each type is kept resident in GPU memory once produced or left to recompute, both consumed by the same layer's backward; offloaded types leave during the forward and restage beneath the backward.
180	Offloaded activations ride pinned buffers with completion events and a
181	guarded prefetch stream: a restage issues only when free GPU memory
182	clears the guard, and its completion event orders it ahead of its
183	consumer, keeping restages off the critical path unless the window
184	closes first (§2.4.2).
185	\end{itemize}
186	
187	An activation type kept in GPU memory has no CPU copy, so the kernels that stream or compute from CPU memory (§3.2) apply only to types the configuration offloads.
188	
189	**Combining Recomputation with Offloading.** Prior systems treat each
190	activation below the checkpoint boundary as either recomputed or
191	offloaded~\cite{superoffload, zero-infinity}; we compose them.
192	An activation type is regenerated in the backward window from a smaller offloaded save; the interconnect carries the save and recomputation supplies the rest. Attention's normalized projections, for instance, are rebuilt
193	exactly from a pair of small offloaded normalization inputs that cost a
194	fraction of the bytes they regenerate. The composition rides the
195	interconnect where it is otherwise idle during a layer's compute,
196	turning idle bandwidth into freed GPU memory at half to two-thirds of
197	offloading's link bytes and no step-time cost over it (Figure M3,
198	§2.4.2).
199	
200	**Asynchronous CPU Execution.** A CPU-side optimizer normally receives
201	gradients computed on the GPU and transferred across the link, and the
202	transfer stands between the backward pass and the optimizer step. For
203	the adapter gradients we remove this transfer. Because the adapters are
204	low-rank and the activations they contract against already reside in
205	CPU memory, a persistent CPU worker computes the gradient on the Grace
206	cores, in parallel with the ongoing backward pass, and writes the fp32
207	result straight into the optimizer's pinned buffer; only the rank-width projection gradient crosses the link. The computation hides inside the
208	dependency windows the backward opens; the GPU alternative would
209	underfill a GEMM and add a transfer to a busy link, four times the
210	added critical path at 256K rows (5.2 versus 1.3~ms, §2.4.3, Figure
211	M4b).
212	
213	**Kernel Dispatch.** Every operator runs on the device where its
214	operands already sit. Arithmetic intensity settles the clear cases:
215	compute-bound frozen-path GEMMs run on the GPU, and the memory-bound
216	ingestion of gradients runs on the CPU. The remaining cases fall to
217	measured thresholds on row counts, bytes, and token counts, gated by model family and free GPU memory. The CPU-placement thresholds are
218	expressed in rows, the quantity that predicts when CPU work outgrows
219	the dependency window it hides in (§2.4.3, Figure M4b); the shipped
220	threshold arms the CPU adapter-gradient placement through 262{,}144
221	rows, inside the measured crossover. The threshold-gated CPU placements are disabled wholesale for the dense families, whose recorded runs exhaust CPU capacity first and whose adapter-gradient sites carry every token, past the crossover of Figure M4b (§2.4.4, §2.4.3); prefetch engages only when free
222	GPU memory clears the same guard the transport layer consults. The
223	rules are fixed once and serve every configuration.
224	
225	## 3.5 Dynamic Expert Load Balancing
226	
227	Each GPU of a Grace–Blackwell superchip reads the shared CPU memory
228	through its own NVLink-C2C link (§2.1), and per-step routing skew
229	leaves a static expert split idling one GPU and its link (§2.4.5). AsymLoRA keeps the weights still and shares the work: each
230	grouped launch executes one shared list of expert workloads, agreed
231	through the memory both GPUs address with no collective communication.
232	
233	**A Shared Expert Work List.** Each shared grouped launch executes the
234	union of both GPUs' expert work rather than two private lists, so
235	either GPU absorbs the other's overload. Sharing applies under the
236	configurations that offload the routed activations (§3.4): the tokens
237	then reside in the shared CPU memory, so either GPU reads the other's
238	tokens directly and computes its portion of the union list by
239	streaming those activations and the expert weights from that memory;
240	other launches take the data-parallel split. The expert
241	weights likewise stay put: each expert's bank streams
242	once from the shared CPU memory regardless of which GPU consumes it.
243	Sharing covers only the frozen grouped GEMM, so adapter computation and
244	gradients are untouched and the mechanism has no effect on training
245	semantics.
246	
247	**Collective-Free Coordination.** Every cross-GPU agreement runs
248	through the shared memory rather than a communication primitive. The
249	balanced cut of the work list is derived identically on both GPUs from
250	routing counts they already hold, so in the common case the two sides
251	exchange nothing at all before launching; results written for the peer
252	land directly in its staging buffers, made visible by host-side flag
253	polling and GPU-side acquire/release ordering. A counter-raced variant,
254	in which the two GPUs consume the list from opposite ends until they
255	meet, remains available when counts are not known in advance; Figure
256	M5b (§2.4.5) is the measured basis for preferring the computed cut,
257	31.2 versus 39.0~ms on the expert GEMM at $z{=}1.5$ on Qwen3.5-122B.
258	Sharing arms only where it can help: launches whose per-expert row
259	counts exceed a measured ceiling fall back to the plain data-parallel
260	split, so the mechanism's floor is the unshared launch, and its gains
261	concentrate where routing skew binds.
262	
263	## 3.6 Implementation
264	
265	AsymLoRA comprises the CUDA/C++ kernel extensions of §§3.2 and 3.5
266	(about X KLOC; exact split to be filled from the repository), a Python
267	placement and transport layer implementing §3.4 (about Y KLOC), and
268	the Profiler of §3.3, integrated into the [stack] fine-tuning
269	stack. The
270	integration is deliberately narrow: the system replaces the frozen-GEMM
271	dispatch, the activation-offload hooks, and the optimizer's gradient
272	ingestion, and leaves the trainer loop, data pipeline, attention
273	implementation, and adapter mathematics untouched.
274	
275	Every mechanism of §§3.2–3.5 is individually switchable and off by
276	default; a launch configuration is an explicit set of flags emitted by
277	the Profiler, and each run records its full configuration in a manifest alongside its artifacts, and its measured peaks and throughput feed the Profiler's record store. CPU-side pinned memory is allocated through a per-family accounting
278	layer that degrades to pageable allocation rather than failing, and
279	every configuration reported in §5 is reproducible from its recorded
280	manifest.

memory comes back as transfers, restages, or recomputation (§2.4.4).
The Dispatcher narrows this cost by overlapping the added work with
the dependency windows the backward pass opens; the cost that remains
is why more resident configurations stay faster and why the Profiler
selects the most resident one that fits (§3.3) (Figure~SYS, center).

**Enacting the Placement.** Weights and activations are placed
independently.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Weights} are staged or streamed (§3.2). Staging copies a
weight into GPU memory for its GEMM and releases it after, holding at
most one layer's weights at once. Streaming leaves it in CPU memory and
reads it tile-by-tile during the GEMM, holding no copy in GPU memory
but moving every tile across the interconnect.

\item \textbf{Activations} are recomputed by default: the forward saves
only each layer's input, and the backward regenerates the rest (§3.1).
Within that recompute, each type is kept resident in GPU memory once produced or left to recompute, both consumed by the same layer's backward; offloaded types leave during the forward and restage beneath the backward.
Offloaded activations ride pinned buffers with completion events and a
guarded prefetch stream: a restage issues only when free GPU memory
clears the guard, and its completion event orders it ahead of its
consumer, keeping restages off the critical path unless the window
closes first (§2.4.2).
\end{itemize}

An activation type kept in GPU memory has no CPU copy, so the kernels that stream or compute from CPU memory (§3.2) apply only to types the configuration offloads.

**Combining Recomputation with Offloading.** Prior systems treat each
activation below the checkpoint boundary as either recomputed or
offloaded~\cite{superoffload, zero-infinity}; we compose them.
An activation type is regenerated in the backward window from a smaller offloaded save; the interconnect carries the save and recomputation supplies the rest. Attention's normalized projections, for instance, are rebuilt
exactly from a pair of small offloaded normalization inputs that cost a
fraction of the bytes they regenerate. The composition rides the
interconnect where it is otherwise idle during a layer's compute,
turning idle bandwidth into freed GPU memory at half to two-thirds of
offloading's link bytes and no step-time cost over it (Figure M3,
§2.4.2).

**Asynchronous CPU Execution.** A CPU-side optimizer normally receives
gradients computed on the GPU and transferred across the link, and the
transfer stands between the backward pass and the optimizer step. For
the adapter gradients we remove this transfer. Because the adapters are
low-rank and the activations they contract against already reside in
CPU memory, a persistent CPU worker computes the gradient on the Grace
cores, in parallel with the ongoing backward pass, and writes the fp32
result straight into the optimizer's pinned buffer; only the rank-width projection gradient crosses the link. The computation hides inside the
dependency windows the backward opens; the GPU alternative would
underfill a GEMM and add a transfer to a busy link, four times the
added critical path at 256K rows (5.2 versus 1.3~ms, §2.4.3, Figure
M4b).

**Kernel Dispatch.** Every operator runs on the device where its
operands already sit. Arithmetic intensity settles the clear cases:
compute-bound frozen-path GEMMs run on the GPU, and the memory-bound
ingestion of gradients runs on the CPU. The remaining cases fall to
measured thresholds on row counts, bytes, and token counts, gated by model family and free GPU memory. The CPU-placement thresholds are
expressed in rows, the quantity that predicts when CPU work outgrows
the dependency window it hides in (§2.4.3, Figure M4b); the shipped
threshold arms the CPU adapter-gradient placement through 262{,}144
rows, inside the measured crossover. The threshold-gated CPU placements are disabled wholesale for the dense families, whose recorded runs exhaust CPU capacity first and whose adapter-gradient sites carry every token, past the crossover of Figure M4b (§2.4.4, §2.4.3); prefetch engages only when free
GPU memory clears the same guard the transport layer consults. The
rules are fixed once and serve every configuration.

## 3.5 Dynamic Expert Load Balancing

Each GPU of a Grace–Blackwell superchip reads the shared CPU memory
through its own NVLink-C2C link (§2.1), and per-step routing skew
leaves a static expert split idling one GPU and its link (§2.4.5). AsymLoRA keeps the weights still and shares the work: each
grouped launch executes one shared list of expert workloads, agreed
through the memory both GPUs address with no collective communication.

**A Shared Expert Work List.** Each shared grouped launch executes the
union of both GPUs' expert work rather than two private lists, so
either GPU absorbs the other's overload. Sharing applies under the
configurations that offload the routed activations (§3.4): the tokens
then reside in the shared CPU memory, so either GPU reads the other's
tokens directly and computes its portion of the union list by
streaming those activations and the expert weights from that memory;
other launches take the data-parallel split. The expert
weights likewise stay put: each expert's bank streams
once from the shared CPU memory regardless of which GPU consumes it.
Sharing covers only the frozen grouped GEMM, so adapter computation and
gradients are untouched and the mechanism has no effect on training
semantics.

**Collective-Free Coordination.** Every cross-GPU agreement runs
through the shared memory rather than a communication primitive. The
balanced cut of the work list is derived identically on both GPUs from
routing counts they already hold, so in the common case the two sides
exchange nothing at all before launching; results written for the peer
land directly in its staging buffers, made visible by host-side flag
polling and GPU-side acquire/release ordering. A counter-raced variant,
in which the two GPUs consume the list from opposite ends until they
meet, remains available when counts are not known in advance; Figure
M5b (§2.4.5) is the measured basis for preferring the computed cut,
31.2 versus 39.0~ms on the expert GEMM at $z{=}1.5$ on Qwen3.5-122B.
Sharing arms only where it can help: launches whose per-expert row
counts exceed a measured ceiling fall back to the plain data-parallel
split, so the mechanism's floor is the unshared launch, and its gains
concentrate where routing skew binds.

## 3.6 Implementation

AsymLoRA comprises the CUDA/C++ kernel extensions of §§3.2 and 3.5
(about X KLOC; exact split to be filled from the repository), a Python
placement and transport layer implementing §3.4 (about Y KLOC), and
the Profiler of §3.3, integrated into the [stack] fine-tuning
stack. The
integration is deliberately narrow: the system replaces the frozen-GEMM
dispatch, the activation-offload hooks, and the optimizer's gradient
ingestion, and leaves the trainer loop, data pipeline, attention
implementation, and adapter mathematics untouched.

Every mechanism of §§3.2–3.5 is individually switchable and off by
default; a launch configuration is an explicit set of flags emitted by
the Profiler, and each run records its full configuration in a manifest alongside its artifacts, and its measured peaks and throughput feed the Profiler's record store. CPU-side pinned memory is allocated through a per-family accounting
layer that degrades to pageable allocation rather than failing, and
every configuration reported in §5 is reproducible from its recorded
manifest.

1	\section{Background and Motivation}
2	\label{sec:motivation}
3

13	\begin{figure}[t]
14	  \centering
15	  \subfigure[Optimizer share of step time]{%
16	    \includegraphics[width=0.465\columnwidth]{figures/optimizer_timing.pdf}%
17	    \label{fig:motivation-optimizer}%
18	  }\hfill
19	  \subfigure[Peak-memory breakdown]{%
20	    \includegraphics[width=0.465\columnwidth]{figures/memory_decomposition.pdf}%
21	    \label{fig:motivation-memory}%
22	  }
23	  \vspace{-3mm}
24	  \caption{Model-state offloading's premise under LoRA. (a) The
25	  optimizer step is a few percent of step time for dense (Qwen3-32B)
26	  and MoE (Qwen3-30B-A3B) LoRA fine-tuning, so runtime machinery
27	  centered on it moves little. (b) With model states off the GPU,
28	  activations dominate the remaining memory peak at long context.}
29	  \label{fig:motivation}
30	\end{figure}
31	
32	\subsection{Background: LoRA Fine-Tuning on Superchips}
33	\label{sec:motivation-background}
34	
35	LoRA fine-tuning replaces each trained weight update with a pair of
36	low-rank factors: a projection $Wx$ gains a correction $BAx$ with
37	$A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d}$, $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d' \times r}$, and
38	rank $r \ll d$ (64 throughout this paper), so the trainable state is a
39	fraction of a percent of the parameters while every forward and
40	backward pass still runs the full frozen model~\cite{lora}.
41	Long-context supervised fine-tuning drives sequence lengths from tens
42	of thousands of tokens to beyond a million, and at these lengths
43	per-layer gradient checkpointing is standard: the forward saves only
44	each layer's input, and the backward recomputes a layer's forward
45	immediately before differentiating it, so at most one layer's
46	activations are live at a time. Placement will act on each type of
47	activation a layer produces (its attention projections, its
48	normalization inputs, its MLP intermediates), uniformly across layers.
49	In MoE models a router assigns each token to a few expert MLPs per
50	layer; a grouped GEMM runs all of a layer's experts in one launch and
51	returns outputs grouped by expert rather than by token.
52	
53	A Grace--Blackwell superchip couples two Blackwell GPUs, each with
54	189~GB of HBM, to one Grace CPU with 72 cores and a memory pool well
55	beyond a single GPU's HBM. Each GPU reaches the CPU's memory over its
56	own coherent NVLink-C2C link: host-to-device streams on our machine
57	achieve about 212~GB/s from the GPU's local memory socket (roughly
58	half from the far socket), well below the [8]~TB/s of the GPU's HBM.
59	The two links are independent, though both draw on the CPU memory's
60	[500]~GB/s, which caps what the two streams and the Grace cores' own
61	kernels can pull from it together. Coherence means a GPU kernel reads
62	CPU memory directly, with no staging copy and no driver round trip;
63	each GPU thereby addresses the whole CPU pool, well beyond its own
64	HBM.
65	
66	\subsection{Model-State Offloading and the Activation Bottleneck}
67	\label{sec:motivation-model-state}
68	
69	The models we target overflow GPU memory. At the large end the weights
70	alone exceed it, a 235B-parameter model holding about 470~GB in bf16
71	against 189~GB of HBM per GPU; across the rest, the weights and the
72	long-context activations together do from [N] tokens on. Part of the
73	training state must therefore live in CPU memory.
74	
75	Existing offloading systems move model states.
76	ZeRO-Offload~\cite{zero-offload} homes the optimizer states and
77	gradients in CPU memory and runs the update there;
78	ZeRO-Infinity~\cite{zero-infinity} moves the parameters as well;
79	SuperOffload~\cite{superoffload} tunes the design for superchips with
80	speculative optimizer execution overlapped with the backward pass, a
81	Grace-tuned Adam, and gradient bucketization over the interconnect.
82	The runtime machinery centers on the optimizer step, and for
83	full-parameter training this is the right center: fp32 master weights
84	and Adam moments exist for every parameter, and their update dominates
85	an offloaded step.
86	
87	LoRA voids this premise twice. First, the adapters are the only
88	trainable state, so the optimizer accounts for a few percent of step
89	time on dense (Qwen3-32B) and MoE (Qwen3-30B-A3B) models alike, and
90	overlapping it with the backward leaves end-to-end step time
91	essentially unchanged (Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-optimizer}). Second,
92	everything these systems move is parameter-proportional and static
93	once homed: the recurring traffic that remains under LoRA is the
94	rank-width adapter exchange plus, where the parameters live in CPU
95	memory, a read-only weight fetch whose bytes are fixed while the
96	step's compute grows with tokens, so as context grows the fetch
97	occupies a shrinking fraction of the step and the interconnect and the
98	Grace cores idle through the rest. What grows is the
99	token-proportional term. Activations scale linearly in tokens: one
100	bf16 activation of hidden width 5120 spans 10.7~GB at a million
101	tokens, a layer produces several such types plus MLP intermediates
102	five times wider, and every layer's saved checkpoint input accumulates
103	beneath the one live layer (Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-memory}). For
104	long-context LoRA fine-tuning the binding term is therefore the
105	activation peak, and model-state offloading reaches it only at the
106	checkpoint boundary, where whole saved tensors are offloaded or
107	recomputed~\cite{zero-infinity, superoffload}; the within-layer
108	activation types beneath that boundary, which dominate the peak, stay
109	on the GPU.
110	
111	\subsection{Streaming Kernels Fall Short for Training}
112	\label{sec:motivation-naive}
113	
114	A different use of the superchip streams operands instead of moving
115	state. An asymmetric GEMM keeps one operand in CPU memory and reads it
116	tile-by-tile over the interconnect while the multiplication proceeds:
117	the streamed operand occupies no GPU memory and needs no staging
118	buffer. The AsymGEMM inference line realizes this for
119	serving~\cite{asymgemm, directkv, c2cserve}. The regime suits the
120	link: the kernel reads the streamed operand in shared-memory-sized
121	tiles and pipelines them beneath the multiplication, so many tiles are
122	in flight at once, per-access latency is hidden, and what the stream
123	asks of the interconnect is sustained bandwidth, which each GPU's
124	private link supplies. CPU memory as operand capacity with the compute
125	staying on the GPU is exactly the shape of the activation problem, if
126	the kernels carry over to training.
127	
128	They do not carry over, though the trivial re-aim runs: a GEMM is
129	general, and the operand rule is a single clause, the large once-read
130	operand streams while the small reused one stays resident, so the
131	frozen path $Y{=}XW^\top$ streams $W$, and the adapter contractions
132	$S{=}XA^\top$ and $dA{=}dS^\top X$ stream the activation $X$ while the
133	megabyte-scale adapters stay resident; deleting the weight-reuse loop
134	looks like all that is left. It is not enough, because reuse in these
135	kernels is not a loop but three structural commitments, and LoRA's
136	dataflows break each one. First, who owns the pipeline: the kernel
137	gives its multi-buffered shared-memory pipeline to the streamed
138	operand because the streamed operand is the reused one; in the adapter
139	contractions the reused operand is the resident factor, so the memory
140	roles must invert, the stream taking a fetch-once slot at full link
141	width and the adapter taking the pipeline, a rewiring of the kernel's
142	memory hierarchy rather than a deletion. Second, where parallelism
143	comes from: the launch grid is keyed to output width, and a rank-64
144	output is 64 columns, one thread block's worth of work, so the GPU
145	serializes; parallelism must be re-extracted from the token rows by
146	partitioning the stream itself, which changes the launch geometry and
147	how partial results combine. Third, when outputs may retire: the
148	kernel retires output tiles as its reduction advances, valid because
149	its reduction axis is resident; the adapter gradient reduces over the
150	streamed axis, so nothing may retire until the whole stream has
151	passed, forcing an output-stationary dataflow, the rank-sized output
152	pinned in registers for the stream's entire lifetime, which the
153	inference kernels do not contain. Fixing any one commitment breaks the
154	other two's assumptions: what results is a rebuilt kernel, not a
155	patched one. The accounting consequence follows: with no streaming
156	kernel for these dataflows, the only fast path under offloading today
157	is staging the activation back, and the staged copy is the offloaded
158	tensor rematerializing in GPU memory at exactly the backward's peak,
159	so the peak saving offloading bought is spent at the moment it binds.
160	Streaming's memory promise is real, and for training it is so far
161	uncollectable; collecting it takes rebuilt kernels
162	(\S\ref{sec:motivation-kernels}).
163	
164	\subsection{Opportunities: Rebuilding Long-Context Activation Offloading for Superchips}
165	\label{sec:motivation-opportunities}
166	
167	The superchip supplies exactly the resources model-state offloading
168	leaves idle (\S\ref{sec:motivation-model-state}): both directions of
169	each C2C link and the Grace cores. And kernels control their own
170	dataflows: nothing in \S\ref{sec:motivation-naive}'s failure is
171	fundamental to the hardware. \emph{The ideal execution would use CPU
172	memory purely for capacity, run each operator at full rate on the
173	processor where it wins, and pay no step time for the placement.} Five
174	opportunities close the distance to that ideal.
175	
176	\subsubsection{Kernels Rebuilt for Training Dataflows}
177	\label{sec:motivation-kernels}
178	
179	The first opportunity is kernel structure, not tuning. Rebuilt for
180	training, the streaming kernels (i) invert the operand roles of
181	\S\ref{sec:motivation-naive}, the once-read activation taking the
182	fetch-once stream slot and the small resident factor taking the
183	shared-memory pipeline; (ii) accumulate token-axis reductions
184	output-stationary, the rank-sized result living in registers until the
185	stream ends; (iii) fold the routing scatter into the streamed grouped
186	GEMM's epilogue, forward and backward: a grouped GEMM returns outputs
187	in expert order, and where that output is streamed or offloaded, the
188	separate re-ordering pass first materializes an expert-ordered copy of
189	it, so the epilogue instead writes each result, scaled by its routing
190	weight, to its token-order address, and both the copy and the pass
191	disappear (the input-side gather stays a staged pass; its fused
192	variant measured about 75$\times$ slower and was rejected); and (iv)
193	instantiate transposed variants for the backward's rereads of the
194	frozen weights.
195	
196	\begin{figure}[t]
197	  \centering
198	  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/m2a-adapter-gemm-placement.pdf}%
199	  \vspace{-4mm}
200	  \caption{Adapter-GEMM placement microbenchmark: the rank-64 attention LoRA-A projection against a CPU-resident activation (Qwen3-32B shapes) across 32K--512K token rows, three executions (Resident / Staged / Streamed): per-GEMM wall time (left, log--log) and the GPU memory the execution's input operands hold (right). Both offload executions are link-bound and scale identically; Streamed holds only the 0.7\,MB adapter on GPU.}
201	  \label{fig:motivation-m2a}
202	\end{figure}
203	
204	Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m2a} measures what the rebuild collects, on
205	one adapter GEMM as the representative microbenchmark: the attention LoRA-A projection
206	$S{=}XA^\top$ at rank 64 and hidden width 5120, the activation $X$
207	CPU-resident, at 32K and 256K token rows. Three executions: Resident,
208	both operands pre-placed in HBM, the cuBLAS ceiling; Staged, $X$
209	copied to HBM and cuBLAS run on the copy; Streamed, the rebuilt kernel
210	reading $X$ in place. At 32K rows they take 0.053, 1.651, and
211	1.598~ms; at 256K rows, 0.402, 13.080, and 12.701~ms. Both off-GPU
212	executions are link-bound, sustaining the link's achieved rate (about
213	210~GB/s), because at rank 64 the arithmetic is negligible next to
214	moving $X$; Staged then moves the bytes twice, over the link and again
215	out of HBM, which is why Streamed runs about 3\% faster. The decisive
216	difference is what the execution holds: Staged holds the returned
217	activation, 0.34~GB at 32K rows and 2.69~GB at 256K, re-spent at
218	exactly the backward's peak, where Streamed holds the 0.7~MB adapter.
219	Under offloading, the one executable path paid the link and re-bought
220	the memory; the rebuilt kernel pays the same link time and keeps the
221	memory saving the offload was for. The 30$\times$ gap to Resident is
222	the residency premium, the throughput price of any off-GPU placement;
223	it argues for keeping tensors resident whenever they fit
224	(\S\ref{sec:motivation-scheduler}), not for staging.
225	
226	\begin{figure}[t]
227	  \centering
228	  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/m2b-scatter-fused.pdf}%
229	  \vspace{-4mm}
230	  \caption{Output-side scatter fusion (Qwen3-30B-A3B, streamed recipe, 128K tokens): fused epilogue scatter versus unfused grouped GEMM plus a separate scatter pass, on the forward and gate/up-gradient legs -- leg wall time (left) and the expert-order activation copies each leg holds (right); fusion eliminates the 8.6\,GB expert-ordered output copy on both legs.}
231	  \label{fig:motivation-m2b}
232	\end{figure}
233	
234	The routed-expert legs measure the scatter fusion
235	(Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m2b}): Qwen3-30B-A3B expert GEMMs under
236	the streamed recipe at 128K tokens (top-8 of 128 experts, 1.05M routed
237	rows), the fused epilogue against an unfused grouped GEMM plus
238	separate scatter pass. Fusion eliminates the expert-ordered fp32
239	output copy on both legs, 8.59~GB per leg at this length, and the
240	forward leg also runs 13\% faster (41.9 to 36.4~ms); the backward leg
241	pays 12\% (44.0 to 49.1~ms), because its streamed weight is read
242	transposed and the fused mainloop pays more for that than the folded
243	scatter saves. The fusion's claim is therefore the eliminated copy on
244	both legs, with a faster forward, and the backward's 12\% is the
245	stated price of its 8.59~GB.
246	
247	The rebuilt kernels' trade-off is that every streamed tile crosses the
248	interconnect; the GPU-bound C2C direction, idle under model-state
249	offloading (\S\ref{sec:motivation-model-state}), absorbs that traffic
250	(\S\ref{sec:motivation-c2c}). Streaming also fixes a direction, moving
251	the data to the compute; \S\ref{sec:motivation-cpu} opens the inverse
252	route. \textbf{Takeaway:} rebuilt for once-read operands and backward
253	dataflows, streaming runs at staged execution's speed with streamed
254	execution's memory: the promise \S\ref{sec:motivation-naive} called
255	uncollectable, collected.
256	
257	\subsubsection{Idle Interconnect as Activation Capacity}
258	\label{sec:motivation-c2c}
259	
260	The second opportunity spends the idle link on activations. Below the
261	checkpoint boundary, each activation type is independently offloaded,
262	leaving the GPU in the forward and returning beneath the backward's
263	compute, restaged or consumed in place by the kernels of
264	\S\ref{sec:motivation-kernels} and \S\ref{sec:motivation-cpu}, or
265	recomputed, regenerated by the layer's forward inside the backward
266	window. The per-type mix inside one layer is the composition prior
267	systems lack: they choose once per saved tensor at the checkpoint
268	boundary (\S\ref{sec:motivation-model-state}). Attention shows why the
269	mix pays: its two small normalization inputs regenerate the wide
270	normalized projections, so offloading the parents moves a fraction of
271	the bytes of the children they rebuild.
272	
273	\begin{figure}[t]
274	  \centering
275	  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/m3-composition.pdf}%
276	  \vspace{-4mm}
277	  \caption{Per-module composition: one Qwen3-32B layer at 128K tokens under recompute-all, offload-all, and the shipped composed per-type mix, split by module: peak HBM, link bytes, and module time (the composition acts in the backward; forward time is policy-independent).}
278	  \label{fig:motivation-m3}
279	\end{figure}
280	
281	Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m3} measures one full Qwen3-32B layer,
282	forward and backward, at 128K tokens under three per-type policies,
283	recompute-all (pure checkpointing), offload-all (every offloadable
284	type leaves and restages), and the composed mix the system ships, with
285	peak HBM, link bytes, and backward-window time split by module
286	(attention, MLP). In the MLP the composition does what the levers
287	promise: offload-all cuts the module's backward peak from
288	recompute-all's 44.0~GiB to 26.6, composed holds 31.5 (the 5-GiB gap
289	is a prefetch trade: gate and up staged early, their gradients kept on
290	the GPU), and composed moves 0.67$\times$ offload-all's link bytes
291	(51.3 versus 76.3~GiB) while running 11\% faster than it over the
292	backward window (1230 versus 1360~ms). In attention the win
293	moves to the wires. Composed moves 0.48$\times$ offload-all's link
294	bytes (14.6 versus 30.5~GiB), the parent-to-child ratio visible
295	directly, and holds 7.8~GiB of pinned host memory to offload-all's
296	16.9; but no policy lowers this module's GPU peak at this length,
297	because in every policy the peak instant sits inside the query-norm
298	backward, where the fp32 upcasts and their gradient chain hold about
299	six 4-GiB tensors at once: offload-all restages the two fp32 saves at
300	exactly that instant, re-spending the bytes it freed, and composed
301	rebuilds the same chain inside its recompute while its side-stream
302	staging runs beside it (36.5 versus 30.5~GiB). At this length the
303	composition's attention win is link and host bytes; its peak win lives
304	in the MLP. On time, the figure reports the backward window, where
305	the composition acts (forward time is policy-independent): composed
306	beats offload-all in both modules (4\% faster in attention, 11\% in
307	the MLP). Recompute-all is the fastest policy in this isolated
308	single-layer run, 12\% ahead of composed in attention and 77\% in the
309	MLP: with the whole GPU and an idle link, its extra FLOPs cost nothing
310	while the offload policies wait on restages. What it cannot shed is
311	residency, the 44.0~GiB MLP backward above, which is the term that
312	does not scale (\S\ref{sec:motivation-model-state}).
313	
314	The trade-off is that freed GPU memory returns as link traffic,
315	absorbed while each transfer fits inside its layer's dependency
316	window, the span the layer's compute opens between an operand's
317	production and its consumption. \textbf{Takeaway:} spent on
318	activations, the idle interconnect becomes GPU-memory headroom at no
319	step-time cost over offloading, and the per-type composition cuts the
320	bytes that conversion pays to half to two-thirds.
321	
322	\subsubsection{Idle Grace Cores as a Second Compute Engine}
323	\label{sec:motivation-cpu}
324	
325	\input{sections/cpu_scope_table}
326	
327	Streaming moves the operand to the compute; the third opportunity is
328	the inverse, moving the compute to the operand. The Grace cores idle
329	outside the few-percent optimizer step
330	(\S\ref{sec:motivation-model-state}), 72 cores against the CPU
331	memory's [500]~GB/s, and memory-bound gradient work fits them when its
332	operands already live in CPU memory. Two placements ship, both SVE
333	kernels built for Grace. The CPU adapter-gradient kernel computes $dA$
334	where the offloaded activation lies, contracting it in place and
335	depositing the fp32 result directly into the optimizer's pinned
336	buffer, so all that crosses the link is the rank-width projection
337	gradient, 34~MB at 256K rows against the 2.7~GB activation a GPU-side
338	gradient would restage. The gradient-ingestion kernel fuses the
339	bf16-to-fp32 widen into the gradient-norm reduction the optimizer
340	already performs: gradients cross the link in bf16, half the fp32
341	bytes, and one SVE pass replaces the stock two, 7.2$\times$ faster on
342	a 1-GiB gradient batch (12.1 versus 86.7~ms).
343	Table~\ref{tab:cpu-scope} scopes the CPU's role against
344	SuperOffload's: GraceAdam~\cite{superoffload} runs the fp32 update
345	loop on these cores and leaves the ingestion pass untouched, and
346	Superchip-Aware Casting~\cite{superoffload} chose to cast on the GPU
347	and transmit fp32, a conclusion that inverts once the CPU cast is
348	fused into a reduction the optimizer already requires. (A fused SwiGLU
349	elementwise kernel for the same placement is built and bit-accurate
350	but ships disabled: the device-to-host transfer it removes is fully
351	overlapped on this machine, so removing it buys no step time, a
352	negative result that sharpens the gating below.)
353	
354	\begin{figure}[t]
355	  \centering
356	  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/m4-crossover.pdf}%
357	  \vspace{-4mm}
358	  \caption{Grace-kernel placement microbenchmark: the CPU
359	  adapter-gradient deposit (MoE attention $dA$) across 64K--1M rows.
360	  Left: critical path added to a busy backward by the CPU and GPU
361	  routes; the CPU route stays $\sim$1.3\,ms while its work hides under
362	  the 64\,ms window and inverts between 512K and 1M -- the shipped
363	  $\leq$262K gate (dashed) sits conservatively inside the measured
364	  crossover. Right: serial time against stock CPU matmuls (1.8--60$\times$;
365	  the stock path collapses beyond 256K rows).}
366	  \label{fig:motivation-m4}
367	\end{figure}
368	
369	Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m4} measures the deposit at its shipped
370	site, MoE attention $dA$, across 64K, 256K, and 1M projection rows.
371	Against stock PyTorch CPU matmuls at the same 96-thread budget, the
372	kernel runs 1.8$\times$, 2.4$\times$, and 31$\times$ faster (12.3
373	versus 21.6~ms, 33.3 versus 79.8, and 137 versus 4336: the stock bf16
374	path collapses at scale). Placement, however, is not settled by serial
375	time: run in isolation, the GPU route, restage plus GPU gradient
376	kernel plus gradient transfer, is faster at every size; the shipped
377	question is what each route adds to the critical path of a backward
378	that is already using the SMs and the link. Run concurrently with such
379	a context (63.6~ms of streamed GEMMs), the CPU route adds 1.36~ms at
380	64K rows to the GPU route's 1.29, parity; 1.32~ms at 256K to the GPU's
381	5.19, four times less; and 87.8~ms at 1M to the GPU's 20.7, because
382	137~ms of serial CPU work no longer fits a 64~ms window. The crossover
383	falls between 256K and 1M rows, and the shipped policy arms the CPU
384	placement only through the 256K point (262,144 rows), the last where
385	it wins. The boundary is a time window, not a bandwidth limit: the
386	idle cores absorb CPU seconds only while the backward's dependency
387	window is open, extending the step once it closes, and row count
388	predicts the closure. \textbf{Takeaway:} with the optimizer light, the
389	Grace cores absorb gradient work, but only inside the backward's
390	dependency windows; a gradient computable on either processor, with a
391	measured crossover between them, is exactly why kernel dispatch exists
392	(\S\ref{sec:design-scheduler}).
393	
394	\subsubsection{One Placement Does Not Fit All Jobs}
395	\label{sec:motivation-scheduler}
396	
397	\begin{figure}[t]
398	  \centering
399	  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/m6-tradeoff.pdf}%
400	  \vspace{-2mm}
401	  \caption{Memory--throughput tradeoff: training throughput and peak
402	  GPU memory (allocator peak) across the configuration order (T1
403	  resident / T2 partial / T3 streamed; Qwen3-32B, batch 1) at 32K and
404	  512K tokens; the crossed marker is T1's measured out-of-memory abort
405	  at 512K.}
406	  \label{fig:motivation-m6}
407	\end{figure}
408	
409	The fourth opportunity is the choice among the first three. Every
410	placement off the GPU frees memory and costs throughput: a streamed
411	weight holds no GPU memory where a staged one holds a layer's buffer,
412	an offloaded activation type frees its bytes but pays a restage, a
413	recomputed type pays FLOPs instead, and beneath them all sits
414	\S\ref{sec:motivation-kernels}'s 30$\times$ residency premium. The
415	placements also share a wire: a configuration's weight streams,
416	activation streams, and restages all ride the same GPU-bound link, so
417	their costs add, and the configuration measurements of
418	Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m6} price them together. Overlap narrows
419	these costs but does not erase them, so configurations, each an
420	assignment of a placement to every weight and activation type, order
421	from most resident, the fastest, to fully streamed, the leanest.
422	Shorter jobs fit near-resident configurations and run fastest there;
423	only the longest need the streamed end: at 32K the most resident of
424	the three measured configurations is the fastest and holds the most
425	GPU memory (2063 versus 1524 versus 698~tok/s; 14.1 versus 11.8
426	versus 8.4~GiB; Qwen3-32B, batch 1), and at 512K the most resident
427	aborts out of memory in an attempted run, so the best feasible
428	configuration shifts to the partial one, 327 versus the streamed
429	one's 264~tok/s, a near-wall fit at 172 of the GPU's 184~GiB
430	(Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m6}). Near the capacity wall a
431	wrong pick ends in an out-of-memory abort, not a slowdown, and beyond
432	a short anchor zone where kernel behavior still shifts with length,
433	peak GPU memory is linear in token count for a fixed model and
434	configuration, so records of past runs predict whether a candidate
435	fits. Within a feasible configuration, throughput rises with batch
436	size only to a knee, [the batch where the step's kernels reach full
437	device occupancy, reached at small batch for long sequences], and is
438	flat past it, so the largest fitting batch is not worth taking past
439	the knee (\S\ref{sec:design-profiler}). The leanest configurations
440	also trade GPU memory for CPU memory, bounded in turn by its own
441	capacity, a bound the dense families reach first in recorded runs
442	(\S\ref{sec:design-scheduler}). \textbf{Takeaway:} the fastest
443	feasible configuration shifts with model and sequence length, and it
444	is predictable from records: selection must precede launch, and can.
445	
446	\subsubsection{Two GPUs, One Memory: Balancing MoE Without Moving Data}
447	\label{sec:motivation-balancer}
448	
449	\begin{figure*}[t]
450	  \centering
451	  \includegraphics[width=0.92\textwidth]{figures/ep_balance_q35122b_row3.pdf}%
452	  \vspace{-2mm}
453	  \caption{Dynamic expert load (Qwen3.5-122B routed expert GEMMs) across
454	  routing skew $z$, three executions: data-parallel (DP), static
455	  expert-parallel (EP), and the shared-list dynamic EP (ours). All three
456	  process the same routed rows against the same shared-memory pool, so
457	  aggregate activation traffic is identical by construction and no
458	  execution exchanges tokens between GPUs (no all-to-all on a
459	  superchip); per-link activation reads follow the row split of the
460	  left panel. The one traffic component that differs is weight
461	  streaming (middle): the streamed kernel holds no expert weights
462	  resident, re-reading an expert's bank once per executed row segment,
463	  so traffic counts bank \emph{reads}, not banks owned. Skew splits
464	  EP's hot experts into ever more segments -- its fixed half-set is
465	  re-streamed up to 1.8$\times$, crossing DP at $z{=}2$; DP owns every
466	  bank on both GPUs (a constant 2$\times$ floor); the dynamic cut keeps
467	  each expert's rows contiguous on one GPU and reads each bank about
468	  once, the floor, at every $z$. Left: compute imbalance -- EP's hot GPU
469	  carries up to 56\% excess routed rows while DP and ours stay
470	  balanced. Right: Expert-GEMM wall time -- the dynamic cut tracks or
471	  beats the best execution at every skew. Remaining models and the
472	  MoE-block view in the appendix.\label{fig:motivation-m5a}\label{fig:motivation-m5b}\label{fig:motivation-balancer}}
473	\end{figure*}
474	
475	The last opportunity uses the second GPU. MoE routing concentrates
476	tokens on different experts at every step, so under a static expert
477	partition the GPU holding the cold experts finishes early and idles,
478	its private link unused (Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m5a}).
479	Conventional rebalancing moves data, either the tokens, exchanged
480	all-to-all before every expert layer through collectives that stall
481	both GPUs (expert parallelism~\cite{expert-parallelism}), or the
482	expert weights, repartitioned. On a superchip neither has to move: the
483	expert weights already sit in memory both GPUs address over
484	independent links, and under the activation-offloading configurations
485	the long jobs run, the routed tokens sit there too, so what moves is
486	the work list, one shared list of expert workloads per grouped launch,
487	collective-free. We measure four executions of the expert GEMM across
488	routing skew $z$ (larger $z$ concentrates more tokens on fewer
489	experts): the static expert partition; a data-parallel split, each GPU
490	running its own tokens through every expert; and the shared list cut
491	two ways, a computed cut, both GPUs deriving the same balanced split
492	from routing counts they already hold, and a counter-raced cut, both
493	claiming work from the list's opposite ends until they meet. At
494	$z{=}1.5$ on Qwen3.5-122B the computed cut runs the expert GEMM in
495	31.2~ms against 39.0 raced, 42.8 data-parallel, and 44.6
496	expert-partitioned; the static partition pays the skew itself, the
497	data-parallel split runs every expert at half its rows and streams
498	every expert bank over both links, and the raced cut pays coherence
499	traffic on its shared counters where the computed cut's counters are
500	private. The saving carries through to the MoE block, the two GPUs
501	finish near-balanced across the skew sweep, and both GPUs stream from
502	the same CPU memory throughout, so the shared [500]~GB/s ceiling of
503	\S\ref{sec:motivation-background} is priced into the numbers
504	(Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m5b}). The gain needs skew to bind: where
505	per-expert work already saturates both GPUs under the data-parallel
506	split, sharing adds nothing, which sets the per-expert row ceiling
507	above which it is left off, and on Llama-4-Scout, where the
508	data-parallel split is as fast at every skew we sweep, it adds nothing
509	at all. \textbf{Takeaway:} on a superchip, wherever the routed tokens
510	reside in the shared memory, MoE balance is a scheduling property, not
511	a communication cost.
