\section{Background and Motivation}
\label{sec:motivation}

% Synced from agent/impls/s04-p1-dgx-02-c06/motivation_full_v2.md,
% 2026-07-26 measured rewrite: M2a/M2b/M3/M4b numbers in prose, M5b
% confirmed; M6 measured 2026-07-26 (m6-tradeoff.pdf + \S2.4.4 numbers
% filled from profiling_results/motivation/m6.json). Structure:
% definitions -> model-state offloading + voided premise -> streaming
% endorsed + carry-over test -> five opportunity units (microbench +
% trade-off + Takeaway). \motivationplot renders placeholder boxes for
% the figures still pending generation (m5a).

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \subfigure[Optimizer share of step time]{%
    \includegraphics[width=0.465\columnwidth]{figures/optimizer_timing.pdf}%
    \label{fig:motivation-optimizer}%
  }\hfill
  \subfigure[Peak-memory breakdown]{%
    \includegraphics[width=0.465\columnwidth]{figures/memory_decomposition.pdf}%
    \label{fig:motivation-memory}%
  }
  \vspace{-3mm}
  \caption{Model-state offloading's premise under LoRA. (a) The
  optimizer step is a few percent of step time for dense (Qwen3-32B)
  and MoE (Qwen3-30B-A3B) LoRA fine-tuning, so runtime machinery
  centered on it moves little. (b) With model states off the GPU,
  activations dominate the remaining memory peak at long context.}
  \label{fig:motivation}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Background: LoRA Fine-Tuning on Superchips}
\label{sec:motivation-background}

LoRA fine-tuning replaces each trained weight update with a pair of
low-rank factors: a projection $Wx$ gains a correction $BAx$ with
$A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d}$, $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d' \times r}$, and
rank $r \ll d$ (64 throughout this paper), so the trainable state is a
fraction of a percent of the parameters while every forward and
backward pass still runs the full frozen model~\cite{lora}.
Long-context supervised fine-tuning drives sequence lengths from tens
of thousands of tokens to beyond a million, and at these lengths
per-layer gradient checkpointing is standard: the forward saves only
each layer's input, and the backward recomputes a layer's forward
immediately before differentiating it, so at most one layer's
activations are live at a time. Placement will act on each type of
activation a layer produces (its attention projections, its
normalization inputs, its MLP intermediates), uniformly across layers.
In MoE models a router assigns each token to a few expert MLPs per
layer; a grouped GEMM runs all of a layer's experts in one launch and
returns outputs grouped by expert rather than by token.

A Grace--Blackwell superchip couples two Blackwell GPUs, each with
189~GB of HBM, to one Grace CPU with 72 cores and a memory pool well
beyond a single GPU's HBM. Each GPU reaches the CPU's memory over its
own coherent NVLink-C2C link: host-to-device streams on our machine
achieve about 212~GB/s from the GPU's local memory socket (roughly
half from the far socket), well below the [8]~TB/s of the GPU's HBM.
The two links are independent, though both draw on the CPU memory's
[500]~GB/s, which caps what the two streams and the Grace cores' own
kernels can pull from it together. Coherence means a GPU kernel reads
CPU memory directly, with no staging copy and no driver round trip;
each GPU thereby addresses the whole CPU pool, well beyond its own
HBM.

\subsection{Model-State Offloading and the Activation Bottleneck}
\label{sec:motivation-model-state}

The models we target overflow GPU memory. At the large end the weights
alone exceed it, a 235B-parameter model holding about 470~GB in bf16
against 189~GB of HBM per GPU; across the rest, the weights and the
long-context activations together do from [N] tokens on. Part of the
training state must therefore live in CPU memory.

Existing offloading systems move model states.
ZeRO-Offload~\cite{zero-offload} homes the optimizer states and
gradients in CPU memory and runs the update there;
ZeRO-Infinity~\cite{zero-infinity} moves the parameters as well;
SuperOffload~\cite{superoffload} tunes the design for superchips with
speculative optimizer execution overlapped with the backward pass, a
Grace-tuned Adam, and gradient bucketization over the interconnect.
The runtime machinery centers on the optimizer step, and for
full-parameter training this is the right center: fp32 master weights
and Adam moments exist for every parameter, and their update dominates
an offloaded step.

LoRA voids this premise twice. First, the adapters are the only
trainable state, so the optimizer accounts for a few percent of step
time on dense (Qwen3-32B) and MoE (Qwen3-30B-A3B) models alike, and
overlapping it with the backward leaves end-to-end step time
essentially unchanged (Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-optimizer}). Second,
everything these systems move is parameter-proportional and static
once homed: the recurring traffic that remains under LoRA is the
rank-width adapter exchange plus, where the parameters live in CPU
memory, a read-only weight fetch whose bytes are fixed while the
step's compute grows with tokens, so as context grows the fetch
occupies a shrinking fraction of the step and the interconnect and the
Grace cores idle through the rest. What grows is the
token-proportional term. Activations scale linearly in tokens: one
bf16 activation of hidden width 5120 spans 10.7~GB at a million
tokens, a layer produces several such types plus MLP intermediates
five times wider, and every layer's saved checkpoint input accumulates
beneath the one live layer (Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-memory}). For
long-context LoRA fine-tuning the binding term is therefore the
activation peak, and model-state offloading reaches it only at the
checkpoint boundary, where whole saved tensors are offloaded or
recomputed~\cite{zero-infinity, superoffload}; the within-layer
activation types beneath that boundary, which dominate the peak, stay
on the GPU.

\subsection{Streaming Kernels Fall Short for Training}
\label{sec:motivation-naive}

A different use of the superchip streams operands instead of moving
state. An asymmetric GEMM keeps one operand in CPU memory and reads it
tile-by-tile over the interconnect while the multiplication proceeds:
the streamed operand occupies no GPU memory and needs no staging
buffer. The AsymGEMM inference line realizes this for
serving~\cite{asymgemm, directkv, c2cserve}. The regime suits the
link: the kernel reads the streamed operand in shared-memory-sized
tiles and pipelines them beneath the multiplication, so many tiles are
in flight at once, per-access latency is hidden, and what the stream
asks of the interconnect is sustained bandwidth, which each GPU's
private link supplies. CPU memory as operand capacity with the compute
staying on the GPU is exactly the shape of the activation problem, if
the kernels carry over to training.

They do not carry over, though the trivial re-aim runs: a GEMM is
general, and the operand rule is a single clause, the large once-read
operand streams while the small reused one stays resident, so the
frozen path $Y{=}XW^\top$ streams $W$, and the adapter contractions
$S{=}XA^\top$ and $dA{=}dS^\top X$ stream the activation $X$ while the
megabyte-scale adapters stay resident; deleting the weight-reuse loop
looks like all that is left. It is not enough, because reuse in these
kernels is not a loop but three structural commitments, and LoRA's
dataflows break each one. First, who owns the pipeline: the kernel
gives its multi-buffered shared-memory pipeline to the streamed
operand because the streamed operand is the reused one; in the adapter
contractions the reused operand is the resident factor, so the memory
roles must invert, the stream taking a fetch-once slot at full link
width and the adapter taking the pipeline, a rewiring of the kernel's
memory hierarchy rather than a deletion. Second, where parallelism
comes from: the launch grid is keyed to output width, and a rank-64
output is 64 columns, one thread block's worth of work, so the GPU
serializes; parallelism must be re-extracted from the token rows by
partitioning the stream itself, which changes the launch geometry and
how partial results combine. Third, when outputs may retire: the
kernel retires output tiles as its reduction advances, valid because
its reduction axis is resident; the adapter gradient reduces over the
streamed axis, so nothing may retire until the whole stream has
passed, forcing an output-stationary dataflow, the rank-sized output
pinned in registers for the stream's entire lifetime, which the
inference kernels do not contain. Fixing any one commitment breaks the
other two's assumptions: what results is a rebuilt kernel, not a
patched one. The accounting consequence follows: with no streaming
kernel for these dataflows, the only fast path under offloading today
is staging the activation back, and the staged copy is the offloaded
tensor rematerializing in GPU memory at exactly the backward's peak,
so the peak saving offloading bought is spent at the moment it binds.
Streaming's memory promise is real, and for training it is so far
uncollectable; collecting it takes rebuilt kernels
(\S\ref{sec:motivation-kernels}).

\subsection{Opportunities: Rebuilding Long-Context Activation Offloading for Superchips}
\label{sec:motivation-opportunities}

The superchip supplies exactly the resources model-state offloading
leaves idle (\S\ref{sec:motivation-model-state}): both directions of
each C2C link and the Grace cores. And kernels control their own
dataflows: nothing in \S\ref{sec:motivation-naive}'s failure is
fundamental to the hardware. \emph{The ideal execution would use CPU
memory purely for capacity, run each operator at full rate on the
processor where it wins, and pay no step time for the placement.} Five
opportunities close the distance to that ideal.

\subsubsection{Kernels Rebuilt for Training Dataflows}
\label{sec:motivation-kernels}

The first opportunity is kernel structure, not tuning. Rebuilt for
training, the streaming kernels (i) invert the operand roles of
\S\ref{sec:motivation-naive}, the once-read activation taking the
fetch-once stream slot and the small resident factor taking the
shared-memory pipeline; (ii) accumulate token-axis reductions
output-stationary, the rank-sized result living in registers until the
stream ends; (iii) fold the routing scatter into the streamed grouped
GEMM's epilogue, forward and backward: a grouped GEMM returns outputs
in expert order, and where that output is streamed or offloaded, the
separate re-ordering pass first materializes an expert-ordered copy of
it, so the epilogue instead writes each result, scaled by its routing
weight, to its token-order address, and both the copy and the pass
disappear (the input-side gather stays a staged pass; its fused
variant measured about 75$\times$ slower and was rejected); and (iv)
instantiate transposed variants for the backward's rereads of the
frozen weights.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/m2a-adapter-gemm-placement.pdf}%
  \vspace{-4mm}
  \caption{Adapter-GEMM placement microbenchmark: the rank-64 attention LoRA-A projection against a CPU-resident activation (Qwen3-32B shapes) across 32K--512K token rows, three executions (Resident / Staged / Streamed): per-GEMM wall time (left, log--log) and the GPU memory the execution's input operands hold (right). Both offload executions are link-bound and scale identically; Streamed holds only the 0.7\,MB adapter on GPU.}
  \label{fig:motivation-m2a}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m2a} measures what the rebuild collects, on
one adapter GEMM as the representative microbenchmark: the attention LoRA-A projection
$S{=}XA^\top$ at rank 64 and hidden width 5120, the activation $X$
CPU-resident, at 32K and 256K token rows. Three executions: Resident,
both operands pre-placed in HBM, the cuBLAS ceiling; Staged, $X$
copied to HBM and cuBLAS run on the copy; Streamed, the rebuilt kernel
reading $X$ in place. At 32K rows they take 0.053, 1.651, and
1.598~ms; at 256K rows, 0.402, 13.080, and 12.701~ms. Both off-GPU
executions are link-bound, sustaining the link's achieved rate (about
210~GB/s), because at rank 64 the arithmetic is negligible next to
moving $X$; Staged then moves the bytes twice, over the link and again
out of HBM, which is why Streamed runs about 3\% faster. The decisive
difference is what the execution holds: Staged holds the returned
activation, 0.34~GB at 32K rows and 2.69~GB at 256K, re-spent at
exactly the backward's peak, where Streamed holds the 0.7~MB adapter.
Under offloading, the one executable path paid the link and re-bought
the memory; the rebuilt kernel pays the same link time and keeps the
memory saving the offload was for. The 30$\times$ gap to Resident is
the residency premium, the throughput price of any off-GPU placement;
it argues for keeping tensors resident whenever they fit
(\S\ref{sec:motivation-scheduler}), not for staging.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/m2b-scatter-fused.pdf}%
  \vspace{-4mm}
  \caption{Output-side scatter fusion (Qwen3-30B-A3B, streamed recipe, 128K tokens): fused epilogue scatter versus unfused grouped GEMM plus a separate scatter pass, on the forward and gate/up-gradient legs -- leg wall time (left) and the expert-order activation copies each leg holds (right); fusion eliminates the 8.6\,GB expert-ordered output copy on both legs.}
  \label{fig:motivation-m2b}
\end{figure}

The routed-expert legs measure the scatter fusion
(Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m2b}): Qwen3-30B-A3B expert GEMMs under
the streamed recipe at 128K tokens (top-8 of 128 experts, 1.05M routed
rows), the fused epilogue against an unfused grouped GEMM plus
separate scatter pass. Fusion eliminates the expert-ordered fp32
output copy on both legs, 8.59~GB per leg at this length, and the
forward leg also runs 13\% faster (41.9 to 36.4~ms); the backward leg
pays 12\% (44.0 to 49.1~ms), because its streamed weight is read
transposed and the fused mainloop pays more for that than the folded
scatter saves. The fusion's claim is therefore the eliminated copy on
both legs, with a faster forward, and the backward's 12\% is the
stated price of its 8.59~GB.

The rebuilt kernels' trade-off is that every streamed tile crosses the
interconnect; the GPU-bound C2C direction, idle under model-state
offloading (\S\ref{sec:motivation-model-state}), absorbs that traffic
(\S\ref{sec:motivation-c2c}). Streaming also fixes a direction, moving
the data to the compute; \S\ref{sec:motivation-cpu} opens the inverse
route. \textbf{Takeaway:} rebuilt for once-read operands and backward
dataflows, streaming runs at staged execution's speed with streamed
execution's memory: the promise \S\ref{sec:motivation-naive} called
uncollectable, collected.

\subsubsection{Idle Interconnect as Activation Capacity}
\label{sec:motivation-c2c}

The second opportunity spends the idle link on activations. Below the
checkpoint boundary, each activation type is independently offloaded,
leaving the GPU in the forward and returning beneath the backward's
compute, restaged or consumed in place by the kernels of
\S\ref{sec:motivation-kernels} and \S\ref{sec:motivation-cpu}, or
recomputed, regenerated by the layer's forward inside the backward
window. The per-type mix inside one layer is the composition prior
systems lack: they choose once per saved tensor at the checkpoint
boundary (\S\ref{sec:motivation-model-state}). Attention shows why the
mix pays: its two small normalization inputs regenerate the wide
normalized projections, so offloading the parents moves a fraction of
the bytes of the children they rebuild.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/m3-composition.pdf}%
  \vspace{-4mm}
  \caption{Per-module composition: one Qwen3-32B layer at 128K tokens under recompute-all, offload-all, and the shipped composed per-type mix, split by module: peak HBM, link bytes, and module time (the composition acts in the backward; forward time is policy-independent).}
  \label{fig:motivation-m3}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m3} measures one full Qwen3-32B layer,
forward and backward, at 128K tokens under three per-type policies,
recompute-all (pure checkpointing), offload-all (every offloadable
type leaves and restages), and the composed mix the system ships, with
peak HBM, link bytes, and backward-window time split by module
(attention, MLP). In the MLP the composition does what the levers
promise: offload-all cuts the module's backward peak from
recompute-all's 44.0~GiB to 26.6, composed holds 31.5 (the 5-GiB gap
is a prefetch trade: gate and up staged early, their gradients kept on
the GPU), and composed moves 0.67$\times$ offload-all's link bytes
(51.3 versus 76.3~GiB) while running 11\% faster than it over the
backward window (1230 versus 1360~ms). In attention the win
moves to the wires. Composed moves 0.48$\times$ offload-all's link
bytes (14.6 versus 30.5~GiB), the parent-to-child ratio visible
directly, and holds 7.8~GiB of pinned host memory to offload-all's
16.9; but no policy lowers this module's GPU peak at this length,
because in every policy the peak instant sits inside the query-norm
backward, where the fp32 upcasts and their gradient chain hold about
six 4-GiB tensors at once: offload-all restages the two fp32 saves at
exactly that instant, re-spending the bytes it freed, and composed
rebuilds the same chain inside its recompute while its side-stream
staging runs beside it (36.5 versus 30.5~GiB). At this length the
composition's attention win is link and host bytes; its peak win lives
in the MLP. On time, the figure reports the backward window, where
the composition acts (forward time is policy-independent): composed
beats offload-all in both modules (4\% faster in attention, 11\% in
the MLP). Recompute-all is the fastest policy in this isolated
single-layer run, 12\% ahead of composed in attention and 77\% in the
MLP: with the whole GPU and an idle link, its extra FLOPs cost nothing
while the offload policies wait on restages. What it cannot shed is
residency, the 44.0~GiB MLP backward above, which is the term that
does not scale (\S\ref{sec:motivation-model-state}).

The trade-off is that freed GPU memory returns as link traffic,
absorbed while each transfer fits inside its layer's dependency
window, the span the layer's compute opens between an operand's
production and its consumption. \textbf{Takeaway:} spent on
activations, the idle interconnect becomes GPU-memory headroom at no
step-time cost over offloading, and the per-type composition cuts the
bytes that conversion pays to half to two-thirds.

\subsubsection{Idle Grace Cores as a Second Compute Engine}
\label{sec:motivation-cpu}

\input{sections/cpu_scope_table}

Streaming moves the operand to the compute; the third opportunity is
the inverse, moving the compute to the operand. The Grace cores idle
outside the few-percent optimizer step
(\S\ref{sec:motivation-model-state}), 72 cores against the CPU
memory's [500]~GB/s, and memory-bound gradient work fits them when its
operands already live in CPU memory. Two placements ship, both SVE
kernels built for Grace. The CPU adapter-gradient kernel computes $dA$
where the offloaded activation lies, contracting it in place and
depositing the fp32 result directly into the optimizer's pinned
buffer, so all that crosses the link is the rank-width projection
gradient, 34~MB at 256K rows against the 2.7~GB activation a GPU-side
gradient would restage. The gradient-ingestion kernel fuses the
bf16-to-fp32 widen into the gradient-norm reduction the optimizer
already performs: gradients cross the link in bf16, half the fp32
bytes, and one SVE pass replaces the stock two, 7.2$\times$ faster on
a 1-GiB gradient batch (12.1 versus 86.7~ms).
Table~\ref{tab:cpu-scope} scopes the CPU's role against
SuperOffload's: GraceAdam~\cite{superoffload} runs the fp32 update
loop on these cores and leaves the ingestion pass untouched, and
Superchip-Aware Casting~\cite{superoffload} chose to cast on the GPU
and transmit fp32, a conclusion that inverts once the CPU cast is
fused into a reduction the optimizer already requires. (A fused SwiGLU
elementwise kernel for the same placement is built and bit-accurate
but ships disabled: the device-to-host transfer it removes is fully
overlapped on this machine, so removing it buys no step time, a
negative result that sharpens the gating below.)

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/m4-crossover.pdf}%
  \vspace{-4mm}
  \caption{Grace-kernel placement microbenchmark: the CPU
  adapter-gradient deposit (MoE attention $dA$) across 64K--1M rows.
  Left: critical path added to a busy backward by the CPU and GPU
  routes; the CPU route stays $\sim$1.3\,ms while its work hides under
  the 64\,ms window and inverts between 512K and 1M -- the shipped
  $\leq$262K gate (dashed) sits conservatively inside the measured
  crossover. Right: serial time against stock CPU matmuls (1.8--60$\times$;
  the stock path collapses beyond 256K rows).}
  \label{fig:motivation-m4}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m4} measures the deposit at its shipped
site, MoE attention $dA$, across 64K, 256K, and 1M projection rows.
Against stock PyTorch CPU matmuls at the same 96-thread budget, the
kernel runs 1.8$\times$, 2.4$\times$, and 31$\times$ faster (12.3
versus 21.6~ms, 33.3 versus 79.8, and 137 versus 4336: the stock bf16
path collapses at scale). Placement, however, is not settled by serial
time: run in isolation, the GPU route, restage plus GPU gradient
kernel plus gradient transfer, is faster at every size; the shipped
question is what each route adds to the critical path of a backward
that is already using the SMs and the link. Run concurrently with such
a context (63.6~ms of streamed GEMMs), the CPU route adds 1.36~ms at
64K rows to the GPU route's 1.29, parity; 1.32~ms at 256K to the GPU's
5.19, four times less; and 87.8~ms at 1M to the GPU's 20.7, because
137~ms of serial CPU work no longer fits a 64~ms window. The crossover
falls between 256K and 1M rows, and the shipped policy arms the CPU
placement only through the 256K point (262,144 rows), the last where
it wins. The boundary is a time window, not a bandwidth limit: the
idle cores absorb CPU seconds only while the backward's dependency
window is open, extending the step once it closes, and row count
predicts the closure. \textbf{Takeaway:} with the optimizer light, the
Grace cores absorb gradient work, but only inside the backward's
dependency windows; a gradient computable on either processor, with a
measured crossover between them, is exactly why kernel dispatch exists
(\S\ref{sec:design-scheduler}).

\subsubsection{One Placement Does Not Fit All Jobs}
\label{sec:motivation-scheduler}

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/m6-tradeoff.pdf}%
  \vspace{-2mm}
  \caption{Memory--throughput tradeoff: training throughput and peak
  GPU memory (allocator peak) across the configuration order (T1
  resident / T2 partial / T3 streamed; Qwen3-32B, batch 1) at 32K and
  512K tokens; the crossed marker is T1's measured out-of-memory abort
  at 512K.}
  \label{fig:motivation-m6}
\end{figure}

The fourth opportunity is the choice among the first three. Every
placement off the GPU frees memory and costs throughput: a streamed
weight holds no GPU memory where a staged one holds a layer's buffer,
an offloaded activation type frees its bytes but pays a restage, a
recomputed type pays FLOPs instead, and beneath them all sits
\S\ref{sec:motivation-kernels}'s 30$\times$ residency premium. The
placements also share a wire: a configuration's weight streams,
activation streams, and restages all ride the same GPU-bound link, so
their costs add, and the configuration measurements of
Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m6} price them together. Overlap narrows
these costs but does not erase them, so configurations, each an
assignment of a placement to every weight and activation type, order
from most resident, the fastest, to fully streamed, the leanest.
Shorter jobs fit near-resident configurations and run fastest there;
only the longest need the streamed end: at 32K the most resident of
the three measured configurations is the fastest and holds the most
GPU memory (2063 versus 1524 versus 698~tok/s; 14.1 versus 11.8
versus 8.4~GiB; Qwen3-32B, batch 1), and at 512K the most resident
aborts out of memory in an attempted run, so the best feasible
configuration shifts to the partial one, 327 versus the streamed
one's 264~tok/s, a near-wall fit at 172 of the GPU's 184~GiB
(Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m6}). Near the capacity wall a
wrong pick ends in an out-of-memory abort, not a slowdown, and beyond
a short anchor zone where kernel behavior still shifts with length,
peak GPU memory is linear in token count for a fixed model and
configuration, so records of past runs predict whether a candidate
fits. Within a feasible configuration, throughput rises with batch
size only to a knee, [the batch where the step's kernels reach full
device occupancy, reached at small batch for long sequences], and is
flat past it, so the largest fitting batch is not worth taking past
the knee (\S\ref{sec:design-profiler}). The leanest configurations
also trade GPU memory for CPU memory, bounded in turn by its own
capacity, a bound the dense families reach first in recorded runs
(\S\ref{sec:design-scheduler}). \textbf{Takeaway:} the fastest
feasible configuration shifts with model and sequence length, and it
is predictable from records: selection must precede launch, and can.

\subsubsection{Two GPUs, One Memory: Balancing MoE Without Moving Data}
\label{sec:motivation-balancer}

\begin{figure*}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.92\textwidth]{figures/ep_balance_q35122b_row3.pdf}%
  \vspace{-2mm}
  \caption{Dynamic expert load (Qwen3.5-122B routed expert GEMMs) across
  routing skew $z$, three executions: data-parallel (DP), static
  expert-parallel (EP), and the shared-list dynamic EP (ours). All three
  process the same routed rows against the same shared-memory pool, so
  aggregate activation traffic is identical by construction and no
  execution exchanges tokens between GPUs (no all-to-all on a
  superchip); per-link activation reads follow the row split of the
  left panel. The one traffic component that differs is weight
  streaming (middle): the streamed kernel holds no expert weights
  resident, re-reading an expert's bank once per executed row segment,
  so traffic counts bank \emph{reads}, not banks owned. Skew splits
  EP's hot experts into ever more segments -- its fixed half-set is
  re-streamed up to 1.8$\times$, crossing DP at $z{=}2$; DP owns every
  bank on both GPUs (a constant 2$\times$ floor); the dynamic cut keeps
  each expert's rows contiguous on one GPU and reads each bank about
  once, the floor, at every $z$. Left: compute imbalance -- EP's hot GPU
  carries up to 56\% excess routed rows while DP and ours stay
  balanced. Right: Expert-GEMM wall time -- the dynamic cut tracks or
  beats the best execution at every skew. Remaining models and the
  MoE-block view in the appendix.\label{fig:motivation-m5a}\label{fig:motivation-m5b}\label{fig:motivation-balancer}}
\end{figure*}

The last opportunity uses the second GPU. MoE routing concentrates
tokens on different experts at every step, so under a static expert
partition the GPU holding the cold experts finishes early and idles,
its private link unused (Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m5a}).
Conventional rebalancing moves data, either the tokens, exchanged
all-to-all before every expert layer through collectives that stall
both GPUs (expert parallelism~\cite{expert-parallelism}), or the
expert weights, repartitioned. On a superchip neither has to move: the
expert weights already sit in memory both GPUs address over
independent links, and under the activation-offloading configurations
the long jobs run, the routed tokens sit there too, so what moves is
the work list, one shared list of expert workloads per grouped launch,
collective-free. We measure four executions of the expert GEMM across
routing skew $z$ (larger $z$ concentrates more tokens on fewer
experts): the static expert partition; a data-parallel split, each GPU
running its own tokens through every expert; and the shared list cut
two ways, a computed cut, both GPUs deriving the same balanced split
from routing counts they already hold, and a counter-raced cut, both
claiming work from the list's opposite ends until they meet. At
$z{=}1.5$ on Qwen3.5-122B the computed cut runs the expert GEMM in
31.2~ms against 39.0 raced, 42.8 data-parallel, and 44.6
expert-partitioned; the static partition pays the skew itself, the
data-parallel split runs every expert at half its rows and streams
every expert bank over both links, and the raced cut pays coherence
traffic on its shared counters where the computed cut's counters are
private. The saving carries through to the MoE block, the two GPUs
finish near-balanced across the skew sweep, and both GPUs stream from
the same CPU memory throughout, so the shared [500]~GB/s ceiling of
\S\ref{sec:motivation-background} is priced into the numbers
(Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m5b}). The gain needs skew to bind: where
per-expert work already saturates both GPUs under the data-parallel
split, sharing adds nothing, which sets the per-expert row ceiling
above which it is left off, and on Llama-4-Scout, where the
data-parallel split is as fast at every skew we sweep, it adds nothing
at all. \textbf{Takeaway:} on a superchip, wherever the routed tokens
reside in the shared memory, MoE balance is a scheduling property, not
a communication cost.

28	
29	\subsection{System Overview}
30	\label{sec:design-overview}
31	
32	AsymLoRA is a fine-tuning system for Grace--Blackwell superchips, which
33	couple two Blackwell GPUs to a Grace CPU over the coherent NVLink-C2C
34	interconnect, so that both GPUs read the CPU's memory directly. It
35	targets long-context LoRA fine-tuning of large language models, dense
36	and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) alike, at sequence lengths from tens of thousands of tokens to beyond a million, where model weights and long-context activations together exceed GPU memory (from [N] tokens on; at the largest models the weights alone do).
37	
38	AsymLoRA therefore trains with the base weights homed in CPU memory,
39	as prior offload systems do~\cite{zero-infinity, superoffload}, and with per-layer gradient checkpointing enabled: the
40	forward saves only each layer's input, and the backward recomputes a
41	layer's forward before differentiating it, so at most one layer's
42	activations are live at a time. Under a memory budget, AsymLoRA
43	determines where each of these tensors resides across a run and how
44	each reaches its consumer. AsymLoRA introduces no approximations:
45	training computes the same optimization step as standard LoRA fine-tuning, up to floating-point reduction order [and device rounding].
46	
47	Figure~\ref{fig:design-overview} shows the four modules: (1)--(2) are
48	fixed before launch, the kernel portfolio and the configuration;
49	(3)--(4) act during the step. (1) The training kernels
50	(\S\ref{sec:design-kernels}) run GEMMs that stream CPU-resident
51	operands over the interconnect and CPU kernels that consume them in
52	place. (2) The Profiler (\S\ref{sec:design-profiler}) searches
53	measured past runs for the configuration and batch size that maximize
54	throughput under the user's model, maximum sequence length, and memory
55	budget. (3) The Dispatcher (\S\ref{sec:design-scheduler}) enacts the
56	configuration's placements each step and routes every operator to the
57	kernel where its operands sit. (4) The Expert Balancer
58	(\S\ref{sec:design-balancer}) shares one routed-expert work list
59	between both GPUs through the shared CPU memory, absorbing routing
60	skew without moving weights.
61	
62	\subsection{Training Kernels for CPU-Resident Tensors}
63	\label{sec:design-kernels}
64	
65	Our kernels stream a CPU-resident operand tile-by-tile over the
66	interconnect during the GEMM, holding no copy in GPU memory, the
67	streaming scheme of the AsymGEMM inference library~\cite{asymgemm}.
68	Training keeps the frozen-weight stream and adds a second streamed role, the once-read activation, together with the backward's token-axis reductions and transposed rereads (\S\ref{sec:motivation-naive}, \S\ref{sec:motivation-kernels}); the kernels below serve these dataflows.
69	
70	\paragraph{AsymLoRA Adapter Kernels.}
71	The adapter path has three kernels. (1) The forward-projection kernel
72	computes the low-rank projections on the GPU, directly against
73	CPU-resident activations. The once-read activation takes the
74	fetch-once slot in shared memory while the small resident factor is
75	pipelined. This arrangement inverts the inference kernels, whose
76	reused weight is the streamed operand. Its launch grid is partitioned
77	over row segments rather than experts: at rank 64, an
78	expert-partitioned grid would collapse to one thread block per expert.
79	(2) The GPU adapter-gradient kernel streams the activation as one
80	operand of the weight-gradient contraction. Because that contraction
81	reduces over the token axis, no output can retire until the stream has
82	passed, so the kernel holds its rank-sized accumulators in registers
83	across the entire segment and writes them once. (3) The CPU
84	adapter-gradient kernel computes the same gradient on the Grace cores
85	instead, writing fp32 results directly into the optimizer's pinned
86	buffer, so that only the rank-width projection gradient, not the activation, crosses the link. Whether kernel (2) or (3) computes an operator's
87	adapter gradient is a dispatch decision, deferred to
88	\S\ref{sec:design-scheduler}.
89	
90	\paragraph{Scatter-Fused Asymmetric Grouped GEMMs for Routed Experts.}
91	A grouped GEMM computes an MoE layer's experts in a single launch but
92	returns each expert's outputs in expert order, so a separate pass must
93	scatter them back to token order; when its output is streamed or offloaded, that pass materializes an expert-ordered copy of it first. Our kernels
94	fold the token-order scatter into the epilogue of the streamed grouped
95	GEMM, forward and backward (\S\ref{sec:motivation-kernels}): the
96	epilogue scatters each result while the mainloop is still streaming
97	weight tiles across the interconnect. (1) The forward kernel
98	multiplies each expert's partial results by their routing weights and
99	writes them straight to token-order addresses, so the output leaves
100	the GEMM already in token order, with no separate pass and no permuted
101	copy. (2) The backward kernel does the same for the gate and up
102	projections' input gradients. Both stream weights and scatter results
103	within one launch. The fusion covers the output side only; the
104	expert-order input gather remains a separate staged pass
105	(\S\ref{sec:motivation-kernels}). Under configurations that stream the
106	routed activations, the Dispatcher (\S\ref{sec:design-scheduler}) uses
107	these kernels, chosen for the expert-ordered output copy they
108	eliminate (\S\ref{sec:motivation-kernels}); where the activations stay
109	GPU-resident, the scatter is a cheap on-GPU pass and the unfused
110	grouped GEMM is used instead.
111	
112	\paragraph{CPU Kernels for Host-Resident Data.}
113	Memory-bound gradient work whose operands already reside in CPU memory
114	runs on the Grace cores; computing it on the GPU would cross the link
115	twice, to fetch the operands and return the result. We compute it in
116	kernels written for the length-agnostic vector model of Arm's Scalable
117	Vector Extension (SVE), operating on the bf16 operands in place
118	(\S\ref{sec:motivation-cpu}). Two such kernels ship. (1) The CPU
119	adapter-gradient kernel is kernel (3) of the adapter path above. (2)
120	The gradient-ingestion kernel converts each incoming gradient from
121	bf16 to fp32 and fuses this conversion with the gradient-norm
122	reduction the optimizer already performs, so the gradient is read once
123	rather than twice, 7.2$\times$ faster than the stock two-pass path
124	(\S\ref{sec:motivation-cpu}). The backward emits gradients in bf16, so
125	transferring them in bf16 rather than fp32 is exact, and the
126	conversion introduces no additional pass over memory.
127	
128	Together these form a portfolio of three execution targets: streamed
129	AsymLoRA GEMMs, resident cuBLAS GEMMs, and Grace CPU kernels. The
130	streamed family covers the frozen path in both directions: the
131	base-weight GEMMs ship transposed instantiations for the backward's
132	input gradients, reading the same CPU-resident weight under the
133	transposed access pattern and degrading to a staged GEMM where the
134	transposed tiling constraints do not hold. Which target executes
135	which operator, and under which placement, is fixed by the
136	configuration (\S\ref{sec:design-profiler}) and its dispatch
137	(\S\ref{sec:design-scheduler}).
138	
139	\subsection{Offline Profiling for Configuration Selection}
140	\label{sec:design-profiler}
141	
142	A configuration assigns every weight a transport, staged or streamed, and every activation type (\S\ref{sec:motivation-background}) a placement: kept in GPU memory, offloaded to CPU memory, or recomputed (transport in \S\ref{sec:design-scheduler}). From measured past runs
143	alone, the Profiler answers a job request (model, maximum sequence
144	length, memory budget) with the configuration and batch size predicted
145	to maximize throughput within the capacity the budget leaves free; no profiling sweep precedes launch; the one exception, near the capacity wall, is a single guarded feasibility probe. A model family enters the record store once, through an anchor sweep of [k] short runs per configuration, at [two] sequence lengths beyond the anchor zone from which the linear fits extrapolate plus [j] in-zone lengths that seed the verbatim tables; every later run appends its manifest and measured peaks to the store (\S\ref{sec:design-impl}).
146	
147	\paragraph{Peak-Memory Prediction.}
148	For every model and configuration the Profiler maintains a linear model of peak GPU memory in the token count (\S\ref{sec:motivation-scheduler}), fitted to past runs, alongside CPU-side peaks recorded the same way [verify: linear fit versus anchor scaling in the shipped checker]. A configuration
149	that offloads more to CPU memory uses less GPU memory but more CPU
150	memory, so it can run out of either, and the Profiler checks both. The
151	user's budget is a reservation, subtracted from each physical capacity
152	before the fits are checked, so headroom for anything else on the
153	machine is expressed in the check itself. Where linear fits are
154	invalid (the short-sequence anchor zone, where kernels change
155	behavior), measured tables are used verbatim. Near the capacity wall
156	the Profiler does not trust either: any decision within a fixed band
157	of the limit is flagged, and the emitted configuration carries the exact probe command that validates it with a short run, [a few] steps at the job's maximum sequence length, at the emitted batch and one below.
158	% (Figure F5: predicted versus measured peak GPU memory across sequence
159	% lengths for each configuration of one model: the linear fits, the
160	% anchor zone, and the probe band near the wall.)
161	
162	\paragraph{Configuration Search.}
163	The configurations form a fixed ladder per model family, each the previous with one more activation type moved off the GPU, so residency orders them totally; more residency is faster, a property the measurements confirm for every family we ship
164	(\S\ref{sec:motivation-scheduler}, Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m6}).
165	The search therefore needs no runtime timing; the Profiler considers
166	configurations from most to least resident and takes the first that
167	fits. It then chooses the largest batch that passes both capacity
168	checks; where a measured throughput knee exists
169	(\S\ref{sec:motivation-scheduler}, Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m6}),
170	the batch is capped there, because larger batches no longer pay; in recorded runs the knee falls below every feasible configuration's batch ceiling, so the cap forfeits nothing a leaner configuration could reclaim [verify against M6]. Every
171	change to the fitted constants is gated by self-tests over the
172	prediction properties and by replay of all recorded decisions, so a change that would have altered a past decision is caught before it can misconfigure a run.
173	
174	\subsection{Runtime Placement and Kernel Dispatch}
175	\label{sec:design-scheduler}
176	
177	The Dispatcher executes each training step under the configuration the
178	Profiler selected (\S\ref{sec:design-profiler}), reading only the
179	runtime state: free GPU memory and per-operator shapes. It enacts each
180	placement through staging, streaming, offloading, or recomputation,
181	and routes each operator to the kernel of the device holding its
182	operands. Every placement off the GPU trades throughput for memory:
183	the freed memory comes back as transfers, restages, or recomputation
184	(\S\ref{sec:motivation-scheduler}). The Dispatcher narrows this cost by
185	overlapping the added work with the dependency windows the backward
186	pass opens; the cost that remains is why more resident configurations
187	stay faster and why the Profiler selects the most resident one that
188	fits (\S\ref{sec:design-profiler})
189	(Figure~\ref{fig:design-overview}, center).
190	
191	\paragraph{Enacting the Placement.}
192	Weights and activations are placed independently.
193	
194	\begin{itemize}
195	\item \textbf{Weights} are staged or streamed
196	(\S\ref{sec:design-kernels}). Staging copies a weight into GPU memory
197	for its GEMM and releases it after, holding at most one layer's
198	weights at once. Streaming leaves it in CPU memory and reads it
199	tile-by-tile during the GEMM, holding no copy in GPU memory but moving
200	every tile across the interconnect.
201	
202	\item \textbf{Activations} are recomputed by default: the forward
203	saves only each layer's input, and the backward regenerates the rest
204	(\S\ref{sec:design-overview}). Within that recompute, each type is kept resident in GPU memory once produced or left to recompute, both consumed by the same layer's backward; offloaded types leave during the forward and restage beneath the backward. Offloaded activations ride pinned buffers with completion events and a guarded prefetch stream: a restage issues
205	only when free GPU memory clears the guard, and its completion event
206	orders it ahead of its consumer, keeping restages off the critical
207	path unless the window closes first (\S\ref{sec:motivation-c2c}).
208	\end{itemize}
209	
210	An activation type kept in GPU memory has no CPU copy, so the kernels that stream or compute from CPU memory (\S\ref{sec:design-kernels}) apply only to types the configuration offloads.
211	
212	\paragraph{Combining Recomputation with Offloading.}
213	Prior systems treat each activation below the checkpoint boundary as
214	either recomputed or offloaded~\cite{superoffload, zero-infinity}; we
215	compose them. An activation type is regenerated in the backward window from a smaller offloaded save; the interconnect carries the save and recomputation supplies the rest. Attention's normalized projections,
216	for instance, are rebuilt exactly from a pair of small offloaded
217	normalization inputs that cost a fraction of the bytes they
218	regenerate. The composition rides the interconnect where it is
219	otherwise idle during a layer's compute, turning idle bandwidth into
220	freed GPU memory at half to two-thirds of offloading's link bytes and
221	no step-time cost over it (Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m3},

234	underfill a GEMM and add a transfer to a busy link, four times the
235	added critical path at 256K rows (5.2 versus 1.3~ms,
236	\S\ref{sec:motivation-cpu}, Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m4}).

238	\paragraph{Kernel Dispatch.}
239	Every operator runs on the device where its operands already sit.
240	Arithmetic intensity settles the clear cases: compute-bound
241	frozen-path GEMMs run on the GPU, and the memory-bound ingestion of
242	gradients runs on the CPU. The remaining cases fall to measured thresholds on row counts, bytes, and token counts, gated by model family and free GPU memory. The CPU-placement thresholds are expressed
243	in rows, the quantity that predicts when CPU work outgrows the
244	dependency window it hides in (\S\ref{sec:motivation-cpu},
245	Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m4}); the shipped threshold arms the CPU
246	adapter-gradient placement through 262,144 rows, inside the measured
247	crossover. 248	same guard the transport layer consults. The rules are fixed once and
249	serve every configuration.
250	
251	\subsection{Dynamic Expert Load Balancing}
252	\label{sec:design-balancer}
253	
254	Each GPU of a Grace--Blackwell superchip reads the shared CPU memory
255	through its own NVLink-C2C link (\S\ref{sec:motivation-background}),
256	and per-step routing skew leaves a static expert split idling one GPU
257	and its link (\S\ref{sec:motivation-balancer}). AsymLoRA keeps the weights still and
258	shares the work: each grouped launch executes one shared list of
259	expert workloads, agreed through the memory both GPUs address with no
260	collective communication.
261	
262	\paragraph{A Shared Expert Work List.}
263	Each shared grouped launch executes the union of both GPUs' expert
264	work rather than two private lists, so either GPU absorbs the other's
265	overload. Sharing applies under the configurations that offload the
266	routed activations (\S\ref{sec:design-scheduler}): the tokens then
267	reside in the shared CPU memory, so either GPU reads the other's
268	tokens directly and computes its portion of the union list by

270	other launches take the data-parallel split. The expert weights
271	likewise stay put: each expert's bank streams once from the shared CPU
272	memory regardless of which GPU consumes it. Sharing covers only the

279	identically on both GPUs from routing counts they already hold, so in
280	the common case the two sides exchange nothing at all before

290	measured ceiling fall back to the plain data-parallel split, so the
291	mechanism's floor is the unshared launch, and its gains concentrate
292	where routing skew binds.

294	\subsection{Implementation}
295	\label{sec:design-impl}

298	\S\ref{sec:design-kernels} and \S\ref{sec:design-balancer} (about

\section{AsymLoRA Design}
\label{sec:design}

% Synced from agent/impls/s04-p1-dgx-02-c06/system_writing_full_v2.md in the
% AsymGEMM repo, 2026-07-26 (measured update: SwiGLU CPU kernel removed
% per toconfirm #1 DISPROVEN, two CPU kernels ship; scatter fusion
% output-side only; dispatch/async grounded on M4b, 262,144-row arming
% ceiling; M3/M5b numbers attached to composition and balancer).
% Conventions:
%   - \cite{key} are citation placeholders until the bibliography lands.
%   - [bracketed] values are pending verification; "(Figure F5: ...)"
%     comment blocks describe figures still to be drawn.
%   - Subsection titles are working names pending author confirmation.
%   - GATE: figures/AsymLoRA.pdf still numbers the modules in the old
%     order (Kernels, AsymScheduler, Balancer, Profiler); renumber to
%     Kernels, Profiler, Dispatch, Balancer and relabel boxes to the
%     final titles before submission (gate C5).

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  % system overview: single column. The diagram is authored at 223.9pt wide,
  % so \columnwidth (234.9pt) renders it at ~1.05x -- internal labels land at
  % 6.3--9.4pt, comfortably under the 10pt body text.
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/AsymLoRA.pdf}%
  \caption{AsymLoRA system overview: asymmetric GEMM kernels split operands between GPU HBM and Grace CPU DRAM (left); the runtime streams activations over NVLink-C2C and balances dynamic experts across the Superchip (middle); the scheduler profiles the model and memory budget to pick the configuration that fits in HBM (right).}
  \label{fig:design-overview}
\end{figure}

\subsection{System Overview}
\label{sec:design-overview}

AsymLoRA is a fine-tuning system for Grace--Blackwell superchips, which
couple two Blackwell GPUs to a Grace CPU over the coherent NVLink-C2C
interconnect, so that both GPUs read the CPU's memory directly. It
targets long-context LoRA fine-tuning of large language models, dense
and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) alike, at sequence lengths from tens of thousands of tokens to beyond a million, where model weights and long-context activations together exceed GPU memory (from [N] tokens on; at the largest models the weights alone do).

AsymLoRA therefore trains with the base weights homed in CPU memory,
as prior offload systems do~\cite{zero-infinity, superoffload}, and with per-layer gradient checkpointing enabled: the
forward saves only each layer's input, and the backward recomputes a
layer's forward before differentiating it, so at most one layer's
activations are live at a time. Under a memory budget, AsymLoRA
determines where each of these tensors resides across a run and how
each reaches its consumer. AsymLoRA introduces no approximations:
training computes the same optimization step as standard LoRA fine-tuning, up to floating-point reduction order [and device rounding].

Figure~\ref{fig:design-overview} shows the four modules: (1)--(2) are
fixed before launch, the kernel portfolio and the configuration;
(3)--(4) act during the step. (1) The training kernels
(\S\ref{sec:design-kernels}) run GEMMs that stream CPU-resident
operands over the interconnect and CPU kernels that consume them in
place. (2) The Profiler (\S\ref{sec:design-profiler}) searches
measured past runs for the configuration and batch size that maximize
throughput under the user's model, maximum sequence length, and memory
budget. (3) The Dispatcher (\S\ref{sec:design-scheduler}) enacts the
configuration's placements each step and routes every operator to the
kernel where its operands sit. (4) The Expert Balancer
(\S\ref{sec:design-balancer}) shares one routed-expert work list
between both GPUs through the shared CPU memory, absorbing routing
skew without moving weights.

\subsection{Training Kernels for CPU-Resident Tensors}
\label{sec:design-kernels}

Our kernels stream a CPU-resident operand tile-by-tile over the
interconnect during the GEMM, holding no copy in GPU memory, the
streaming scheme of the AsymGEMM inference library~\cite{asymgemm}.
Training keeps the frozen-weight stream and adds a second streamed role, the once-read activation, together with the backward's token-axis reductions and transposed rereads (\S\ref{sec:motivation-naive}, \S\ref{sec:motivation-kernels}); the kernels below serve these dataflows.

\paragraph{AsymLoRA Adapter Kernels.}
The adapter path has three kernels. (1) The forward-projection kernel
computes the low-rank projections on the GPU, directly against
CPU-resident activations. The once-read activation takes the
fetch-once slot in shared memory while the small resident factor is
pipelined. This arrangement inverts the inference kernels, whose
reused weight is the streamed operand. Its launch grid is partitioned
over row segments rather than experts: at rank 64, an
expert-partitioned grid would collapse to one thread block per expert.
(2) The GPU adapter-gradient kernel streams the activation as one
operand of the weight-gradient contraction. Because that contraction
reduces over the token axis, no output can retire until the stream has
passed, so the kernel holds its rank-sized accumulators in registers
across the entire segment and writes them once. (3) The CPU
adapter-gradient kernel computes the same gradient on the Grace cores
instead, writing fp32 results directly into the optimizer's pinned
buffer, so that only the rank-width projection gradient, not the activation, crosses the link. Whether kernel (2) or (3) computes an operator's
adapter gradient is a dispatch decision, deferred to
\S\ref{sec:design-scheduler}.

\paragraph{Scatter-Fused Asymmetric Grouped GEMMs for Routed Experts.}
A grouped GEMM computes an MoE layer's experts in a single launch but
returns each expert's outputs in expert order, so a separate pass must
scatter them back to token order; when its output is streamed or offloaded, that pass materializes an expert-ordered copy of it first. Our kernels
fold the token-order scatter into the epilogue of the streamed grouped
GEMM, forward and backward (\S\ref{sec:motivation-kernels}): the
epilogue scatters each result while the mainloop is still streaming
weight tiles across the interconnect. (1) The forward kernel
multiplies each expert's partial results by their routing weights and
writes them straight to token-order addresses, so the output leaves
the GEMM already in token order, with no separate pass and no permuted
copy. (2) The backward kernel does the same for the gate and up
projections' input gradients. Both stream weights and scatter results
within one launch. The fusion covers the output side only; the
expert-order input gather remains a separate staged pass
(\S\ref{sec:motivation-kernels}). Under configurations that stream the
routed activations, the Dispatcher (\S\ref{sec:design-scheduler}) uses
these kernels, chosen for the expert-ordered output copy they
eliminate (\S\ref{sec:motivation-kernels}); where the activations stay
GPU-resident, the scatter is a cheap on-GPU pass and the unfused
grouped GEMM is used instead.

\paragraph{CPU Kernels for Host-Resident Data.}
Memory-bound gradient work whose operands already reside in CPU memory
runs on the Grace cores; computing it on the GPU would cross the link
twice, to fetch the operands and return the result. We compute it in
kernels written for the length-agnostic vector model of Arm's Scalable
Vector Extension (SVE), operating on the bf16 operands in place
(\S\ref{sec:motivation-cpu}). Two such kernels ship. (1) The CPU
adapter-gradient kernel is kernel (3) of the adapter path above. (2)
The gradient-ingestion kernel converts each incoming gradient from
bf16 to fp32 and fuses this conversion with the gradient-norm
reduction the optimizer already performs, so the gradient is read once
rather than twice, 7.2$\times$ faster than the stock two-pass path
(\S\ref{sec:motivation-cpu}). The backward emits gradients in bf16, so
transferring them in bf16 rather than fp32 is exact, and the
conversion introduces no additional pass over memory.

Together these form a portfolio of three execution targets: streamed
AsymLoRA GEMMs, resident cuBLAS GEMMs, and Grace CPU kernels. The
streamed family covers the frozen path in both directions: the
base-weight GEMMs ship transposed instantiations for the backward's
input gradients, reading the same CPU-resident weight under the
transposed access pattern and degrading to a staged GEMM where the
transposed tiling constraints do not hold. Which target executes
which operator, and under which placement, is fixed by the
configuration (\S\ref{sec:design-profiler}) and its dispatch
(\S\ref{sec:design-scheduler}).

\subsection{Offline Profiling for Configuration Selection}
\label{sec:design-profiler}

A configuration assigns every weight a transport, staged or streamed, and every activation type (\S\ref{sec:motivation-background}) a placement: kept in GPU memory, offloaded to CPU memory, or recomputed (transport in \S\ref{sec:design-scheduler}). From measured past runs
alone, the Profiler answers a job request (model, maximum sequence
length, memory budget) with the configuration and batch size predicted
to maximize throughput within the capacity the budget leaves free; no profiling sweep precedes launch; the one exception, near the capacity wall, is a single guarded feasibility probe. A model family enters the record store once, through an anchor sweep of [k] short runs per configuration, at [two] sequence lengths beyond the anchor zone from which the linear fits extrapolate plus [j] in-zone lengths that seed the verbatim tables; every later run appends its manifest and measured peaks to the store (\S\ref{sec:design-impl}).

\paragraph{Peak-Memory Prediction.}
For every model and configuration the Profiler maintains a linear model of peak GPU memory in the token count (\S\ref{sec:motivation-scheduler}), fitted to past runs, alongside CPU-side peaks recorded the same way [verify: linear fit versus anchor scaling in the shipped checker]. A configuration
that offloads more to CPU memory uses less GPU memory but more CPU
memory, so it can run out of either, and the Profiler checks both. The
user's budget is a reservation, subtracted from each physical capacity
before the fits are checked, so headroom for anything else on the
machine is expressed in the check itself. Where linear fits are
invalid (the short-sequence anchor zone, where kernels change
behavior), measured tables are used verbatim. Near the capacity wall
the Profiler does not trust either: any decision within a fixed band
of the limit is flagged, and the emitted configuration carries the exact probe command that validates it with a short run, [a few] steps at the job's maximum sequence length, at the emitted batch and one below.
% (Figure F5: predicted versus measured peak GPU memory across sequence
% lengths for each configuration of one model: the linear fits, the
% anchor zone, and the probe band near the wall.)

\paragraph{Configuration Search.}
The configurations form a fixed ladder per model family, each the previous with one more activation type moved off the GPU, so residency orders them totally; more residency is faster, a property the measurements confirm for every family we ship
(\S\ref{sec:motivation-scheduler}, Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m6}).
The search therefore needs no runtime timing; the Profiler considers
configurations from most to least resident and takes the first that
fits. It then chooses the largest batch that passes both capacity
checks; where a measured throughput knee exists
(\S\ref{sec:motivation-scheduler}, Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m6}),
the batch is capped there, because larger batches no longer pay; in recorded runs the knee falls below every feasible configuration's batch ceiling, so the cap forfeits nothing a leaner configuration could reclaim [verify against M6]. Every
change to the fitted constants is gated by self-tests over the
prediction properties and by replay of all recorded decisions, so a change that would have altered a past decision is caught before it can misconfigure a run.

\subsection{Runtime Placement and Kernel Dispatch}
\label{sec:design-scheduler}

The Dispatcher executes each training step under the configuration the
Profiler selected (\S\ref{sec:design-profiler}), reading only the
runtime state: free GPU memory and per-operator shapes. It enacts each
placement through staging, streaming, offloading, or recomputation,
and routes each operator to the kernel of the device holding its
operands. Every placement off the GPU trades throughput for memory:
the freed memory comes back as transfers, restages, or recomputation
(\S\ref{sec:motivation-scheduler}). The Dispatcher narrows this cost by
overlapping the added work with the dependency windows the backward
pass opens; the cost that remains is why more resident configurations
stay faster and why the Profiler selects the most resident one that
fits (\S\ref{sec:design-profiler})
(Figure~\ref{fig:design-overview}, center).

\paragraph{Enacting the Placement.}
Weights and activations are placed independently.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Weights} are staged or streamed
(\S\ref{sec:design-kernels}). Staging copies a weight into GPU memory
for its GEMM and releases it after, holding at most one layer's
weights at once. Streaming leaves it in CPU memory and reads it
tile-by-tile during the GEMM, holding no copy in GPU memory but moving
every tile across the interconnect.

\item \textbf{Activations} are recomputed by default: the forward
saves only each layer's input, and the backward regenerates the rest
(\S\ref{sec:design-overview}). Within that recompute, each type is kept resident in GPU memory once produced or left to recompute, both consumed by the same layer's backward; offloaded types leave during the forward and restage beneath the backward. Offloaded activations ride pinned buffers with completion events and a guarded prefetch stream: a restage issues
only when free GPU memory clears the guard, and its completion event
orders it ahead of its consumer, keeping restages off the critical
path unless the window closes first (\S\ref{sec:motivation-c2c}).
\end{itemize}

An activation type kept in GPU memory has no CPU copy, so the kernels that stream or compute from CPU memory (\S\ref{sec:design-kernels}) apply only to types the configuration offloads.

\paragraph{Combining Recomputation with Offloading.}
Prior systems treat each activation below the checkpoint boundary as
either recomputed or offloaded~\cite{superoffload, zero-infinity}; we
compose them. An activation type is regenerated in the backward window from a smaller offloaded save; the interconnect carries the save and recomputation supplies the rest. Attention's normalized projections,
for instance, are rebuilt exactly from a pair of small offloaded
normalization inputs that cost a fraction of the bytes they
regenerate. The composition rides the interconnect where it is
otherwise idle during a layer's compute, turning idle bandwidth into
freed GPU memory at half to two-thirds of offloading's link bytes and
no step-time cost over it (Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m3},
\S\ref{sec:motivation-c2c}).

\paragraph{Asynchronous CPU Execution.}
A CPU-side optimizer normally receives gradients computed on the GPU
and transferred across the link, and the transfer stands between the
backward pass and the optimizer step. For the adapter gradients we
remove this transfer. Because the adapters are low-rank and the
activations they contract against already reside in CPU memory, a
persistent CPU worker computes the gradient on the Grace cores, in
parallel with the ongoing backward pass, and writes the fp32 result
straight into the optimizer's pinned buffer; only the rank-width projection gradient crosses the link. The computation hides inside the
dependency windows the backward opens; the GPU alternative would
underfill a GEMM and add a transfer to a busy link, four times the
added critical path at 256K rows (5.2 versus 1.3~ms,
\S\ref{sec:motivation-cpu}, Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m4}).

\paragraph{Kernel Dispatch.}
Every operator runs on the device where its operands already sit.
Arithmetic intensity settles the clear cases: compute-bound
frozen-path GEMMs run on the GPU, and the memory-bound ingestion of
gradients runs on the CPU. The remaining cases fall to measured thresholds on row counts, bytes, and token counts, gated by model family and free GPU memory. The CPU-placement thresholds are expressed
in rows, the quantity that predicts when CPU work outgrows the
dependency window it hides in (\S\ref{sec:motivation-cpu},
Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m4}); the shipped threshold arms the CPU
adapter-gradient placement through 262,144 rows, inside the measured
crossover. The threshold-gated CPU placements are disabled wholesale for the dense families, whose recorded runs exhaust CPU capacity first and whose adapter-gradient sites carry every token, past the crossover of Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m4} (\S\ref{sec:motivation-scheduler}, \S\ref{sec:motivation-cpu}); prefetch engages only when free GPU memory clears the
same guard the transport layer consults. The rules are fixed once and
serve every configuration.

\subsection{Dynamic Expert Load Balancing}
\label{sec:design-balancer}

Each GPU of a Grace--Blackwell superchip reads the shared CPU memory
through its own NVLink-C2C link (\S\ref{sec:motivation-background}),
and per-step routing skew leaves a static expert split idling one GPU
and its link (\S\ref{sec:motivation-balancer}). AsymLoRA keeps the weights still and
shares the work: each grouped launch executes one shared list of
expert workloads, agreed through the memory both GPUs address with no
collective communication.

\paragraph{A Shared Expert Work List.}
Each shared grouped launch executes the union of both GPUs' expert
work rather than two private lists, so either GPU absorbs the other's
overload. Sharing applies under the configurations that offload the
routed activations (\S\ref{sec:design-scheduler}): the tokens then
reside in the shared CPU memory, so either GPU reads the other's

streaming those activations and the expert weights from that memory;
other launches take the data-parallel split. The expert weights

\subsection{Implementation}
\label{sec:design-impl}

AsymLoRA comprises the CUDA/C++ kernel extensions of
\S\ref{sec:design-kernels} and \S\ref{sec:design-balancer} (about
[X]~KLOC; exact split to be filled from the repository), a Python
placement and transport layer implementing
\S\ref{sec:design-scheduler} (about [Y]~KLOC), and the Profiler of
\S\ref{sec:design-profiler}, integrated into the [stack] fine-tuning
stack. The integration is deliberately narrow: the system replaces the
frozen-GEMM dispatch, the activation-offload hooks, and the
optimizer's gradient ingestion, and leaves the trainer loop, data
pipeline, attention implementation, and adapter mathematics untouched.

Every mechanism of \S\ref{sec:design-kernels}--\S\ref{sec:design-balancer}
is individually switchable and off by default; a launch configuration
is an explicit set of flags emitted by the Profiler, and each run records its full configuration in a manifest alongside its artifacts, and its measured peaks and throughput feed the Profiler's record store.
CPU-side pinned memory is allocated through a per-family accounting

Figure M2a measures what the rebuild collects, on one adapter GEMM as
a case study: the attention LoRA-A projection $S{=}XA^\top$ at rank 64
and hidden width 5120, the activation $X$ CPU-resident, at 32K and
256K token rows. Three executions: Resident, both operands pre-placed
in HBM, the cuBLAS ceiling; Staged, $X$ copied to HBM and cuBLAS run
on the copy; Streamed, the rebuilt kernel reading $X$ in place. At 32K
rows they take 0.053, 1.651, and 1.598~ms; at 256K rows, 0.402,
13.080, and 12.701~ms. Both off-GPU executions are link-bound,
sustaining the link's achieved rate (about 210~GB/s), because at rank
64 the arithmetic is negligible next to moving $X$; Staged then moves
the bytes twice, over the link and again out of HBM, which is why
Streamed runs about 3\% faster. The decisive difference is what the
execution holds: Staged holds the returned activation, 0.34~GB at 32K
rows and 2.69~GB at 256K, re-spent at exactly the backward's peak,
where Streamed holds the 0.7~MB adapter. Under offloading, the one
executable path paid the link and re-bought the memory; the rebuilt
kernel pays the same link time and keeps the memory saving the offload
was for. The 30$\times$ gap to Resident is
the residency premium, the throughput price of any off-GPU placement;
it argues for keeping tensors resident whenever they fit (§2.4.4), not
for staging.

Figure M4b measures the deposit at its shipped site, MoE attention
$dA$, across 64K, 256K, and 1M projection rows. Against stock PyTorch
CPU matmuls at the same 96-thread budget, the kernel runs 1.8$\times$,
2.4$\times$, and 31$\times$ faster (12.3 versus 21.6~ms, 33.3 versus
79.8, and 137 versus 4336: the stock bf16 path collapses at scale).
Placement, however, is not settled by serial time: run in isolation,
the GPU route, restage plus GPU gradient kernel plus gradient
transfer, is faster at every size; the shipped question is what each
route adds to the critical path of a backward that is already using
the SMs and the link. Run concurrently with such a context (63.6~ms of
streamed GEMMs), the CPU route adds 1.36~ms at 64K rows to the GPU
route's 1.29, parity; 1.32~ms at 256K to the GPU's 5.19, four times
less; and 87.8~ms at 1M to the GPU's 20.7, because 137~ms of serial
CPU work no longer fits a 64~ms window. The crossover falls between
256K and 1M rows, and the shipped policy arms the CPU placement only
through the 256K point (262{,}144 rows), the last where it wins. The
boundary is a time window, not a bandwidth limit: the idle cores
absorb CPU seconds only while the backward's dependency window is
open, extending the step once it closes, and row count predicts the
closure.

Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-m2a} measures what the rebuild collects, on
one adapter GEMM as the representative microbenchmark: the attention LoRA-A projection
$S{=}XA^\top$ at rank 64 and hidden width 5120, the activation $X$
CPU-resident, at 32K and 256K token rows. Three executions: Resident,
both operands pre-placed in HBM, the cuBLAS ceiling; Staged, $X$
copied to HBM and cuBLAS run on the copy; Streamed, the rebuilt kernel
reading $X$ in place. At 32K rows they take 0.053, 1.651, and
1.598~ms; at 256K rows, 0.402, 13.080, and 12.701~ms. Both off-GPU
executions are link-bound, sustaining the link's achieved rate (about
210~GB/s), because at rank 64 the arithmetic is negligible next to
moving $X$; Staged then moves the bytes twice, over the link and again
out of HBM, which is why Streamed runs about 3\% faster. The decisive
difference is what the execution holds: Staged holds the returned
activation, 0.34~GB at 32K rows and 2.69~GB at 256K, re-spent at
exactly the backward's peak, where Streamed holds the 0.7~MB adapter.
Under offloading, the one executable path paid the link and re-bought
the memory; the rebuilt kernel pays the same link time and keeps the
memory saving the offload was for. The 30$\times$ gap to Resident is
the residency premium, the throughput price of any off-GPU placement;
it argues for keeping tensors resident whenever they fit
(\S\ref{sec:motivation-scheduler}), not for staging.

site, MoE attention $dA$, across 64K, 256K, and 1M projection rows.
Against stock PyTorch CPU matmuls at the same 96-thread budget, the
kernel runs 1.8$\times$, 2.4$\times$, and 31$\times$ faster (12.3
versus 21.6~ms, 33.3 versus 79.8, and 137 versus 4336: the stock bf16
path collapses at scale). Placement, however, is not settled by serial
time: run in isolation, the GPU route, restage plus GPU gradient
kernel plus gradient transfer, is faster at every size; the shipped
question is what each route adds to the critical path of a backward
that is already using the SMs and the link. Run concurrently with such
a context (63.6~ms of streamed GEMMs), the CPU route adds 1.36~ms at
64K rows to the GPU route's 1.29, parity; 1.32~ms at 256K to the GPU's
5.19, four times less; and 87.8~ms at 1M to the GPU's 20.7, because
137~ms of serial CPU work no longer fits a 64~ms window. The crossover
falls between 256K and 1M rows, and the shipped policy arms the CPU
placement only through the 256K point (262,144 rows), the last where
it wins. The boundary is a time window, not a bandwidth limit: the
idle cores absorb CPU seconds only while the backward's dependency
window is open, extending the step once it closes, and row count
predicts the closure.

**Dispatcher — and your instinct about why is correct.** "Kernel Scheduler" is odd because the phrase already means something else: in GPU-land a kernel scheduler is the driver/hardware machinery that orders kernel *launches* (streams, thread blocks). Your module never reorders launches — it picks **which of several kernel implementations runs an operator** (streamed AsymLoRA vs. resident cuBLAS vs. Grace CPU). That act has an exact standard name: **kernel dispatch** — it's literally what PyTorch's ATen "dispatcher" does (one operator, multiple backends, runtime routes), so every MLSys reviewer parses it instantly and correctly.

1. Your §3.4 already contains a "Kernel Dispatch" paragraph and already calls the component "the Dispatcher" — the name becomes a zero-churn lexical match with the section (your rule D).

One more real option exists — a single concrete word that genuinely *means* both duties at once: **dataflow**.

**Dataflow Engine** (15)

Here's the key realization: placement and kernel choice aren't actually two separate duties in your system — they're **two views of one decision**. Pick the streamed kernel ⇒ the tensor stays in DRAM and flows over C2C; pick cuBLAS ⇒ it stages to HBM first; pick the Grace kernel ⇒ the data doesn't move and the compute comes to it. Where the data sits, how it travels, and which kernel consumes it — that single joint choice is exactly what "dataflow" names. So a coordination ("Tensor and Kernel …") was never needed; the right single word existed.
