# Task: Name the §3 system components of the AsymLoRA paper (module 3 is the hard one)

You are helping name the system-design components of an MLSys'26 submission.
Three of the four names are (near-)settled; **module 3 has gone through ~15
candidates and none satisfied the author**. Your job: propose names that
actually pass the criteria below, with reasoning, and recommend one.

## Paper context (1 minute version)

Working title: *AsymLoRA: Long-Context LoRA Fine-Tuning of LLMs on
Grace-Blackwell Superchips*. A GB200 superchip couples two Blackwell GPUs to
one Grace CPU over coherent NVLink-C2C links; GPU kernels can read CPU memory
directly. The system trains LoRA at 32K–1M+ token contexts by keeping base
weights and offloaded activations in the large CPU memory, streaming them
tile-by-tile into GPU GEMMs (or computing on the Grace cores directly), and
picking, per job, how much stays GPU-resident.

§3 (System Design) has four components, walked in this order:

1. **§3.2 Kernel portfolio** — GPU kernels that stream CPU-resident operands
   during the GEMM (ours), stock resident cuBLAS GEMMs, and Grace CPU (SVE)
   kernels that compute on host-resident data in place. A *pool of execution
   targets to choose among*. The system-figure box for this module already
   draws the three choices: "AsymLoRA GEMM / cuBLAS GEMM / Grace SVE2".
2. **§3.3 Profiler** — offline; given (model, max sequence length, memory
   budget), answers from *recorded past runs only* (no profiling sweep before
   launch) with the configuration + batch size that maximizes throughput and
   fits both GPU and CPU memory. A **configuration** = an assignment of a
   transport to every weight (staged or streamed) and a placement to every
   activation type (kept / offloaded / recomputed).
3. **§3.4 The module to name** — the per-step online component. Full duty
   description below.
4. **§3.5 Balancer** — MoE-only; both GPUs execute one shared list of expert
   workloads read from the shared CPU memory, rebalancing per-step routing
   skew without moving weights or tokens and without collectives.

## Module 3: what it actually does (from §3.4, "Runtime Placement and Kernel Dispatch")

Executes each training step under the configuration the Profiler selected,
reading only runtime state (free GPU memory, per-operator shapes). Two duties
that are really two sides of one decision:

- **Storage/placement side**: enacts every tensor's placement — stages
  weights (copy in, release after), streams them (read tile-by-tile over
  C2C, no GPU copy), offloads activation types in the forward and restages
  them beneath the backward (pinned buffers, completion events, a guarded
  prefetch stream), or recomputes them in the backward window. Overlaps all
  of this into the dependency windows the backward opens.
- **Compute side**: dispatches every operator to the kernel of the device
  holding its operands — streamed AsymLoRA GEMM vs. resident cuBLAS vs.
  Grace CPU kernel — via fixed rules plus measured row-count thresholds
  (e.g., CPU adapter-gradient placement armed only ≤262,144 rows).

Note the coupling (the author cares about this): **placement is fixed first
(by the configuration) and the kernel choice follows from it** — "every
operator runs where its operands sit." Choosing the streamed kernel *is*
choosing not to stage the tensor; choosing cuBLAS implies staging it;
choosing the CPU kernel means the data doesn't move at all.

## Naming requirements (the author's criteria, distilled from many rounds)

1. **Reader-transparent**: a first-time reader should roughly know what the
   module does from the name alone. Style exemplars the author loves:
   "**Dynamic Expert Load Balancer**", "**KV Resizer**" — concrete object +
   plain action. Names must NOT encode mechanism or timing (KV Resizer
   doesn't say how or when it resizes).
2. **Both duties must not be hidden**: a name that reads compute-only
   ("Kernel Dispatcher") or storage-only was rejected. It must at least
   *cover* moving/parking tensors AND routing compute (or name something
   that genuinely implies both).
3. **Natural English, standard systems vocabulary**: no minted jargon, not
   arcane, not "crude" (e.g., "Memory and Compute Scheduler" was called too
   crude), and — this killed most candidates — **no engineered-sounding
   coordinations or hyphenated modifiers** ("Placement and Dispatch
   Runtime", "Placement-Driven Kernel Dispatcher" all "sound odd").
4. **Length**: it is a box title in the system figure; budget ≈ ≤28 chars
   (the longest settled sibling, "Dynamic Expert Load Balancer", is 28).
   Two-line box titles are possible but disliked.
5. **Box = subsection title, identical strings** (the paper's style rule:
   figure sub-box names lexically match subsection titles; short handle in
   running prose, e.g. "the Balancer").
6. **Name-clash constraints**: upstream AsymGEMM (the inference library this
   builds on) ships a kernel-internal component literally named
   `asymScheduler` — a bare "Scheduler" name needs a first-use distinction
   (paper gate C2). Also avoid "Router" (the figure already has an MoE
   "Expert Router") and "Resource Manager" (YARN association).
7. **Parallel with the settled siblings** (see below): plain agent nouns.

## Current status of the four names

| # | Module | Status |
|---|--------|--------|
| 1 | Kernel portfolio | Near-settled: **Training Kernel Pool** (author proposed "Kernel Pool"; "Kernel Repos" and "Training Kernel Library" rejected as odd; "Portfolio" was acceptable but Pool preferred) |
| 2 | Profiler | **Configuration Selector** — settled |
| 3 | Runtime placement + dispatch | **UNSETTLED — your task** |
| 4 | Expert balancer | **Dynamic Expert Load Balancer** — settled (author's favorite; the style anchor) |

## Module-3 candidates already REJECTED (do not re-propose; reasons matter)

| Candidate | Rejection reason |
|---|---|
| AsymScheduler (current figure label) | Nondescriptive + upstream `asymScheduler` clash (gate C2) |
| Dispatcher / Placement Dispatcher | "Placement Dispatcher" sounds weird (dispatch–placement verb-object mismatch) |
| Runtime Placement and Kernel Dispatcher | Too long, engineered |
| Placement and Dispatch Runtime / Placement Runtime | "Sounds odd" |
| Configuration Executor | "A bit weird" (though the Selector→Executor pairing was noted as elegant) |
| Tensor and Kernel Scheduler | "Kernel scheduler" collocation feels off; also collides with GPU launch-scheduling meaning |
| Memory and Compute Scheduler | Too crude / OS-textbook |
| Runtime Resource Manager | Too generic; YARN's ResourceManager association |
| Placement-Aware Execution Engine | Author briefly liked it, then judged "-Aware" weak/confusing and the whole thing too much info |
| Placement-Driven Kernel Dispatcher | Mechanism modifier confuses readers ("what even is placement-driven?") |
| Kernel Dispatcher | Natural + standard (PyTorch-dispatcher precedent) **but hides the offloading/staging duty** — author explicitly objected |
| Tensor and Kernel Dispatcher | "Sounds so odd", zeugma (you don't dispatch tensors) |
| Step Executor / Training Step Executor | Too vague |
| Execution Engine | "Too vague" |
| Dataflow Engine / Dataflow Scheduler / Dataflow Dispatcher | Conceptually strongest so far (dataflow = the one decision covering both sides) but "still sounds weird" to the author |

The author has effectively hit this trilemma: name one duty (sharp but
incomplete) vs. name both (complete but engineered-sounding) vs. name the
role one level up (natural but vague). They rejected a representative of
every branch. A winning name must either find a genuinely natural single
word/phrase implying both duties, or be so idiomatic that its incompleteness
or genericity stops mattering.

## Files for deeper context (repo-relative; prefix with the repo root)

Repo root: `third_party/AsymGEMM/` inside the AsymGEMM-SFT tree
(`/home/kevinni/AsymGEMM-SFT/` on the author's machine; `/workspace/AsymGEMM-SFT/` in containers).

- `agent/overleaf/[MLSys 26 Sub] Superchip-based LoRA/sections/system.tex` —
  the current §3 text; §3.4 is the module to name ("Runtime Placement and
  Kernel Dispatch", component handle "the Dispatcher").
- `agent/overleaf/[MLSys 26 Sub] Superchip-based LoRA/sections/motivations.tex`
  — §2; §2.4.3–§2.4.4 motivate why dispatch/placement decisions exist.
- `agent/impls/s04-p1-dgx-02-c06/system_writing_full_v2.md` — same §3 text
  in markdown (ground truth draft).
- `agent/impls/s04-p1-dgx-02-c06/system_writing_v2.md` — §3 skeleton +
  back-matter: style rules (section D), gates C2/C5 (scheduler name clash;
  figure-relabel pass pending — boxes will be renamed and renumbered to
  match whatever titles are chosen).
- `agent/overleaf/[MLSys 26 Sub] Superchip-based LoRA/figures/AsymLoRA.pdf`
  — the system figure. Current box titles: "Kernels", "AsymScheduler",
  "Profiler", "Dynamic Expert Balancer". The module-3 box contains: HBM,
  SMEM, Weights, Activations, Staging, Streaming, NVLink C2C.

## Deliverable

1. 5–10 fresh candidate names for module 3 (not in the rejected list), each
   with: the reading a first-time reviewer would get, how it covers (or
   honestly frames) both duties, char count, and the §3.1 walk sentence it
   would produce.
2. A ranked recommendation (top 1–2) judged against criteria 1–7.
3. Sanity-check the full 4-name set for parallelism, and flag if your
   module-3 pick argues for adjusting a sibling (e.g., Selector/Executor-style
   pairing).
4. Do NOT edit the paper; output the analysis only. The author (Kevin) picks.

   module does from the name alone. Style exemplars the author loves:
   "**Dynamic Expert Load Balancer**", "**KV Resizer**" — concrete object +
   plain action. Names must NOT encode mechanism or timing (KV Resizer
   doesn't say how or when it resizes).
2. **Both duties must not be hidden**: a name that reads compute-only
   ("Kernel Dispatcher") or storage-only was rejected. It must at least
   *cover* moving/parking tensors AND routing compute (or name something
   that genuinely implies both).
3. **Natural English, standard systems vocabulary**: no minted jargon, not
   arcane, not "crude" (e.g., "Memory and Compute Scheduler" was called too
   crude), and — this killed most candidates — **no engineered-sounding
   coordinations or hyphenated modifiers** ("Placement and Dispatch
   Runtime", "Placement-Driven Kernel Dispatcher" all "sound odd").
4. **Length**: it is a box title in the system figure; budget ≈ ≤28 chars
   (the longest settled sibling, "Dynamic Expert Load Balancer", is 28).
   Two-line box titles are possible but disliked.
5. **Box = subsection title, identical strings** (the paper's style rule:
   figure sub-box names lexically match subsection titles; short handle in
   running prose, e.g. "the Balancer").
6. **Name-clash constraints**: upstream AsymGEMM (the inference library this
   builds on) ships a kernel-internal component literally named
   `asymScheduler` — a bare "Scheduler" name needs a first-use distinction
   (paper gate C2). Also avoid "Router" (the figure already has an MoE
   "Expert Router") and "Resource Manager" (YARN association).

\subsection{System Overview}
\label{sec:design-overview}

AsymLoRA is a fine-tuning system for Grace--Blackwell superchips, which
couple two Blackwell GPUs to a Grace CPU over the coherent NVLink-C2C
interconnect, so that both GPUs read the CPU's memory directly. It
targets long-context LoRA fine-tuning of large language models, dense
and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) alike, at sequence lengths from tens of thousands of tokens to beyond a million, where model weights and long-context activations together exceed GPU memory (from [N] tokens on; at the largest models the weights alone do).

AsymLoRA therefore trains with the base weights homed in CPU memory,
as prior offload systems do~\cite{zero-infinity, superoffload}, and with per-layer gradient checkpointing enabled: the
forward saves only each layer's input, and the backward recomputes a
layer's forward before differentiating it, so at most one layer's
activations are live at a time. Under a memory budget, AsymLoRA
determines where each of these tensors resides across a run and how
each reaches its consumer. AsymLoRA introduces no approximations:
training computes the same optimization step as standard LoRA fine-tuning, up to floating-point reduction order [and device rounding].

Figure~\ref{fig:design-overview} shows the four modules: (1)--(2) are
fixed before launch, the kernel portfolio and the configuration;
(3)--(4) act during the step. (1) The training kernels
(\S\ref{sec:design-kernels}) run GEMMs that stream CPU-resident
operands over the interconnect and CPU kernels that consume them in
place. (2) The Profiler (\S\ref{sec:design-profiler}) searches
measured past runs for the configuration and batch size that maximize
throughput under the user's model, maximum sequence length, and memory
budget. (3) The Dispatcher (\S\ref{sec:design-scheduler}) enacts the
configuration's placements each step and routes every operator to the
kernel where its operands sit. (4) The Expert Balancer
(\S\ref{sec:design-balancer}) shares one routed-expert work list
between both GPUs through the shared CPU memory, absorbing routing
skew without moving weights.

This section outlines the overall architecture of AsymLoRA, a system
that fine-tunes large language models, dense and Mixture-of-Experts
(MoE) alike, with LoRA at sequence lengths from tens of thousands of
tokens to beyond a million, on Grace--Blackwell superchips whose two
Blackwell GPUs read the Grace CPU's memory directly over coherent
NVLink-C2C links. AsymLoRA integrates training kernels that compute
against CPU-resident tensors with record-driven configuration
selection and per-step placement control, adapting the execution to
each job's model, sequence length, and memory budget, as shown in
Figure~\ref{fig:design-overview}. Training runs with the base weights
homed in CPU memory, as prior offload systems
do~\cite{zero-infinity, superoffload}, and with per-layer gradient
checkpointing enabled, the forward saving only each layer's input and
the backward recomputing a layer's forward before differentiating it,
so at most one layer's activations are live at a time. Under a user's
memory budget, AsymLoRA determines where every tensor resides and how
it reaches its consumer, and it introduces no approximations: training
computes the same optimization step as standard LoRA fine-tuning, up
to floating-point reduction order [and device rounding]. Four core
components divide this work: the Training Kernels (1) and the
Configuration Selector (2) are fixed before launch; the Runtime
Controller (3) and the Dynamic Expert Balancer (4) act during each
training step.

The \textbf{Training Kernels} (1) run the training GEMMs directly
against CPU-resident tensors: the streamed AsymLoRA kernels read
frozen weights and once-read activations tile-by-tile over the
interconnect while the multiplication proceeds, holding no copy in GPU
memory, and the Grace SVE kernels compute memory-bound gradient work
on the CPU cores, in place. Together with the resident cuBLAS GEMMs,
they form a portfolio of three execution targets, so that every
operator has an implementation on whichever device holds its operands
(\S\ref{sec:design-kernels}).

The \textbf{Configuration Selector} (2) turns a job request (model,
maximum sequence length, memory budget) into a launch plan offline,
from recorded past runs alone: it predicts every candidate
configuration's peak GPU and CPU memory and emits the most resident
configuration that fits, with the batch size that maximizes throughput
within the budget. It runs no profiling sweep before launch, so
selection precedes the first training step
(\S\ref{sec:design-profiler}).

The \textbf{Runtime Controller} (3) executes each training step under
the selected configuration, reading only runtime state. It enacts
every tensor's placement, staging, streaming, offloading, or
recomputing it, overlaps the added transfers with the dependency
windows the backward pass opens, and dispatches every operator to the
kernel of the device holding its operands
(\S\ref{sec:design-scheduler}).

The \textbf{Dynamic Expert Balancer} (4) absorbs per-step MoE routing
skew across the two GPUs. Rather than exchanging tokens or
repartitioning expert weights, both GPUs execute one shared list of
expert workloads through the CPU memory they both address, restoring
balance with no collective communication and no data movement
(\S\ref{sec:design-balancer}).

## 3.1 System Overview

AsymLoRA is a fine-tuning system for Grace–Blackwell superchips, which
couple two Blackwell GPUs to a Grace CPU over the coherent NVLink-C2C
interconnect, so that both GPUs read the CPU's memory directly. It
targets long-context LoRA fine-tuning of large language models, dense
and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) alike, at sequence lengths from tens of thousands of tokens to beyond a million, where model weights and long-context activations together exceed GPU memory (from [N] tokens on; at the largest models the weights alone do).

AsymLoRA therefore trains with the base weights homed in CPU memory,
as prior offload systems do~\cite{zero-infinity, superoffload}, and with per-layer gradient checkpointing enabled: the
forward saves only each layer's input, and the backward recomputes a
layer's forward before differentiating it, so at most one layer's
activations are live at a time. Under a memory budget, AsymLoRA
determines where each of these tensors resides across a run and how
each reaches its consumer. AsymLoRA introduces no approximations:
training computes the same optimization step as standard LoRA fine-tuning, up to floating-point reduction order [and device rounding].

Figure~SYS shows the four modules: (1)–(2) are fixed before launch,
the kernel portfolio and the configuration; (3)–(4) act during the
step. (1) The training kernels (§3.2) run GEMMs that stream
CPU-resident operands over the interconnect and CPU kernels that
consume them in place. (2) The Profiler (§3.3) searches measured past
runs for the configuration and batch size that maximize throughput
under the user's model, maximum sequence length, and memory budget.
(3) The Dispatcher (§3.4) enacts the configuration's placements each
step and routes every operator to the kernel where its operands sit.
(4) The Expert Balancer (§3.5) shares one routed-expert work list
between both GPUs through the shared CPU memory, absorbing routing
skew without moving weights.

## 3.1 System Overview

This section outlines the overall architecture of AsymLoRA, a system
that fine-tunes large language models, dense and Mixture-of-Experts
(MoE) alike, with LoRA at sequence lengths from tens of thousands of
tokens to beyond a million, on Grace–Blackwell superchips whose two
Blackwell GPUs read the Grace CPU's memory directly over coherent
NVLink-C2C links. AsymLoRA integrates training kernels that compute
against CPU-resident tensors with record-driven configuration
selection and per-step placement control, adapting the execution to
each job's model, sequence length, and memory budget, as shown in
Figure~SYS. Training runs with the base weights homed in CPU memory,
as prior offload systems do~\cite{zero-infinity, superoffload}, and
with per-layer gradient checkpointing enabled, the forward saving only
each layer's input and the backward recomputing a layer's forward
before differentiating it, so at most one layer's activations are live
at a time. Under a user's memory budget, AsymLoRA determines where
every tensor resides and how it reaches its consumer, and it
introduces no approximations: training computes the same optimization
step as standard LoRA fine-tuning, up to floating-point reduction
order [and device rounding]. Four core components divide this work:
the Training Kernels (1) and the Configuration Selector (2) are fixed
before launch; the Runtime Controller (3) and the Dynamic Expert
Balancer (4) act during each training step.

The **Training Kernels** (1) run the training GEMMs directly against
CPU-resident tensors: the streamed AsymLoRA kernels read frozen
weights and once-read activations tile-by-tile over the interconnect
while the multiplication proceeds, holding no copy in GPU memory, and
the Grace SVE kernels compute memory-bound gradient work on the CPU
cores, in place. Together with the resident cuBLAS GEMMs, they form a
portfolio of three execution targets, so that every operator has an
implementation on whichever device holds its operands (§3.2).

The **Configuration Selector** (2) turns a job request (model, maximum
sequence length, memory budget) into a launch plan offline, from
recorded past runs alone: it predicts every candidate configuration's
peak GPU and CPU memory and emits the most resident configuration that
fits, with the batch size that maximizes throughput within the budget.
It runs no profiling sweep before launch, so selection precedes the
first training step (§3.3).

The **Runtime Controller** (3) executes each training step under the
selected configuration, reading only runtime state. It enacts every
tensor's placement, staging, streaming, offloading, or recomputing it,
overlaps the added transfers with the dependency windows the backward
pass opens, and dispatches every operator to the kernel of the device
holding its operands (§3.4).

The **Dynamic Expert Balancer** (4) absorbs per-step MoE routing skew
across the two GPUs. Rather than exchanging tokens or repartitioning
expert weights, both GPUs execute one shared list of expert workloads
through the CPU memory they both address, restoring balance with no
collective communication and no data movement (§3.5).

## 3.1 System Overview

This section outlines the overall architecture of AsymLoRA, a system
that fine-tunes large language models, dense and Mixture-of-Experts
(MoE) alike, with LoRA at sequence lengths from tens of thousands of
tokens to beyond a million, on Grace–Blackwell superchips whose two
Blackwell GPUs read the Grace CPU's memory directly over coherent
NVLink-C2C links. AsymLoRA integrates training kernels that compute
against CPU-resident tensors with record-driven configuration
selection and per-step placement control, adapting the execution to
each job's model, sequence length, and memory budget, as shown in
Figure~SYS. Training runs with the base weights homed in CPU memory,
as prior offload systems do~\cite{zero-infinity, superoffload}, and
with per-layer gradient checkpointing enabled, the forward saving only
each layer's input and the backward recomputing a layer's forward
before differentiating it, so at most one layer's activations are live
at a time. Under a user's memory budget, AsymLoRA determines where
every tensor resides and how it reaches its consumer, and it
introduces no approximations: training computes the same optimization
step as standard LoRA fine-tuning, up to floating-point reduction
order [and device rounding]. Four core components divide this work:
the Training Kernels (1) and the Configuration Selector (2) are fixed
before launch; the Runtime Controller (3) and the Dynamic Expert
Balancer (4) act during each training step.

The **Training Kernels** (1) run the training GEMMs directly against
CPU-resident tensors: the streamed AsymLoRA kernels read frozen
weights and once-read activations tile-by-tile over the interconnect
while the multiplication proceeds, holding no copy in GPU memory, and
the Grace SVE kernels compute memory-bound gradient work on the CPU
cores, in place. Together with the resident cuBLAS GEMMs, they form a
portfolio of three execution targets, so that every operator has an
implementation on whichever device holds its operands (§3.2).

The **Configuration Selector** (2) turns a job request (model, maximum
sequence length, memory budget) into a launch plan offline, from
recorded past runs alone: it predicts every candidate configuration's
peak GPU and CPU memory and emits the most resident configuration that
fits, with the batch size that maximizes throughput within the budget.
It runs no profiling sweep before launch, so selection precedes the
first training step (§3.3).

The **Runtime Controller** (3) executes each training step under the
selected configuration, reading only runtime state. It enacts every
tensor's placement, staging, streaming, offloading, or recomputing it,
overlaps the added transfers with the dependency windows the backward
pass opens, and dispatches every operator to the kernel of the device
holding its operands (§3.4).

The **Dynamic Expert Balancer** (4) absorbs per-step MoE routing skew
across the two GPUs. Rather than exchanging tokens or repartitioning
expert weights, both GPUs execute one shared list of expert workloads
through the CPU memory they both address, restoring balance with no
collective communication and no data movement (§3.5).

Done and pushed (`e4b4f95`) — local and Overleaf identical. What I did:

**1. New names propagated everywhere.** Decoded your updated figure: **① Training Kernels ② Configuration Selector ③ Runtime Controller ④ Dynamic Expert Balancer** — numbering already in the paper's offline→online walk order. §3.2–3.5 subsection titles now equal the box names verbatim; prose handles are "the Kernels / the Selector / the Controller / the Balancer"; zero leftover "Profiler"/"Dispatcher" in tex or md (§2 needed no changes — it never names components, only concepts). This also closes gates C2 (no "Scheduler" in any paper name, so the upstream `asymScheduler` clash is gone) and C5 (renumber/relabel) — both marked resolved in the skeleton.

**2. §3.1 rewritten in DirectKV's register.** I read their §3 ("Overview of DirectKV Architecture"): one intro paragraph — what the system is, what it *integrates*, figure cite — then **one short paragraph per component**, each with the bolded name as subject, what it does, and a second sentence on what that enables ("The Kernel Generator compiles … offline. It serves as …"). Ours now mirrors that exactly: an intro paragraph (scope, "AsymLoRA integrates training kernels that compute against CPU-resident tensors with record-driven configuration selection and per-step placement control…", the givens + no-approximation guarantee, then the (1)–(4) offline/online split), followed by four numbered component paragraphs — **Training Kernels (1)** … **Configuration Selector (2)** … **Runtime Controller (3)** … **Dynamic Expert Balancer (4)**, each ending with its §-pointer.
